speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans face a uniquely challenging set of circumstances.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The major model of Singaporeans getting on the economic ladder has been jobs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Without a job, you are not able to afford renting a place or buying a Housing and Development Board (HDB) flat.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Without your own place, it is difficult to think about having children.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And for these children, few dream of being entrepreneurs with nine in 10 working here, becoming someone's employee.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For almost all of us, the jobs ladder is the main route up, with not many Singaporeans becoming entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The reasons given are variously these: that the market is small and the cost of business daunting, that they lack social safety nets for risk taking, that not enough true growth capital exists for all the private wealth attracted here, that the biggest competitor to Singaporean startups and small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are the Singaporean Government-linked Companies (GLCs).

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Property has been a lottery ticket to many Singaporeans, but with asset prices as high as they are, it is highly questionable if a new generation can follow this model without parental support, given initial conditions of wages lagging asset prices and declining employment prospects.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The persistence of property as a wealth vehicle breeds a rentier mindset.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: One generation's ideology hardens into the next generation's psychology.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: As inter-generational transfers come to dominate socio-economic status, they threaten to entrench inequity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our job structure rests on being the best place in the region for foreign companies to base themselves.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We host many large companies but build few of them.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Ours came here and can as easily go.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At the high value end, tariffs are pulling production home and to friendly countries, reducing the supply of marginal new investment available to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And less of what moves can be won on tax competition.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For an increasing number of research and development (R&D) and manufacturing jobs, speed of iteration, equipping and supplying are decisive factors.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At the cost sensitive end, high business costs and slow manpower approvals accelerate offshoring to regional centres based in countries like Malaysia and Vietnam.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The examples are not unfamiliar to this House.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: H&M moved its Southeast Asia Regional headquarters (HQ) from Singapore to Kuala Lumpur.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Tiger Beer has been brewed here since 1932.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: By the end of next year, it will not be.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For a younger generation, they face a changed playbook.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The high paying entry level tech jobs that many aspired to have largely dried up.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Many entry level roles have been offshored due to the high cost of business.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And capable artificial intelligence (AI) agents and models are set to reduce the need for entry level hiring.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But whatever the cause, it is undeniably hard for young Singaporeans to find a job today.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Entrepreneurship by necessity, rather than by choice, second and third jobs, structural underemployment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In a high-cost economy, the work most likely to stay is work that cannot be done more cheaply somewhere else.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The standard answer for advanced economies has been R&D.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Of course, we should continue to invest, but the upshot is that our R&D complex is sadly not ready to be our growth engine.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And as individual Chinese provinces and groups thereof become increasingly fiercely competitive ecosystems, every economy will need to reckon with the necessary scale, energy availability and the cost required to compete.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is why I believe we must have greater industrial coordination between Southeast Asian countries and engage in transnational industrial policy, as I elaborated in both my maiden speech last September and my Adjournment Motion this July.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: These are structural challenges to the industrial underpinning of jobs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge the Government continues to try to do its best under these circumstances.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But for it, we get the opposite trend in jobs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The value added expected went from $26.7 billion to $23.5 billion to $18 billion.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, even on official statistics, the engine of investment to jobs is faltering.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Faced with such a panoply of problems, what can and should we hope for?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, we need an updated growth model that cares not only about the headline gross domestic product (GDP) growth figure, but the structure of growth.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we truly believe this is a changed world, then our policies must change with it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The structure of growth matters, and growth and distribution are not two things to be done in sequence.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is acceptable as an exigency to grow first and then redistribute by vouchers and rebates.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But over the medium and long term, we should be building an economy where a fair distribution is produced by the growth itself, rather than repaired afterwards out of the proceeds.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And that is why we need an economic engine driven by dynamic local companies, healthy domestic demand, and Singaporeans and Singaporean capital venturing abroad.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Only when Singaporeans thrive and believe the ladders of opportunity are fair to all, can this country be open.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, we need honest measurement and prioritisation of what matters from growth.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: One, the indigenous share of national income, which captures the contribution to national income of Singaporeans as workers, owners and entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Its internationally comparable cousin is the labour share – how much of what stays in Singapore goes to the people who work here.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should resurrect the indigenous income series and measure the whole of what Singaporeans contribute.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Two, real income growth that keeps pace with productivity, not lag it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singaporean workers have kept their end of the bargain.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Their compensation has not kept up with it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Three, whether Singaporeans can still afford the city they built.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Not how much we produce, but how much variety ordinary Singaporeans on an ordinary wage can enjoy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The diversity of services available, how much they can afford and the leisure they can afford to take.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We cannot in one breath lose our heritage businesses and our art spaces, and in the next tell Singaporeans that the city is thriving.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Cities compete on the variety of things there are to consume, not only on what they produce, and high-amenity cities grow faster.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How varied the choices are and how many choices an ordinary wage can afford.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: These three North Stars point us towards a more equal and inclusive economy, with opportunities for entrepreneurs to experiment, households and businesses to succeed, workers to thrive and ideas and innovation to flourish.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How do we foster a dynamic enterprise and innovation system that maximises value regardless of the high business cost and physical constraints?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, my colleague, Jamus Lim, will discuss dynamic local firms.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How can we create a business climate in which dynamic local firms emerge as drivers of innovation and become future cornerstones of the economy?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Third, my colleague, Louis Chua, will discuss land and the roof over the household.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How do we ensure that attractive affordable housing is available for every Singaporean household?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, my colleague, Andre Low, will discuss the start of a working life and ask how we ensure our tertiary students and young workers find meaningful opportunities and good jobs in a challenging economy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Fifth, my colleague, Gerald Giam, will discuss pathways to a middle-class livelihood.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Taking tradespersons as his exemplar, he will ask how we create accessible pathways for them to earn a middle-class livelihood.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Six, my colleague, Fadli Fawzi, will discuss replacement and re-entry and ask whether our system of continuing education actually works.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We close the WP contributions with our two most expansive views of the economic model.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Seventh, my colleague, He Ting Ru, will discuss the lesser measured parts of the economy, in the domestically oriented sectors and ask what parts of this economy our national statistics fail to capture?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And eighth, my colleague, Eileen Chong, will discuss venturing abroad.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How do we empower Singaporeans to seize opportunities in the region and beyond?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What does it mean to take a changed world seriously?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we mean to rebuild the ladder of opportunity in this generation, the answers to these problems must be the centre-piece of our evolved economic model.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In these speeches, my colleague will lay out in eight steps, structural solutions to structural problems.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Today, the problem I will tackle is enterprise and innovation under constraint.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For two generations, we have been good at bringing other people's companies here.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We have been slow to put the same land that we own behind our people building their own.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Why do we take a high land price as a law like gravity?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Universal land pricing is a coherent and convenient accounting ideology, but in the last accounting, the people of Singapore need to decide if this ideology still serves them.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Tuition is expensive and no tutor can promise a good job 20 years out.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We do not ask a child for an immediate pay-off.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should remake the system with the young as the first consideration rather than the last adjustment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Today, we tweak – a discount on a co-living room, a grant, a priority band in a ballot.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Adjustments at the edge of a system designed around somebody else in a different decade.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Treating the young as a first order principle means the opposite.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We design for the 20-something year old foremost.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This is a supply side problem of policy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Before we can remake society to be young, we must remake society for the young.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This experiment will span land rates for both residential and commercial space, spanning co-living, local enterprise and R&D.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It must be centred around an existing core, a university – because one cannot rustle up a cluster from nothing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But one can take one that exists and play to its strengths.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It will be zoned for organic messiness, a district that is pro-worker and pro-business, built around the needs of young people and young companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If it does not work, we can simply revert to the Master Plan.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But surely, today's Singaporeans should have as much say over scarce land as the master planners of decades ago.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, let me take the argument in this order: land, our tertiary institutions, then governance and money.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Thirty years, tens of billions in R&D and more again on fostering entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Both R&D and the ladder of growing local giants have underperformed.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We are worldclass at marshalling inputs but commercial outcomes, in terms of Singaporean-grown companies, have not appeared at the rate the spending implies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: On talent, we want to attract the very best to work alongside a strong local core.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: On capital, we disagree about design but perhaps not ideology.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Which is why risk capital belongs in a policy investment bank rather than inside Government, as the Prime Minister proposes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Where we do have an ideological disagreement is the price of land.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: My colleague, Mr Louis Chua will also speak about this later.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Economic Strategy Review (ESR) organises itself around inputs to production: capital, labour, productivity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But land is an input distinct from capital.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is discussed as revenue and not as a cost – a constraint to live within and not as a lever to change.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But of course, we can test and change this cost.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Centre for Liveable Cities, the Government's own urban research arm, records what happens when One-North was planned: "The idea of providing residential uses in the form of affordable housing was put forth.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: However, it was difficult for HDB to change its public housing policies for a single project like One-North.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, the JTC approached the private sector." National policy then could not bend for One-North.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What we need for R&D and entrepreneurship matters more than dogmatic inflexibility.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It prices out the independent kitchen and the lab with no revenue yet, and leaves to whoever can pay the rent – chains and franchises.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And market scarcity rate, selects for what can be proven in advance – and nothing new can be proven in advance.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: By definition, the novel has no track record.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Thus, the experimental messiness of life is competed out.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A zone of lower commercial pressure is a zone for messiness, a zone where land is cheap enough for the young to make their own places and their own future organically – the first variable and not an accommodation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If land pricing is an unnecessary drag on the young, on enterprise, on an R&D cluster, how do we test it?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There is a formidable constraint: Singaporeans need land prices low – to start something, to live somewhere – and we need them high, because many of our savings sit in HDB flats and the state leans on land revenue.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To have both high land pricing and low land pricing simultaneously, we must do away with the constraint of universal land pricing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There are at least three ways to vary a price.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, across a policy-targeted group, as the Build-To-Order (BTO) does for young parents.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Third, across a geographic boundary – fence one area and change the pricing function inside, in service of agglomeration and enterprise, people and firms packed close enough to make each other more productive.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I believe that the third is the least disruptive theory of change if one believes that our land pricing assumptions need to be tested.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And the question becomes where to test such a zone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For the young, for the R&D economy and for an entrepreneurial spirit.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And looking at the map, I believe NTU is the obvious candidate.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A large number of labs are sited on campus.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is another industrial park – the same answer the Party opposite has given again and again.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we are to clear scarce greenery, the use case must be distinctive enough to be worth the sacrifice.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I believe ours is, and another industrial park is not.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is something priceless and irreversible, traded for something cookie cutter.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is 50 hectares, JTC-developed and anchored on Singapore Institute of Technology's (SIT's) campus.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It proves that the Government will build a district around a university.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But it is more of the same we have done – a business park with a campus in it, on market terms.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If one accepts the first-principle case for a special zone, then two empirical facts must be dealt with.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, the Jurong Region Line is being dug into NTU, with campus stations arriving at the end of the decade.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Kept as separate plans, they make one more park that people commute into.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The better bargain is a district for living, working and playing, and for enterprise, and this new district around NTU would be our last chance to run this sort of experiment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Whatever we settle on this parcel becomes how we price the ground beside every campus after it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is an experiment we must try to make succeed.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But for all our hopes on foreign economic policy, it sits in another country and carries the risk that comes with that.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We can and should run these experiments for ourselves, by ourselves, if we can – and we can.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we want to re-orient our culture towards the spirit of independent living, towards the spirit of risk taking, towards the spirit of collaboration, then we must provide the conditions for the spirit to flourish.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should not be distracted by procedural arguments that Bahar and Jurong are already zoned in a Master Plan.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The experiment can be run as things stand.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, NTU as a centre of a live, work, build district, distinguished by charging land for housing at cost recovery.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: By cost, I mean cost in the ordinary sense, with all scarcity value excluded – the actual cost of constructing, financing, servicing, maintaining and renewing the buildings, not the hypothetical market value of the ground beneath them.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At NUS, a double in hall runs about $494.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The one at Boon Lay is about four kilometres from NTU and cost roughly five times what the university charges its own students.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The median fresh graduate from our six autonomous universities earns $4,500 a month last year.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: After Central Provident Fund (CPF), about $3,600 in hand.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Boon Lay rate, plus its fixed utility charge, takes about 60% of it after the discount.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This is not treating our young as a first order consideration.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our young want space of their own and financial autonomy as a precondition for life, not as a byproduct of marriage.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And 30% below market is measured against the scarcity market.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Before the discount, the same room took more than three quarters of a graduate's take-home pay.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Affordability must be benchmarked against what a young Singaporean actually has to spend rather than market rate discounts.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, what can we offer with a different basis?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: On a cost recovery basis, a room comes to well under the half the going rate, closer to a third.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Take one calculation that owes nothing to a university subsidy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Stretch amortisation to 20 years and it is $1.32 per square foot.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The university's own rate, annualised over 12 months rather than the 35 weeks a term, actually runs, comes out to about $478 to $549 a room.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The universities are already housing people at close to cost.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, we can arrive at a figure between $350 and $550 a month a room.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: All state lands form part of the reserves.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Land must be sold at fair market value.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, let us look at practice and not just theory.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Start with an instrument we have already written.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Land Betterment Charge (Concessionary Relief) Order 2022, waives the betterment charge on state lease university land, put to education and institutional use, and defines "university" as NUS and NTU.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Nor is that the only place the state prices by decision.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Land for a place of worship or a civic and community institution is already valued at half of full land value.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: On the Land Betterment Charge Table effective this March, this is about a tenth of what residential land in the same sector is assessed at.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That red line is not only for rates of places of worship.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Educational and institutional use sits in the same group and is charged at three rates across the whole island, while every residential and commercial rate moves across 118 sectors.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For one class of use, the state already sets a price by decision rather than location.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And in 2023, the Government moved places of worship from competitive tender to fixed price ballot, precisely because bidding had driven prices to levels that distracted religious bodies into fundraising.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For the Party opposite, fair market value is already a function of the interest granted.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is not a single number attached to a plot.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Once you change the use class, the fair market value changes with it lawfully, with the Chief Valuer still doing the valuing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Government identified a market mechanism was pricing a use out of its own purpose, replaced it with an administered price, got a lower number and the Chief Valuer still called it fair market value.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, let us use the rules as they are.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Let us create a use category for non-tradable restricted-tenure, mixed housing and enterprise land, and let the Chief Valuer value that restricted interest.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A clear valuation to build productive capacity for the next generation is not a raid on the reserves.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is the outlay side of an investment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is what every family who pays for tuition for better economic prospects for their kids already knows: it is long-term economic foresight over short-term economic thinking.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How would the zone work if demand exceeds supply?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Once in, the rent stays low once you are part of the zone – studying, working, building or serving it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A firm gets a fixed term and an option to renew and graduates out upon success.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And a person who loses a job or whose startup dies, gets a year's of grace before the rent resets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And if the housing is rented, never sold, it does not become an asset to be traded.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But it is not sufficient on its own.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: You must get the other conditions right too.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: On governance, an innovation district is a place where things are tried and most of them failed.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Most of what I am asking requires no new legislation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should aim to devolve operational decisions to the zone's own board, small and nimble, with the anchor university on it, able to make the bundled decisions on space, pilots, housing allocation, visas and procurements.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And the board should be responsive to the people living in the zone who should have a say in how it is run.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: On money, we should give this zone the ability to back its founders and enterprises.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The bigger draw should be growth capital – the zone taking a stake in the enterprises that grow inside it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singapore and China established Suzhou Industrial Park in 1994.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, while we are not involved in Oriza Holdings, a zone-based financing body is not unknown to us.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: China's New Third Board, its national over-the-counter equity market for unlisted small companies, began in 2006 as a Zhongguancun Science Park Share Transfer pilot and went nationwide in 2013.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, we should capitalise a zone authority that can invest while providing optimal conditions for its startups and enterprises to succeed, taking a capped equity or revenue stake, and allow it to appropriate a portion of the funds it generates to further develop the zone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A zone of lower immediate commercial pressure for these enterprises is a place where experimentation and diversity can flourish.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is a controlled experiment in whether Singapore's land pricing regime is suppressing agglomeration, entrepreneurship and indigenous capital formation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If there is a Singaporean secret sauce that inheres beyond the cost pressures of land and wages, then a zone here, alongside the one in Johor, will tell us.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is a test we should run for our younger generation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We have spent 30 years making this country a good place for other people's companies to succeed.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I am asking that we spend the next 30 making it a place where our owners can – not just a better deal for the young, a country which is built categorically for the young.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, in closing, there has been much talk that the world has changed and it is not changing back.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, here is the test of whether we are serious.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We must reform significant parts of our present economic structure to deal with a changed world, to pursue growth that distributes more fairly and to measure what makes that growth worth having – a fair share of national income, real income growth in line with productivity and a widening range of what an ordinary wage can afford.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Many of these changes must come at the national level, but some are assumptions, long in the tooth, that must be tested.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And a policy laboratory at real scale is how we test it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In this Motion, each of my hon friends will bring another – structural solutions to structural problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will also weave in constructive critique on the recently released ESR.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To start, it is useful to sketch out what our traditional growth model has been.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Accumulate more of what economists call factors of production, to ride on increases in the labour force due to demographic change, while simultaneously building up complementary capital, both manufactured in the form of machines, factories, equipment, as well as human through education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For the former, we marshalled foreign savings with heavy foreign direct investments from MNCs in the early years and since the turn of the century, inward portfolio investment from global funds and family offices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We supplemented this with forced domestic saving from households in the form of CPF and from the state by maintaining large fiscal surpluses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For the latter, we cranked up educational attainment by rapidly educating our school-aged children, then starting in the 1990s, by increasingly absorbing skilled workers from abroad.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We coupled this build-up of factors with fundamentals, exploiting our geographical location, we fostered an economy open to trade in goods, services and finance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding how we were already ahead in the 1960s, at least relative to the rest of the developing world, our growth story is undeniably impressive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It was successfully deployed by Japan in its early industrialisation and the approach, with some idiosyncratic variations, was how the other East Asian dragon economies of Hong Kong, Taiwan and South Korea became wealthy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And starting in the 1980s, China has adapted the self-save model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As successful as this traditional model was, it had embedded within it several pathologies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It made us obsessed somewhat with courting foreign capital and fearful of right-minded pro-worker policies that would reduce our attractiveness as regional headquarters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our educational system to churn out a formidable number of excellent operators, but far fewer risk-taking entrepreneurs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And in the drive to economise on scarce land, our Government's leasehold model has fostered a rent-seeking mindset in real estate, rather than treating land as just another normal input to production.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, this was also the case with the other dragon economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet even among them, Singapore has fared the worst.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Just as important, these other economies, once they entrenched their high-income status, began to evolve their model toward a more internally driven, self-sustaining productivity led one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some may argue that we should make no excuses for growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe that this is incomplete at best and misguided at worst.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, we already know how to drive good growth – crank up capital expenditure to the detriment of labour income and productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, this has been the consistent criticism of Singapore's growth model during its rapid growth phase from the 1960s through to the 1990s and was arguably the impetus for the menagerie of productivity campaigns and bodies that, alas, has not overturned our nation's productivity woes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And while it is tempting for us to look at bolstering growth from tried and tested tools, such as building up yet more of our already intensive capital stock, we must resist because it is clear that disproportionately prioritising resource allocation into hard infrastructure investment, especially in real estate, is running up against diminishing returns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We must instead promote bottom-up formation and growth of our indigenous companies and unleash the innovative and entrepreneurial spirit of our local workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means weaning our companies off a race-to-the-bottom focus on cost cutting as the only means to be competitive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Revenue and wages should instead hinge on productivity gains, not a relentless search for cheaper inputs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Margins can and should be driven by elevating value add and quality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What we want is a "made in Singapore" to be synonymous with better, not just faster or cheaper, which is best left to economies lower down the income ladder.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, this is not simply an appeal for faster growth, not just for growth's sake.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is of existential importance, especially in the age of AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Research shows that worldwide, small firms drive destructive innovation, and startups are the bulwark of sustainable growth through this process of creative destruction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If our SMEs are stifled because business or funding opportunities are crowded out by the bigger players, we will never discover our own homegrown globally competitive unicorns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or if they simply choose to coast along without feeling empowered to challenge large incumbent firms, we will never build a vibrant body of SMEs that form the backbone of our economy, like Germany's Mittelstand or Japan's Taiheiyo Industrial Belt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To enable this transformation, we need a domestic body of medium-sized enterprises capable of growing to become the next wave of national corporate champions and driving a 21st century innovation-led economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We need Singaporeans to start Singaporean companies and for these companies to grow and succeed domestically and on the world stage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore is no stranger to support for SMEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government would undoubtedly point to a veritable grab bag of schemes, such as the Productivity Solutions Grant, SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit, Enterprise Development Grant, Market Readiness Assistance, Enterprise Workforce Transformation Package – I could go on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The question is not whether these are useful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The issue is whether these catalytic grants will spur SME activity sufficiently to allow them to systematically advance to the next stage of growth, or whether there are other structural impediments that inhibit them from transforming themselves from small local firms to medium sized, globally competitive ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Businesses themselves report several key constraints to growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many report an inability to attract and retain the sort of talent that will allow them to elevate their efficiency and output.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, our SMEs have to confront business costs among the highest in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And to compound the challenge, SMEs must secure financing for investment, which is especially scarce once they exit the startup stage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our SMEs must stand ready to be the source of development innovation, the "D" in R&D.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have shared with this House previously about how at less than 2% of GDP, our nation's R&D remains squarely below the global average and significantly behind that of leading innovation nations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I also explained that this was because of anaemic R&D spending by the private sector, not the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The overwhelming majority of business R&D expenditure (BERD) is likely to be from large enterprises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will bring our public expenditure to around 1%, which will be among the global leaders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we need to accelerate private R&D, not just with more public funding, but with complementary funding from our private capital markets as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: SMEs have been major beneficiaries, making up 85% of R&D claims.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But improving productivity is not about innovation alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Research has shown that one important impediment to improving the efficiency of smaller firms is the quality of management.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means there may therefore be a case to expand the scope of qualifying R&D activities for the purposes of tax deductions for this group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is especially for activities aimed at product commercialisation, enhanced internal business operation or overseas expansion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is also missing is a coherent innovation pathway for all SMEs, not just those oriented towards sexy, cutting-edge fields.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Founders of old economy startups may not necessarily possess the technological sophistication to navigate the GoBusiness Directory or the awareness to seek out business advisors in Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They may not be able to string together the myriad packages available or even put together credible applications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is needed is a push rather than pull strategy, where new business registrants are automatically and routinely offered information on how they can access support from the Government to roll out business development innovations over the course of their initial years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even better, startups can match with seconded experts that grow their R&D capabilities in-house, akin to the Agency for Science, Technology and Research's (A*STAR's) Technology for Enterprise Capability Upgrading (T-Up) programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There remains additional room for the state to act as well, through its indirect influence on GLCs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our GLCs can lead the way by dedicating more of their retained earnings toward expenditures in applied R&D, subject to a reasonable return on investment period.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Over the medium run, they can look more towards elevating their spending to more closely match those of other MNCs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Speaking to SMEs, the subject of crushing manpower and rent inevitably emerges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet scaling up and relocating is not always an option.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Market rents will still prevail in the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, doing so will give time for businesses to adjust to jumps in their fixed costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such restrictions have been employed by many jurisdictions worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if we limit it to Government and agency landlords, such as the HDB or JTC, it will be a major step forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It may also be time to revisit the dependency ratio ceiling for certain sectors, like F&B, where Singaporeans continue to shun open positions that are advertised even at attractive wages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singaporeans often view small firm jobs as small-time, second-tier operations compared to a more lucrative prestigious MNC career.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The ESR report, while rightly emphasising the importance of good jobs, remains largely silent on the gap between SME and MNC positions and how they may be bridged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Bridging this gap must recognise that smaller firms often struggle to round up sufficient financing for investment compared to larger ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relieving internal and external access to finance for the purposes of easing cash flow that will unlock hiring is first order if we wish to improve the viability of our young dynamic companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are already schemes that support small enterprise business development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, the Enterprise Development Grant (EDG) is aimed at projects and the Productivity Solutions Grant (PSG) is aimed at IT equipment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The EDG even explicitly recognises human capital development projects as a core capability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our PSG should do the same since productivity is boosted as much by human capital as it is by IT equipment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While one may argue that the Workforce Development Grant (WDG) does much the same thing, the WDG appears overly restrictive, reliant on an approved consultant panel and is not available on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe the scope should be more flexible and allow SMEs to bolster compensation and benefits to better match starting salaries offered by MNCs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Beyond salaries, jobseekers may be attracted to work in SMEs because of the promise of greater work variety and flexibility, and greater exposure to business roles and functions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Internship and apprenticeship programmes, including those from polytechnics, universities and the Graduate Industry Traineeships (GRIT) Programme should actively look to enfold SMEs into their slate of potential employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Career Conversion Programmes should not be limited to the wholesale trade but be expanded to encompass a wider range of SME sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, application and reporting requirements for these programmes are often onerous, stretching the already thin resources of small businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I accept the need for prudence in managing public funds, we should not turn SMEs into another Government bureaucracy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There should be a simplified application process for grants and reporting process requirements should focus on fraud audit rather than extensive documentation compliance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, funds are provided on a reimbursement basis at the moment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But any small business owner, especially one that is starting up, knows that one of the principal challenges that they face is sustaining cash flow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should also reimburse any support we offer upfront and trust SME owners to deploy these grants wisely.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, supporting SMEs with young talent can occur even earlier upstream.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: SMEs in search of skilled workers often seek out interns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unfortunately, many young would-be graduates remain unmatched to potential SME employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Most tertiary institutions already include a job exposure scheme, but take-up remains low.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is despite how attachments often translate into jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One factor behind the low take-up rate could be because companies that hope to partner with tertiary institutions must co-design and co-deliver bespoke curricula.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet even when directed towards hiring talent, there is little structure to ensure the systematic transfer of skills such that the benefits of human capital are spread across the firm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is especially the case for foreign talent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is room to place greater emphasis on local capability development built into schemes, such as the Pioneer Certificate Incentive, and Development and Expansion Incentive to better embed skills transfer to Singaporean employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When local employees are sent for skills upgrading, employers of micro and small enterprises can be partially reimbursed with make-up pay to cover the costs of temporary hiring or overtime, similar to make-up pay when NSmen fulfil their reservist commitments.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Lim, you have a minute left.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Sidelining these actors would amount to killing off the golden goose, which have established themselves as cornerstones of our corporate and industrial landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Our GLCs have also been increasingly competitive on international shores, projecting the economic influence of Singapore Inc worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Nor am I proposing that we abandon our foreign investment and shut the door to foreign capital flows.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These are not Government aspirations or Opposition aspirations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The real question is not whether we want them.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is how we achieve them and who must act.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: On the ground, I have heard that unless your business is AI, then it must be BI, BI means "bei ai" (悲哀), which means "to be sorrowful", in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Many businesses, especially domestic-facing ones, continue to grapple with uncertain demand and persistently high manpower, rental and operating costs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For these businesses and their workers whose livelihoods depend on them, headline GDP does not feel like growth.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our response must therefore work on two horizons – practical, time-bound relief for viable businesses under immediate pressure and longer-term transformation support to help them raise productivity, scale and reach new markets.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But relief without transformation merely postpones the problem.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Government must build the runway for our economy through sound regulation, infrastructure, education, fair regulation and a strong social safety net.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But firms, entrepreneurs and workers are the planes that must still take off.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: From a business perspective, this means three imperatives – enabled enterprises, expand opportunity and embed responsibility.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To enable enterprise, we must build an inclusive economy, one that gives people and businesses equal dignity, genuine access to opportunity and meaningful support when they face disadvantage or disruption.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A traditional SME trying to digitise has different needs from a technology start-up developing intellectual property.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A promising local enterprise preparing to expand overseas needs different support from a company whose business model that may no longer be viable.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Fairness means understanding what each business needs to progress and being clear about the outcomes public support should achieve.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If support is spread too thinly, we fail to give enough runway to companies with the potential to break out internationally.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, inclusion cannot mean guaranteeing the survival of every business.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A dynamic economy requires entry, experimentation, occasional failure and renewal.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Entrepreneurs should have the room to fail responsibly and try again.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But public support cannot remove every commercial risk or socialise every business loss.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Government's role is to create a fair and enabling environment.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses' role is to use it to improve, invest and compete.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is where our business institutions must step up.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Whatever stage of development you are at, your first port of call should be SBF or your relevant chamber and trade association.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A company should not need to understand the entire Government organisational chart before it can obtain help.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If you need to understand a policy or regulation, start with us.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If you need guidance on financing, start with us.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If you need to transform your workforce, adopt AI, enter a new market or find the right Government support, start with us.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But we will own the handover and help every company find the right door.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As it grew, manual processes led to mounting errors and delays.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Through SBF's Technology Implementation Advisory Service, developed with support from Enterprise Singapore and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), we helped the company adopt a single integrated tech solution.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Manual data entry fell by half, reports became almost immediate and the staff gained more time to train and support learners.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For an established SME, the next step may be new financing, stronger management capabilities or entry into an overseas market.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: UTRACON, a Singapore engineering firm seeking to grow in the Middle East, had the capability but lacked local partners and market access.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our role is not to venture for companies but to shorten the distance to their first opportunity abroad.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Enabling enterprise also means ensuring our regulations remain fit-for-purpose.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Regulations are necessary to protect workers, consumers, public safety, the environment and the integrity of our economy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But over time, rules can accumulate and create unintended friction.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The answer is not deregulation for its sake.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Test changes carefully, learn from evidence and adjust where rules no longer work.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Alliance for Action (AfA) on Business Competitiveness demonstrates how this can work.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The value of the AfA was not that Government agreed with every business request.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It was that businesses explained where rules created problems, and that agencies explained the safeguards and trade-offs they had to manage.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, businesses changed their views after understanding the policy reasons.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In other cases, agencies adjusted the rules after understanding operational realities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Not Government always saying yes, not business always being right.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But policy learning through engagement and improving over time.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For Singapore, domestic demand can only provide a buffer, but it cannot be our principal engine of scale.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That is the ambition we need to enable – Singapore companies venturing out, while keeping their most valuable capabilities anchored here.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is why the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) matters.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Its potential can be strengthened by linking it more closely with Batam, Bintan and Karimun (BKK).

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: SBF has initiated a strategic study on how better physical and digital connectivity, smoother customs arrangements and closer regulatory coordination could bring the JS-SEZ and BBK together as a wider regional cooperation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But expanding our hinterland is no free lunch.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Better connectivity also gives consumers more choices and exposes businesses here to greater competition.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: SBF's Johor Bahru–Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link study, done together the Restaurant Association of Singapore and the Singapore Retailers Association illustrates this trade-off.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our response cannot be to stop people from crossing the border.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Neither can Singapore businesses compete on price alone.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must compete on quality, trust, productivity, innovation, distinctive products and better experiences.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As we expand markets to create new opportunities, competition will come.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is to help Singapore companies build the capabilities to venture abroad, anchor value here and become strong enough to compete.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my third point on embedding responsibility.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Companies that benefit from access to global talent must also help develop Singaporeans by mentoring them, build local successors and give Singapore employees regional and global exposure.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We should not frame this as a choice between developing Singaporeans and remaining open to foreign or global talent.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Foreign professionals bring networks, technical knowledge and experience in overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But openness will remain socially sustainable only if it comes with real integration, knowledge transfer and investment in local leadership.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Alliance for Action on the Integration of Foreign Professionals, convened by the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY), Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) and SBF, shows how this can be done.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It produced practical recommendations to strengthen workplace integration while keeping Singapore open to global talent.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: SBF, with support from MCCY, now has an Integration of Foreign Professionals Programme Office.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It works with trade associations and chambers to run orientation for new Employment Pass holders, provides workplace-integration resources and conducts cultural-sensitivity workshops.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses benefit from Singapore's stability, infrastructure, educated workforce, rule of law and social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Giving back to society is not charity, but reinvestment in the foundations that enterprise depends on.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That is why the work of the SBF Foundation and our social impact programmes matters.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Through VolunteerInc., we help companies, including SMEs, mobilise their employees to contribute skills and time in the community.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Through EmployWell and MigrantWell, we create employment pathways for vulnerable groups and support migrant workers' well-being.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is how businesses strengthen the social compact.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: They show what becomes possible when businesses and Government work together.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Business leaders serve in SBF and our trade associations and chambers not because they have time to spare.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But because they know that no company can build a competitive ecosystem alone.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Government cannot know every operational difficulty that businesses face.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses may not fully appreciate every national trade-off that Government must manage.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Unions must understand that better jobs depend on viable companies, while employers must recognise that transformation cannot succeed without workers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That is why our tripartite and public-private partnerships remain important.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The parties do not need to agree on everything.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But there must be enough trust to discuss difficult trade-offs honestly and enough commitment to act after the discussion.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If each of us plays our part, Singapore will not merely respond to the future.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That is the economy of the future I believe Singapore must build.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the current global economic outlook is uncertain.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Fluctuating oil prices and frequent tariff changes have seriously affected economies and business worldwide.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore, as a small open nation with no natural resources, is likewise under considerable pressure.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Looking ahead, we still face several structural challenges.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These challenges are real and cannot be ignored.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our differences lie only in the path forward.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As the saying goes, if you want to go fast, go alone; if you want to go far, go together.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If everyone acts independently and looks only after their own interests, some short-term progress may be made, but it will not last.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Only by supporting one another and working together can we move forward steadily and sustainably.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, businesses should actively seize opportunities while giving back to society.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I firmly believe that as long as the tripartite partners work together, we will be able to weather the difficulties and achieve long-term development. : In conclusion, Mr Speaker, the wording of the Motion suggest that these aspirations somehow stand apart from the ESR.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I am not entirely persuaded by that framing.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Okay, I see you have four proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will get this distributed to all Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Alright, looks like every Member here has been given a copy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: First, it makes clear that the aspirations of inclusion, entrepreneurship, innovation and good jobs are aligned with the ESR, not pursued in spite of it.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Second, it recognises that the Singapore's future economy needs both dynamic local companies and global enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Third, it recognises that healthy domestic demand must be supported by strong external demand, especially for a small and open economy, like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: I will therefore speak to the proposed amended Motion by making three points.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: First, is that the ESR provides a strategic foundation for an inclusive and innovative economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: The ESR recognises that the world has changed fundamentally.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: In a more fractious environment, Singapore cannot simply preserve what worked in the past.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: The ESR was shaped through extensive engagements with businesses, unions, workers and industry stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: It should therefore be seen not merely as a Government report, but as a national strategy, co-created, shaped with the people and enterprises that helped carry it out.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Investments in R&D have anchored research talent in Singapore and also catalysed business expenditure in R&D.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: So, what we need to do next is to strengthen research translation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Singapore not only must produce more research, but translate more ideas into products; more intellectual property to businesses; more innovation into globally competitive Singapore enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: This requires strong partnerships between our universities, research institutions, investors and enterprise.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We need clearer pathways for promising technology to commercialise more industry-led research collaborations and better access for startups and SMEs to capital, customers and global markets.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Second, we must help workers move up, move across and move forward.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Even as technology disrupts jobs, the answer is not to slow down technology adoption.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: That will make our firms less competitive and ultimately, weaken opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: The answer is to give workers access to relevant training, better career guidance, industry-recognised skills and real pathways into growth sectors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: An economy that works for all must create a broad range of good jobs for technicians, operational specialist, tradespeople, associates, and professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs), service workers, mid-career workers and mature workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: My second point is that Singapore's economic engine must be powered by both dynamic local companies and global enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Dynamic local companies matter, but we should not frame local companies and global enterprises as competing choices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Singapore's success has never been built on such false choice.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Instead, our focus should be on helping MNCs, large local companies, SMEs and startups build up one another.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Global enterprises bring investments, technology and international networks while local enterprises contribute agility, innovation and specialised capabilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Together, they create an ecosystem that builds capabilities, accelerates innovations and creates better job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We have already seen how this works in practice.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: AEM, a homegrown Singapore company, designs an advance system that test semiconductors before they reach the market, including the thermal control technology needed to screen today's power-hungry AI chips.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Through a partnership with a global semiconductor MNC in the 2010s, AEM evolved from a contract manufacturer into a trusted innovative engineering partner to the semiconductor industry, delivering tests, thermal automation solutions to AI, high-performance computing and memory devices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: From a Singapore base, it has grown into a global test leader, with operations across Asia, Europe and the US, and it is now extending its expertise to the world's most advanced AI processors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: So, the challenge before us is to deepen these partnerships so that more Singapore enterprises can innovate, scale and internationalise.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: These connections strengthen research translations by bringing researchers, startups, SMEs, investors and industry together to move innovation more quickly from the laboratory to the marketplace.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We must help our SMEs and startups scale while ensuring that global enterprises continue to find Singapore a trusted and valuable base.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: If we become less open, less connected and less attractive to global capital and talent, it is actually our local companies that will lose access to markets, partners, technology and opportunity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: This is why we need both healthy domestic and external demand.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: It sustains many local enterprises, supports jobs and reflects confidence among households and businesses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Yet our whole market alone cannot provide the scale needed for every sector.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We therefore need both a vibrant domestic market where locally focused enterprises can thrive and strong global connections that help other firms reach larger markets.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We must continue to serve the world from Singapore as a trusted hub for finance, trade, technology, logistics, aviation, maritime, data, arbitration, greenfields, professional services and innovation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: At the same time, the benefits of this external orientation must flow back to Singaporeans through good jobs, wages, skills and enterprise opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: This is why the ESR emphasis on Singapore as a connected and trusted hub is so important.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: In a more fragmented world, connectivity alone is not enough.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We must become a place where flows are orchestrated, finance governed, translated into economic value.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: This is important, but this must be done from a strong and open Singapore base from which capital, talent and enterprise can scale into the region.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We want Singaporeans to lead, manage, invest, build and operate across borders.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We also want global partners to use Singapore as a launchpad and to create opportunities for Singaporeans from Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Our region is growing, but it is also diverse, complex and uneven.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Singapore companies need support to understand local regulations, build partnerships, manage risk, access financing and scale operations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: But this must sit within an open and outward-looking strategy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We become stronger by helping the world solve problems from Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Sometimes, economic debates frame equality and competitiveness as opposing objectives.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: For Singapore, competitiveness is what gives us the resources to be inclusive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Without fiscal resource, we cannot fund education, housing, healthcare, social support and skills upgrading.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: So, the question is not whether we choose growth or inclusion.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: The question is what kind of growth we pursue and how we ensure that Singaporeans will benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We want growth that will create good jobs; growth that allows workers to move into better roles; growth that strengthens local enterprises; and growth that supports families, seniors, lower-wage workers and mid-career workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: This is the exactly the kind of growth the Government has emphasised in its broader economic strategy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: The Forward Singapore agenda strengthens social support across different life stages.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: The ESR builds on this by focusing on good jobs, lifelong learning, enterprise transformation and resilience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: There is also another dimension to enterprise that we should not overlook.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We should view enterprises not only as economic units but also as social actors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Companies create jobs, pay wages and generate growth, but at their best they can also strengthen communities, support vulnerable groups, care for the environment and contribute to a stronger society.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: The movement encourages companies to act across five areas: people, society, governance, environment and economic.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: It is about how companies execute purpose through their core business and operations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Some companies do this through inclusive hiring and people-first workplace cultures.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Others do this through employee volunteering, mentoring SMEs, supporting community partners, reducing waste, improving sustainability practices or using their products, services and supply chains to create wider social impact.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Examples include Sheng Siong's people-first culture, HPE's waste recycling, HP's Planet Partners programme and Fraser's Property's efforts to shape environments and communities through its role as a real estate developer.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: This is encouraging progress with room to grow further.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: This matters because an inclusive economy cannot be built by the Government alone.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Startups, SMEs, large local enterprises and MNCs can be a force for good when they embed purpose into how they hire, buy, build, serve and grow.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: A future economy that works for all must be one where businesses do well and also do good.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
