text: The role of the Government is not to freeze the economy in place.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Instead, the role of the Government is to help workers and businesses adapt before disruption hits and to provide support when transitions are difficult.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: The reality is that not every existing job will remain unchanged.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Not every firm will survive in its current form and Singapore cannot avoid global competition.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We can commit to helping Singaporeans build new skills, access new opportunities and navigate change with confidence.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We can commit to helping businesses transform, adopt new technologies, access new markets and build the capabilities needed to compete in a changing world.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: It supports dynamic local companies and global enterprises as part of one ecosystem that creates opportunities for Singaporean entrepreneurs and workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: It values healthy domestic demand while recognising the necessity of strong external demand.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: It encourages Singaporeans and Singaporean capital to venture abroad while remaining anchored in a trusted, open and resilient Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Our future economy must be open, competitive and inclusive at the same time.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We must attract the best from the world while developing the best in Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: It is built by making change less frightening, because Singaporeans know that we will face it together.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It may be convenient that the debate on the original Motion and on any other amendments moved by Members be proceeded with simultaneously as a debate on a single question.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do I have hon Members' agreement to this?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Assent of the majority of Members is given.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The question is the amendments as moved by Mr Edward Chia.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The debate can range over the original Motion and the amendments.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call on Mr Louis Chua, Mr Tiong, do you want to make a clarification?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You certainly have the right of reply at the end, at the closing.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do you want to raise a clarification now?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Just one clarification for the hon Member Edward Chia.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: While we will have comments on some of the other amendments, for the second amendment, which is to delete "economic engine driven" and insert "economy powered", I am not quite sure what the purpose of this amendment is.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: It appears to me, to use a favourite word from a Minister opposite.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: But I think it is basically really saying that an economy must be powered by both local companies and global enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: And I think we could hear from the Member at his closing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: And to support local companies, we must also take the view that global enterprises must be part of the single ecosystem that in turn supports local companies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is a serious piece of work and I commend those involved.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But as I noted in this House last September, Singapore has never lacked task forces and committees – the Economic Strategies Committee in 2009, the Committee on the Future Economy in 2016, the Future Economy Council, the Industry Transformation Maps, the Emerging Stronger Task Force in 2020, and now the ESR and the Singapore Economic Resilient Task Force.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At this rate, reviewing the economy risks becoming a growth industry in its own right.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The ESR asks searching questions of our businesses and our workers: sharpen our value proposition, be agile, be resilient.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But there is one economic actor of whom the report asked remarkably little – the Government itself and specifically, the Government in its most lucrative role as our landlord.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The ESR ambitions for enterprise and innovation will not be realised so long as the Government continues to see itself as a landlord and as long as Singaporeans continue to share in the Government's rentier mindset.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have shared in my speech at the opening of this term in Parliament, policy should not inevitably reward the highest bidder at the expense of wider societal outcomes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And it is in upstream land costs that we must go further.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: State land forms part of our reserves, but excessive land prices push up development costs and rents, impacting tenants and companies, and eventually consumers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: They cascade from developer to tenant, from tenant to hawker, clinic, shopkeeper and finally, to every consumer.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I anticipate the familiar reply that rental is not the largest cost businesses face.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, when this House debated hawker culture, the Senior Minister of State cited a National Environment Agency (NEA) survey showing that rental forms less than 10% of store holders' operating costs against 56% for raw materials and 20% for manpower.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A rented industrial unit on state priced land.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Where does the wholesaler store his goods, the logistics firm parks its lorries, the essential kitchen prepares its ingredients?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: All on land whose price the state sets and extracts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: High land prices feed into rentals and rentals feed into every line of the cost structure, including the 56% we are told to look instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is a cost embedded in all the others and an important, fixed overhead that cannot be avoided.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Members will recall the $52,000 monthly rental bid for a general practitioner (GP) clinic in an HDB estate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung himself acknowledged that this must feed through to healthcare costs one way or another and that the highest rental bid does not deliver the best care for the community.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I agreed with his view then and I continue to hold this view.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: During this year's Committee of Supply, I appreciate that HDB is expanding the Price Quality Method for commercial tenders of neighbourhood shops.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But if we accept this logic downstream at the level of a single shop tender, we must have the intellectual honesty to apply upstream to land policy itself.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our land sales system is built so that prices can only ratchet upwards.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Sites are awarded to the highest bidder generally, subject to a reserve price that is not published for any individual site.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When the market bids above the reserve, the land is sold and a new benchmark is set.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When the market bids below it, the tender is simply not awarded, barring other specific circumstances and the state waits for a better day.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Tails, land prices are not allowed to fall.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That is roughly one in eight tenders aborted rather than allowed to clear at what the market was actually prepared to pay.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The pattern continues in February 2024, when the URA declined to award the Marina Gardens Crescent white site because the sole bid of $770 million, or $984 per square foot per plot ratio, was assessed to be too low.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The history of Paya Lebar Quarter, one of my favourite mixed-use sites in the East, tells the same story.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In November 2011, URA rejected the sole bid from a consortium of UOL Group and Singapore Land for a mixed-use site in Paya Lebar Central at $529.5 million, or $566 per square foot per plot ratio on the grounds that it was too low.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The consortium asked for reserve prices to be made public, given the cost and efforts of submission of such a scale.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: URA declined, saying disclosure would not be in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The land waited four years; the price went up by about two thirds.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The state coffers are higher by a billion, even as the site area is now bigger, and we saw private residential prices in that area reach new highs after Park Place Residences was eventually launched.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The irony is that the Government understands this perfectly well in certain cases.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: NEA proudly sets no reserve rent at all for hawker stall tenders since 2012 and does not set a minimum bid price for hawker stall tenders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My first call, therefore, is that maximising revenues from land and building should no longer be a primary consideration of land policy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have argued in this House before, we should bring back the two-envelope concept and price tenders as the default for strategic and community facing sites, so that land is awarded on the quality and value of what is built and not simply to whoever bids the most.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Government is the biggest landlord of all benefits, but it does so at everyone else's expense.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our own regulatory framework, the total debt servicing ratio, contemplates households committing up to 55% of gross monthly income to debt service obligations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A household servicing a 30-year mortgage at anywhere near that level does not leave the perceived security of a monthly paycheck to start a company with no visibility over cash inflows for years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It optimises for the next paycheck because it must.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is no wonder that risk aversion in Singapore is not some cultural mystery, but a lived balance sheet reality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That is why in the last term of Parliament, I moved an Adjournment Motion calling for rental housing to be developed as a genuine housing model and not merely a residual safety net for those with no other options.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The build-to-own model has served asset accumulation well, but it frontloads a lifetime of leverage onto Singaporeans in precisely the decades when they are most able to take entrepreneurial risk.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In many other global cities, young professionals rent for years without stigma, preserving the flexibility to move, retrain and build.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We already have a variance of this in the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme for married or engaged couples with more modest incomes and who wish to rent a temporary flat while waiting for their new home to be built.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we want a generation of founders, we should stop shackling them to mortgages in their 20s and 30s.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is however only meant to be a short-term programme that will only run for one year for the respective launch dates of each cloud service provider.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: By October 2025, we had reportedly paired some 1,000 firms with cloud partners, but this is a very modest figure as compared to the 385,000 or so firms in Singapore's enterprise landscape in 2024, as identified in the ESR's final report.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I also recognise that the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) AI-Ready SG subsidises half the subscription cost of eligible AI tools for members, if you first go for an approved course.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In other words, the principle of subsidised access to compute has been accepted by the Government.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The questions that remain are of scale, duration and ambition.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hong Kong built its own AI Supercomputing Centre at Cyberport and allocated HK$3 billion to a three-year AI subsidy scheme, under which eligible users receive subsidies of up to 70% of a centre's service list price.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That is a state-owned facility with a published rate card and a discount.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Canada's Sovereign AI Compute Strategy pairs public supercomputing investment with a C$300 million Access Fund that covers two-thirds of eligible costs for local cloud-based AI computing services, on projects with compute costs of up to C$5 million.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Note the word local, and that these are targeted at SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The United Kingdom (UK) having found itself with only 1.3% of global compute capacity in late 2022, committed up to £2 billion by 2030 under its Compute Roadmap, and its AI Research Resource now allocates compute directly: 10,000 GPU hours for first-time users and 20,000 GPU hours for SMEs, awarded as capacity rather than cash.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I could not have summed it up better than a 2025 World Bank report on Digital Progress and Trends report, that governments should create an enabling environment to facilitate access to compute resources, catalysing AI adoption, adaptation and innovation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This can include targeted interventions such as compute subsidies for SMEs and researchers, regional data centres and public-private partnership.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More recently, NVIDIA CEO, Jensen Huang, also remarked that a strong AI ecosystem is not a foregone conclusion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is not a one off or time limited effort, but instead we should spare no effort until a significant majority of our local enterprises have truly embedded AI into their core business processes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My third call is therefore a so-called "HDB model for compute".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The HDB public housing model made the Government's objective of home ownership for the people programme during our early years attainable through subsidised access to state land.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As what Liang Wenfeng, chief executive officer (CEO) of DeepSeek said recently, "人才的差距，本质上也是因为算力的差距".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Let us not have a talent gap in Singapore, simply because of a lack of access to compute.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First, the reserves belong to all Singaporeans, not to the government of the day.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Foregone rent extraction that flows into the productive capacity of Singaporean households and firms is not a raid, but an investment in our collective future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is the owners of the reserves investing in themselves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, on the Government's own explanation to this House, leasehold land reverts to the state at the end of its term and is protected as past reserve once again.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The debate is therefore about the pricing philosophy for the use of land over 99 years, not about giving the freehold away.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Why is a discount for a foreign MNC prudent economic strategy, but a discount for a Singaporean entrepreneur a raid on the reserves?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to conclude in Mandarin, Mr Speaker, on what the real risks are for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, what are the real risks facing our country and our economy?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is it that we are pricing a small number of land parcels, rental flats or GPU clusters below the highest level that the market can bear?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Or is it that generation after generation, Singaporeans will quietly come to the conclusion that, in their own country, the most lucrative business is to be a landlord and the safest life is to become a homeowner burdened by mortgage repayments for half their lives?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Government should stop seeing itself as Singapore's biggest landlord and should instead see itself as more actively as the people's greatest enabler.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If Singaporeans feel anxious about the future, it is our job to listen carefully.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Understanding how people feel is not the same as understanding why they feel that way and more importantly, what to do about it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And that brings me to the central question before this House: how does a small country like Singapore continue to create prosperity in a changing, more volatile world?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is a question every generation of Singaporeans has had to answer.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore's answer has never been abundant resources nor a domestic market of scale.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Everything we have achieved has depended on our ability to create far more value than our size would suggest possible.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That has been Singapore's story for the last 60 years.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It must be Singapore's story for the next 60.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But they must be answered in the right order, because no nation has every captured value it did not first create.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One lesson has remained remarkably constant: the strongest organisations do not succeed because of one advantage.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They succeed because they build complementary capabilities that reinforce one another – technology, talent, capital, customers, partnerships, compounding together.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: None of these strengths is sufficient on its own.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Together, they create greater value than the sum of the parts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The modern 21st century economy works the same way.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is not built around one company or one sector.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has never competed by trying to be bigger than anyone else.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have competed by bringing complementary strengths together faster and better than other countries many times our size.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We connect capital with ideas, research with enterprise, talent with opportunity, local ambition with global markets, global enterprises with capable local suppliers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Over time, those connections become an ecosystem that is far more competitive than any individual company, institution or sector can be on its own.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I suspect there is broad agreement across this House that we want more Singaporean enterprises to succeed globally.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is the path we believe gets us there.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That is why we should be careful about thinking of our choices as trade-offs, a tug of war, a zero-sum game – local enterprises versus global enterprises, domestic demand versus external demand, growth versus inclusion.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Take the relationship between global enterprises and local enterprises.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Dynamic local companies are essential to Singapore's future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We should want more of them, larger ones, more productive ones, more that succeed well beyond our shores.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Global enterprises are equally indispensable, not because they are larger, not because they create jobs, but because they expand the productive frontier of the entire economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They develop Singaporean talent, some of whom will one day set up their own companies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They connect Singapore companies to global customers and supply chains even if those supply chains are re-configuring.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They expose our companies to international best practices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They raise the standards of the ecosystem around them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In short, they expand the frontier of what Singapore's economy is capable of achieving.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It also asks what capabilities will be anchored here and how Singapore enterprises will benefit.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is deliberate capability building, deliberate ecosystem deepening.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A small precision engineering firm here might start by supplying components to an MNC here.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If the ecosystem is working, that story does not stop here.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Exposure to global standards, new technologies and production methods, and demanding customers lets that firm deepen what it can do – move from making parts to designing solutions, from serving one market to several, from supplier to competitor in its own right.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Eventually, it is no longer simply benefiting from the system.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is strengthening the system for the next generation of Singaporean companies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That is how stronger Singapore enterprises are built.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have had the privilege, particularly over the last few years, to work with more local SMEs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is holding them back from scaling globally is rarely a lack of ambition or a lack of demand for what they make.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These are capability gaps and they are unlikely to be closed simply by wining ourselves off connections with our global capital.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If anything, they are closed by making those connections work better for many more Singaporean enterprises.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That is why the real question is not whether local enterprises matter.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is not whether we should support them more strongly.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The real question is how we can build an economy where local and global enterprises reinforce one another, makes the other stronger.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The real question is whether we are helping enough Singaporean enterprises get connected to the ecosystems, acquire the capabilities that allow them to climb the value chain, compete internationally and ultimately, become ecosystem builders themselves.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And that is precisely what the ESR seeks to do.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The same logic applies to domestic and external demand.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But for a country of six million people, domestic demand cannot sustain the growth, wages and opportunities we aspire to.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must continue to compete in far larger markets.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Of course, many Singapore enterprises are not exporters.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As the Member of Parliament for Woodlands, I perhaps feel more keenly than others, that heartland businesses are feeling the pressure and the RTS Link may accelerate this.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But the answer cannot be simply to strengthen domestic demand.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We cannot ask consumers to ignore value, we cannot ask consumers to spend differently, we cannot ask them not to spend their money elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our response has to be to help business compete differently.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Also, ultimately, domestic demand, for every hawker, every family business, every heartland retailer, ultimately depends on Singaporeans' spending power.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That spending power comes from productive jobs, rising wages, competitive industries and companies succeeding in global markets.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In turn, a vibrant domestic economy provides the stability, talent and confidence that enable more firms to grow and venture abroad.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But I think we should answer it in the right way.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It matters who owns the next generation of globally competitive companies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But ownership does not just become reality simply because we declare it to be our objective.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is built patiently, capability by capability, enterprise by enterprise, institution by institution.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Ownership is most durable when it is built on capability, because capability is what allows ownership to endure and grow.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore will not own every company shaping the global AI economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These companies create enormous value for Singaporeans, through jobs, supplier ecosystems, knowledge spillovers, capability building.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And yes, an MNC may one day leave Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The most important question is whether Singaporeans are building the capabilities to create value alongside them – as founders, as engineers, as researchers, as investors, as suppliers, as technology leaders and increasingly, as owners of globally competitive enterprises themselves.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Ownership in a modern economy takes many forms: a founder building the next regional champion, an employer with stock options in a growing company, a Singapore supplier moving into higher-value-added design and engineering, an investor participating in the growth of world-class businesses, our sovereign wealth funds investing on behalf of every Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These are all ways in which Singaporeans participate in, capture and own the value that our economy creates.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The goal is therefore not simply to own more assets.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is to build an economy where more Singaporeans have meaningful ownership in the value they help create.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And we do this by building the whole innovation ecosystem: research, talent, capital, patient financing, market access, regulation, strong global partnerships.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And when they come together, they create something larger than any one policy, say on research, could achieve.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I want to go back to where I started.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If an SME owner says, "I don't feel these benefits," we should listen.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If they say, "I feel crowded out," we should listen.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If they say, "This ecosystem seems to work for everyone except businesses like mine," we should listen.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Global firms do compete with local ones for talent, for capital.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Wages feel the pressure and it falls unevenly and this is real.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But the answer to that real cost is not to become a less open economy, when openness is where the capability comes from.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The answer is to make sure more Singaporeans capture the upside instead of only absorbing the cost, skills that move a worker toward the frontier rather than away from it, capital markets deep enough, partnerships between MNCs and local firms that help more local firms becoming suppliers, adopters, internationalisers and owners in their own right.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And that is firmly, firmly embedded in the ESR strategies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But if we make rebalancing the organising principle of our strategy, we may not end up with more of those companies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Target ownership before capability and competitiveness, and we do not own more of the pie.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That is why I support the hon Member Mr Edward Chia's amendments.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They recognise something this House has known for 60 years and cannot afford to forget for the next 60.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our strength has never come from any one source alone.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It comes from strengthening the connections between them – dynamic local companies, global enterprises, domestic demand and external demand, Singaporeans and Singaporean capital venturing confidently into the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These were never separate engines to be weighed against each other.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They are complementary strengths, working together as one system, working together to lift ordinary Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It proposes training, pathways and career bridges between jobs.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it gives far less attention to the all-important first transition from education or National Service (NS) into stable work, and to whether young people get a fair start.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In February, during the Budget debate, I called this phenomenon the broken bottom rung of the career ladder – when young Singaporeans are unable to make that first meaningful step.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first job is where someone takes a chance on you.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is where you gain the experience that every subsequent employer expects you to have.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A young person cannot create that opportunity alone.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When firms stop taking chances on beginners, Singapore eventually stops producing experienced workers.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I want to ask the Government a practical question: if a young Singaporean has prepared for work, searched earnestly and still cannot secure stable employment, what must change so that their sustained effort can lead them somewhere?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, most graduates still manage to find work.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, eight out of nine graduates found work last year, but that figure is a broad measure.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That means only three out of four – down from four out of five – found more stable, long-term roles and could start building an actual career.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would not sound the klaxons just yet, but these are among several worrying signals, both in Singapore and from around the world, that it is getting harder for our youngest amongst us to find work.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The signals grow stronger when we look across different educational paths.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, another 24% were in part-time or temporary work, including 9.7% who said this was involuntary.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is clearly not a bed of roses for everyone.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The transition into stable work looks materially different depending on where you graduate.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Behind these figures are young people who have done what was asked of them and still cannot get started.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have heard from young graduates who told me about searches running into the hundreds of applications.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One submitted more than 500 applications over six months and received few interviews.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another submitted close to 200 in four months without securing a single one.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For these young people, the first transition meant repeated effort, very little response and no clear place to turn should their efforts repeatedly fail to net a reward.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A confluence of factors is likely driving the cooling job market for young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the increased adoption of both AI and "old-school" technological and productivity advancements, a firm may make the entirely rational decision to automate away the basic tasks once given to junior employees.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may decide that training a beginner is too costly in today's high cost environment and when that person can ultimately leave after gaining critical experience.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Take those same rational decisions and scale them across the economy, and we can start to see the problem.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If every firm, local companies and global enterprises alike, makes the same calculation, the economic engine gradually stops producing experienced workers.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What works for one company's balance sheet damages the national workforce.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has introduced several measures to support the transition into work.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SG Youth Plan has introduced Job Tasters to help young people explore an occupation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Work-Study and Company-Led Training can combine a real job with structured workplace learning.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Taken together, however, a young person can still move from exposure to training to job matching without getting a fair start.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If you are a young Singaporean under 30 making the transition from education or NS into working life, that you will get a fair start, through stable employment or a proper paid career-building pathway.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That means we must rebuild the broken bottom rung of the career ladder.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The establishment of the Skills and Workforce Development Agency (SWDA) gives us an important opportunity to make this promise real.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By bringing skills and employment under one roof, the Government can now judge the whole journey by one outcome: whether young Singaporeans actually get a fair start.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the individual young Singaporean, what this means is targeted and individualised support from SWDA case officers and that should begin early.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Six months into the transition is a sensible checkpoint at which to assess outcomes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Any young person still searching at that point should continue to receive active support and no one should be left to flounder alone.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But a national goal alone will not create opportunities.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, we must create more genuine ways for young people to get their fair start.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague Eileen Chong spoke during the SWDA Bill debate about the implementation gap in skills-based hiring.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore has produced tool kits and established institutions to promote this, but we still do not know clearly whether employers are changing how they hire or if they are lagging behind.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: She called for the Public Service to lead by example and for a published baseline tracking skills-based job postings by sector and employer size.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have also previously proposed that the Careers and Skills Passport evolve from a digital filing cabinet into a dynamic, living credential.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I now propose extending that idea: making it work better for hiring.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Passport already allows Singaporeans to share verified qualifications, training and employment records with employers.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For a fresh graduate, however, that record will naturally be thinner.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers should then match that evidence to the actual skills required for the job and where appropriate, let applicants demonstrate these skills through a structured practical assessment.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Public Service should apply the same discipline to its own entry-level roles: identify what must genuinely be known on the first day, remove degree and prior-experience requirements that cannot be justified and publish whether its hiring practices are changing.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These measures would improve the match between capable beginners and entry-level jobs that already exist in the market.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But matching alone cannot build the workplace experience that some jobs genuinely require and Singapore must therefore also create more places where beginners can acquire it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In some occupations, competence can only be built through sustained, supervised practice.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers want experience because the work genuinely takes time to learn.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, every firm has an incentive to wait for another firm to bear the cost of producing that experienced worker.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore already has workplace programmes for young entrants.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is why Singapore should build a national market for proper paid apprenticeships.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That means recruiting firms and coordinating the teaching assessment and supervision needed to build competence while making sure every place provides enough real work.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A smaller firm may have valuable work but lack a training department, a full curriculum or enough varied tasks to train an apprentice alone.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sector bodies and consortia can provide common teaching roving mentors and independent assessment while coordinating rotations between these SMEs, where these are needed to fully develop a range of competence.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers would still provide the job and the wages and the workplace supervision as well as their own share of investment.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should carry a contract of service, wages, CPF and ordinary workplace protections.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The apprentice should perform productive work, learn through a structured plan and have a named mentor.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These skills should also be recognised independently of any one employer and carry value elsewhere across the market.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same employer need not guarantee permanent conversion, but before the pathway ends, there should be credible decision on conversion or progression.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should support the shared infrastructure and portable occupational training that individual firms are unlikely to provide alone.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers must remain substantial investors from the first day.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government solves the coordination problem, firms provide real work and help build the worker.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Proper apprenticeships are central to a fair start for young people.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same principles have wider application across the economy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague, Mr Gerald Giam, will speak next about the application to the skilled trades, where verified competence should lead to recognised mastery and real progression.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third, the Government should use its economic leverage to create genuinely additional job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some employers have productive work but still hesitate to hire a beginner because of the initial wages, supervision and lower productivity.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One lever is expanding targeted temporary risk-sharing arrangements.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The employer must contribute throughout and take responsibility for wages, CPF, real work supervision and development.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The purpose is to connect public purchasing demand to the development of Singapore's future workforce without imposing a blanket quota on every contractor.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Both levers should face the same test: did public intervention change the employer’s decision and create a productive opportunity that would not otherwise have existed?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Public money should not pay employers to relabel planned vacancies, displace existing workers or cycle young people through temporary seats.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Support should depend on additional work and real development.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These measures will not eliminate every difficult transition for our youths, but they can however increase the number of genuine first opportunities without compelling private employers to hire or manufacturing make work in the economy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Fair Start Promise should be judged by whether they enter stable employment or a proper paid career building pathway and can build from it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should report whether employment lasts, whether job responsibilities and wages progress, and whether the results differ across groups.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A youth should not disappear from the figures because a referral failed or a programme ended.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Keeping these outcomes visible will show where vacancies, training capacity or practical support remain inadequate.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A downturn may also make progress towards the Fair Start Promise harder.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It tells Parliament and the public how much opportunity has disappeared and whether the national response is strong enough.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Fair Start Promise sets the national ambition.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Transparent results will also show where progress is being made and where the Government must do more.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Young people must prepare, search earnestly and engage with suitable opportunities.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers must provide real jobs and invest in beginners.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government must build the conditions in which sustained effort can lead to progress and lead to a stable career.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government must not stand aside when every employer waits for someone else to provide a first chance.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It must not let young people disappear between programmes and institutions.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I rise to speak on the Motion "An Economy of the Future that Works for All".

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I would just like to highlight that the Motion itself is quite important.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly is the collaboration between the private sectors and the Government.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The reason I say this is because we do not want to go into a Motion whereby we want to re-invent everything.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I think the most important part is not break what is already working.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I say this in my context of travelling with the SME Centre to one of the Central Asian countries.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The government of the day or the chamber that we met was quite amazed with what we have – a system, from the Ministry of Trade and Industry, down to Enterprise Singapore, down to the SME Centre, that creates a cohesiveness between the Government to the ground.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that we should be proud of.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We should retain – the ability to grow together.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: In such a climate, the instinct of many nations is to build walls.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Our strategy must clear, open, connected, trusted and resilient.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must double down on what makes Singapore unique – a credible, rules-based hub that can link markets, capital, talent and ideas across a fragmented world.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Member Mark Lee has commented on how important the trade chambers are.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: There are seven parts to my speech which I believe will put a clear perspective to achieve a concentrated network of help as one ecosystem of support to tackle the challenges ahead and devise a set of common strategies to ensure we progress and be very successful.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Trade as our lifeblood in a protectionist world.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: In a world where major economies are derisking, diversifying and sometimes decoupling, we must be the connector others can rely on.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Every new FTA is a new door for our SMEs, a new channel for our services and a new vote of confidence in Singapore's open economy.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: While others raise tariffs and impose quotas, we must lower friction.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must be the neutral ground where East meets West, where North connects with South.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Our legal system, financial infrastructure and logistical capabilities make us ideal for this role.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Empower Enterprise Singapore to be a global conduit in creating Queen Bee companies from GLCs that supports SMEs.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that I would like to share for us to be able to be a strong economy which is unique to our country – whereby the cohesiveness of working together is very important.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Enterprise Singapore's international presence must be leveraged more aggressively.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Their overseas centres should act as business matchmakers, linking Singapore companies with partners, distributors and joint venture opportunities abroad.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: They should not just be officers, they should be deal makers.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Recently, I attended an Enterprise Singapore talk on the Middle East situation and shared with local businesses about what to expect and what are the opportunities.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: But through that informed setting, we are able to make good judgements on whether we should come in or should not come in.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: But overall, the value that is given to companies is that it allowed us to evaluate with certainty and with clarity.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: That is the part that I see as going together, of having Enterprise Singapore overseas and bringing information back to the ground.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: For GLCs, I think they play an important role as well.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, I attended a session organised by the SBF, where they were trying to connect the Queen Bee or GLCs to local businesses in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We are overdue on such kind of collaborations.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We have companies that go all over the world, that tender for big projects.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The ability to work together is more important than ever.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Through that collaboration and interaction, we also show that we have the right sentiment whereby businesses can work with the Government and GLCs very, very well.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Moving on, we can reduce the cost of error for SMEs going overseas.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This includes shared warehousing or logistic hubs in key markets, tax incentives for re-investing overseas profit back into R&D or capability building.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: When we reduce the cost of failure, we increase the courage to try.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: That is how Singaporean companies grow into regional and global champions.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must consciously position ourself as a: financial hub – continue to deepen our capital markets, attract asset managers and investment, and become the leading centre for green finance and fintech in Asia; logistics hub – leverage our port and airport connectivity to be the premier transshipment and distribution centre for the world; transport hub – expand our aviation and maritime networks to remain the gateway between various countries; education hub – attract top global universities and research institutions and nurture homegrown talent to serve regional and global needs; management hub – position Singapore as a regional headquarters for MNCs and the base for professional services in law, accounting, consulting and so on; medical hub – build our world-class healthcare system to attract medical tourism, clinical trials and biotech innovation; and of course, AI hub – invest in AI research, talent and infrastructure to become the leading AI ecosystem in Southeast Asia; sustainability hub – another part that is important in creating a centre of excellence and trust for sustainability reporting and deployment.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This "hub of hubs" strategy is not about doing everything ourselves.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: It is about creating an ecosystem where global players want to base their operations, where Singaporean SMEs can plug into global value chains and where talent from around the world wants to work and innovate with.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Third, empowering SMEs to thrive locally and globally.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Yet they face rising costs, tight labour markets and intense competition.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must do more to help them not just survive but thrive.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: SME Centres, which are one of the hubs that can offer to companies, must be the first port of call for every small and medium business.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: They have provided and should enhance their services.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: SME Centres do provide business advisory services, free of charge, with the support of the Government, workshops on digitalisation, sustainability and internationalisation, access to templates, tools and best practices for governance and compliance.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Organisations like SBF, the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry, SMCCI, the Singapore Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the Association of Small and Medium Enterprise and others must be empowered to do more and not limited to the following: organise business missions and networking events; host sector-specific forums on growth areas like green economy, AI and healthcare; educate members on regulatory changes and emerging opportunities; advocate for SME concerns at the policy level.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: And I think one that has been doing very well is mentorship programmes, pairing seasoned entrepreneurs with startups.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that even the SMCCI has started doing.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Next, to encourage businesses to adapt to changing demand.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs must be ready to pivot, whether it is adopting e-commerce, shifting to sustainable products, or tapping into new customer segments.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Government, and the trade associations and chambers can help by providing real-time market intelligence and trend analysis.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The next part is promoting "Buy Singapore, Support Singapore".

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The reason I raised this issue is regarding GLCs supporting local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I think that is where we can work together to lift everybody up.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: And doing so, this recognises every dollar spent is circulated in our economy, creates jobs and builds resilience.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Government procurement can lead by example, prioritising local SMEs where quality and value are comparable.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The fourth part, embracing sustainability as a competitive edge.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The Government should expand grants for energy-efficient or even increase the grant and of course, carbon accounting and reporting tools, sustainable packaging and supply chain solutions and build green capabilities.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Companies that adopt sustainability early will not only comply with regulations but also, gain a competitive edge in global markets where consumers and investors demand responsibility.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Fifth, manpower and lifelong learning in the age of AI.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: AI is not coming; AI is already here.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: It is transforming industries, automating tasks; in some cases, replacing workers.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This is a distant threat; it is a present reality.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot stop technological progress, but we can ensure that no Singaporean is left behind.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Workforce must be ready to learn and relearn.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: What you learned five years ago may be obsolete today.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Every worker must embrace lifelong learning, not as a slogan, but as a survival strategy.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: AI can automate routine tasks, but it cannot replicate creativity, empathy and leadership.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Our education and training systems must emphasise these uniquely human skills.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Constant learning is the only way to stay competitive and employable.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The Government must make it affordable, accessible and relevant.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The sixth part, supporting R&D and reducing cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, the next one is mitigating high cost of living and operating.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: A thriving economy requires both innovation and affordability.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The last part, part seven, keeping the Singapore Dream alive.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: It is the belief that with hard work, determination and a fair chance, every Singaporean can achieve aspirations, whether in arts, sports, academia, business or culture.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must ensure that no one feels left out.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Inclusive growth means that the benefits of progress are shared broadly.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must uplift the vulnerable, support the middle, and celebrate the successful.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: They must see themselves in our economic story, not as bystanders, but as protagonists.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: In a world that is increasingly turning inward, Singapore must stand firm as a beacon of openness.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must empower our SMEs to thrive both locally and globally.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: And we must ensure that the Singapore Dream remains alive for all.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: In a world turning inward, Singapore must stand firm as a beacon of openness.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must be the bridge of trade, not the barrier.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must become the hub of hubs – financial, logistics, transport, education, management, medical, sustainability and AI.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must empower our SMEs to thrive locally and globally.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must embrace sustainability as a competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must prepare our workforce for the AI revolution and we must keep the Singapore Dream alive for all.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Let us build an economy where every Singaporean can prosper, where every enterprise can grow and where our nation continues to punch above its weight on the global stage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We have relied on foreign labour arbitrage and allowed unlicensed workers to perform tasks meant for certified practitioners, inevitably suppressing local trade earnings over time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With a median monthly income of just $2,700 in 2023, skilled trades are seldom seen as a career of first choice for young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, skilled trades persons form the bedrock of our national infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While AI can automate administrative reports, and overseas remote workers can process corporate accounts, they cannot physically rewire a server room, repair a water main, or maintain critical infrastructure in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These crafts are inherently localised, highly skilled and resistant to remote replacement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If we want to offer genuine economic mobility to our vocational graduates, we cannot leave the skilled trades trapped by undercutting from unlicensed workers, rigid licensing regimes and limited career progression pathways.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must elevate these vocations into respected high earning avenues of trade, entrepreneurship and national pride.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While upskilling is essential, classroom retraining has limited utility in technical crafts, compared to master-led apprenticeships, and training alone cannot resolve deeper market distortions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As we look to elevate skilled technical vocations, reliance on frameworks patterned after the Progressive Wage Model or the Career Progression Model will reach natural structural limits.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While these models establish important wage floors across foundational sectors, their design relies heavily on climbing fixed corporate ladders into administrative or supervisory roles, positions that are inherently limited in number, and compel artisans to abandon their practical craft just to earn a higher income.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To enable our artisans to achieve true long-term wage progression, we must look beyond administrative ladders and restructure the underlying market so that technical mastery naturally commands the true market value of their craft.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To achieve this, we must introduce a market-friendly trade competency framework that elevate skilled trades into highly respected avenues of independent enterprise and professional advancement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must enable trades persons to contribute to and build prosperous, scalable businesses, ensuring they do not feel stuck in demanding jobs with limited prospects.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The ESR report rightly acknowledges that essential physical trades are vital to Singapore's economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, its recommendations continue to rely on incremental tweaks within employer-led models.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the ESR points to outsourcing and weak skills recognition, it remains silent on the deeper structural distortions depressing trade wages.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The report features an inspiring young electrician whose grit is truly commendable.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, his pathway is telling – unlocking high earnings required four academic degrees, including a master's degree from Nitec all the way to a master's degree.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I applaud his drive but question the system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why force a master craftsman through an academic obstacle course instead of directly valuing hands-on mastery and independent enterprise?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This paradigm shift must begin with how these essential vocations are regulated and protected in the open market.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Consider all our current licensing regimes, almost all fixed electrical work legally requires an Energy Market Authority (EMA)-licensed electrical worker, while regulated plumbing requires a PUB-licensed plumber.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This economic gap tempts cash constrained buyers to opt for uncertified options across many routine property maintenance tasks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Uncertified electrical work can cause loose connections, arcing, structural fires or electrocution, while improper plumbing joints can lead to concealed leaks, sewage backflow or water supply contamination.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To protect public safety and shield local artisans from wage depressing undercutting, regulators, including EMA and PUB, must enforce strict regulatory baselines for all market players, whether local or foreign, to ensure local artisans compete on a true level playing field of technical quality and safety.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will require the agencies to staff sufficient inspectors and auditors to conduct enforcement and respond to whistle-blowing complaints.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, we must streamline how local talent enters and moves through the vocational talent pipeline.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Local manpower supply is currently constrained by rigid structures that force junior workers and mid-career entrants through a long, uncertain route just to secure a licence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should promote the skills traits to students and mid-career switches as viable, respected alternatives to polytechnic diplomas and university degrees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Training pathways already exist, whether through full-time ITE programmes or certification courses at the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) Academy or Singapore Institute of Power and Gas for mid-career switches.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, despite completing their classroom education, aspiring tradespersons face structural challenges when attempting to translate those qualifications into licenced, independent careers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Each cleared module would legally authorise the tradesperson for that specific scope of work, whether in water heater installations, sanitary piping or wiring loops.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These milestones are verified via hands on practical assessments, customer ratings and structured peer reviews by master practitioners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This allows local apprentices to start practising legally and earning a respectable living for the task they have mastered, while progressively expanding their certified scope over time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It allows tradespersons to log task-specific trade endorsements, verified under the supervision of licensed artisans, creating an immutable record of their practical milestones.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It can also double as a national trades marketplace, connecting buyers, both enterprises and homeowners, directly with licensed tradespersons, based on verified modular competencies, domain expertise and clear rate schedules set transparently by the artisans themselves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Clear benchmark call out rate bands can be established, providing upfront price transparency for property owners, while guaranteeing fair off-hours compensation for artisans, eliminating both predatory surge gouging and artificial wage caps.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By streamlining, matching and reducing administrative overhead for both small contractors and buyers, the system enables tradespersons to establish sustainable commercial clients, secure corporate procurement contracts and build long-term business equity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, we must eliminate the structural overload reliance on an employer's sole discretion to advance an apprentice's career.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Across skilled trades, the Government currently enforces safety through rigid employer-tied licensing requirements, inadvertently, granting employers veto power over an entry-level worker's advancement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Under the current market structure, established employers have little commercial incentive to sign off on the logbooks and testimonials of apprentices, who may later become direct competitors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: An apprentice should be able to submit their immutable digital work logs and project portfolios to an independent technical panel for verification.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This preserves direct supervisory accountability while protecting apprentices from career stagnation and employer hold-up.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Existing industry bodies, like the Singapore Plumbing Society, the Singapore Electrical Contractors and Licensed Electrical Workers Association, and the Specialist Trade Alliance of Singapore, possess relevant sectoral familiarity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These trade societies can be reformed and integrated as dedicated chambers under this guild.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will give every tradesperson a direct voice, remove corporate employer gatekeeping and empower artisans to govern their craft under a self-regulatory model similar to those enjoyed by doctors, engineers and accountants.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Under this four-sided partnership of shared accountability, employers provide structured apprenticeships with all.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Progress and milestones log transparently in the Tradespersons Skills Ledger.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Singapore Guild of Skilled Tradespersons acts as an independent quality auditor and serves as a safety guardian.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Tradespersons maintain verified digital profiles and direct statutory accountability for work within their endorsed scope and consumers gain direct access to a trusted, transparent marketplace with verified quality assurance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It demands restoring the social standing and institutional dignity of our artisans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When we give skilled tradespersons the autonomy to govern their own professions, command transparent commercial returns for their mastery and build independent, high earning businesses, we can fundamentally change how society views this form of blue-collar work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By replacing rigid academic trade mills with direct market rewards for technical excellence, entering a trade will no longer be seen as a second-best option, born of academic detour, but a proud, lucrative and respected pathway into entrepreneurship and master craftsmanship.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I rise to speak on the Motion before this House.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is much in the Motion's aspirations that I support.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We want our entrepreneurs to succeed and internationalise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We want good jobs and rising opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, economic progress must translate into better lives for our people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also recognise the argument made by Members proposing this Motion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore's traditional economic model has served us well, but the competitive environment has changed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Technology has made it easier for corporate functions to move.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Geopolitical fragmentation is reshaping investment and supply chains.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But a more competitive environment does not make external demand or global companies less important to Singapore's next phase of growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It makes our ability to compete successfully for them and to capture greater value from their presence here, even more important.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Healthy domestic demand can strengthen our resilience, but we should be cautious about suggesting that it can substitute for the scale and opportunities provided by our global economic connections.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I agree, but this is precisely what the ESR already seeks to address.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It recognises that assumptions underpinning Singapore's success are changing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Its response is not simply to repeat the strategy of the past six decades; it is to upgrade it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And in fact, many of the ESR's recommendations are strikingly similar to the aspirations contained in today's Motion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The ESR's recommendations will drive the next bound of economic growth and workforce transformation amidst drastically changed global environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The ESR calls for stronger support for entrepreneurship and access to growth capital, more and better jobs, stronger career transition support and lifelong learning for workers, strengthening Singapore's position as a global leader in AI and a hub for global flows, and building a more dynamic enterprise ecosystem so that more Singapore-based companies can start, scale and succeed globally.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many have already begun to find expression in Government policy, including measures announced in recent Budget, enhancing enterprise financing, supporting SMEs and internationalisation, strengthening workforce transitions and investing further in our AI capabilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This suggests there is considerable common ground between the aspiration in today's Motion and the direction Singapore is already taking through the ESR.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The useful question for today's debate, therefore, to me, is where the substantive difference lies, whether they concern the overall economic model or the balance, emphasis and policy choices within that model.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I think that distinction matters because the debate is not really between an old playbook and a new one.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is about what should be in the new playbook, and where we may differ on the balance and emphasis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One area where I believe we should be careful is the weight we place on external demand and global companies in Singapore's next phase of growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
