text: We have heard many speeches before me on this, but I just want to reiterate it again, briefly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is one economic reality Singapore cannot escape.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For a small country, like ours, domestic demand alone cannot provide the scale of opportunities that Singaporeans aspire to.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That gives some sense of just how deeply Singapore's prosperity is connected to demand beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our semiconductor plants do not produce mainly for Singapore consumers; our pharmaceutical facilities do not manufacture only for patients here; our port, airport and financial centres serve markets far beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: External demand provides much of its scale, and the same applies to global companies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should absolutely build more Singapore champions, but this is not a choice between global companies and local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The ESR itself calls for Singapore to support high-potential enterprises, both homegrown and global.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And this remains the very real source of economic opportunity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The relevant question today is no longer simply how much investment did we attract, it should increasingly be how much value do we anchor in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our strategic functions located here – are Singaporeans progressing into specialists and leadership roles?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are technology and capabilities diffusing into the wider economy?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The ESR seeks to address precisely these linkages, as I infer from its report.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It calls for us to go beyond simply attracting investment and to embed these investments more deeply into Singapore through stronger local supplier networks, partnerships with our research institutions, deeper innovation capabilities and stronger pipelines of skilled talent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The next challenge, as the ESR recognises, is to connect these capabilities more tightly to industry needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I can see that the numbers actually do show benefits on Singapore's front.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In other words, the objective is not simply to bring global companies here but to anchor more of their capabilities here and ensure that their presence strengthens Singapore companies and Singaporean workers as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That should increasingly be our test of successful foreign investment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My office is in One Raffles Quay in Raffles Place.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Almost every morning, I take the lift up and down.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I see young Singaporeans going into offices occupied by global companies, including firms, such as ByteDance, financial institutions and technology companies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They work in technology, data, finance, compliance and regional functions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are young Singaporeans, building careers in global businesses while remaining based in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When these companies choose Singapore as a regional hub, they do not simply rent office space.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They create jobs and demand for local services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They contribute to the vibrancy of our business districts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And this brings me to the concern about a "two-speed economy" narrative.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, I note that the ESR itself recognises the capability and cost constraints faced by SMEs and the difficulties smaller firms can face in navigating and accessing existing support.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In areas, such as AI adoption, ESR specifically calls for support to extend beyond leading firms to the wider business base.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, the challenge facing smaller enterprises is not absent from the ESR.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The more important question is whether our transmission mechanisms are strong enough to reach them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the answer is not to slow down firms operating at the productivity frontier.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is to strengthen the transmission mechanisms and help more firms move towards that frontier, to create convergence upwards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A Singapore SME supplying an advanced manufacturer may have to meet exacting global standards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In doing so, it builds capabilities that can help it win other customers and enter new markets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Workers trained in MNCs carry skills and experience throughout the economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Technology and management practices can diffuse, and anchor companies create demand for suppliers, professional services, logistics and specialised skills.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Openness must create capability and this principle applies to workers too.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Take the administrator or driver working in the logistics and supply chain industry, for example – and I serve as a union advisor to the Supply Chain Employees' Union.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As AI, automation and digitalisation transform supply chains, our objective cannot simply be to preserve today's job exactly as it exists.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is precisely the transmission mechanism we should strengthen.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Global expertise anchored here, with Singaporeans progressively equipped to take on more sophisticated roles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is not a retreat from our hub strategy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore cannot compete with much larger economies principally on cost.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must compete on value through skills, connectivity, trust, infrastructure, innovation and our ability to manage complex regional and global operations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think Members on both sides of this House would agree that many local enterprises face significant cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But if business costs are an important concern in today's debate, or in other speeches later on, I hope we can also have greater clarity on the policy choices that would address them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For many SMEs, particularly in sectors, such as services, retail, logistics and F&B, significant cost pressures include labour, rental and energy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, the question I have is: so, what are the policy choices?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have heard some from the earlier speeches.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If rental costs are the concern, are Members proposing some form of rent regulation or greater intervention in commercial leasing?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If energy costs are the issue, are Members suggesting energy price controls or longer-term subsidies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We all want our businesses to remain competitive and to manage their costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But measures to reduce one cost can have consequences elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I hope today's debate and later speeches can therefore move beyond identifying the challenges facing SMEs, on which there is considerable common ground, towards a clearer discussion of which policy choices we or they are prepared to make and which trade-offs we are prepared to accept.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Essentially, economic policy ultimately requires choices, and choices require prioritisation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a small country, Singapore cannot depend on domestic demand alone.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need global markets, global investment and international economic linkages to create greater scale for growth and opportunities for our people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But our objective is not simply to bring more global companies to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What matters more is how much value, capability and opportunity we can anchor in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are Singaporeans getting better jobs and opportunities to progress?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are our local SMEs becoming suppliers and partners to global companies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are technology, skills and expertise spreading across our wider economy?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Efforts to address these questions are aligned with the key thrusts of the Economic Strategy Review, or ESR, report.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We do not have to choose between global companies and local companies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to ensure that both can grow together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If different parts of our economy are moving at different speeds, the answer is not to slow down those that are most competitive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead, we need to help more enterprises and workers build their capabilities so that they can progress together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Economic openness and inclusion are also not conflicting objectives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our challenge is to remain open to the world, while ensuring that more Singaporeans, workers and Singapore enterprises can seize the opportunities that this openness creates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: All this is aligned with the recommendations of the Economic Strategy Review report.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is also the spirit that we want to bring to the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: National strategies will only bring about meaningful change when our communities understand the changes taking place and are able to seize the opportunities available.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our purpose is not to create a separate economic strategy for the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our objective is to ensure that our community is prepared for change and well positioned to seize and create new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is where M³+, business leaders and community networks can serve as a bridge between national programmes and needs on the ground.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For enterprises with the aspiration and potential, Singapore should be their starting point, not their limit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We want to help more enterprises build capabilities, become suppliers and partners to global companies, and eventually venture into ASEAN and wider markets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Technology will change jobs and the skills required.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to help workers understand these changes early, upgrade their skills and seize opportunities in growth sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should not wait until someone loses his or her job before we act.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Economic resilience also means preparing before change occurs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to move from awareness to participation in the ESR strategy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can more Malay/Muslim SMEs become suppliers and business partners to global companies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can more of our entrepreneurs expand into ASEAN?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Inclusion is not simply about redistributing the gains from growth after they have been created.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Inclusion also means widening opportunities so that more members of our community can participate in the very process that creates that growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Malay/Muslim community should not merely be prepared for the economy of the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should have the confidence, skills and capabilities to help shape that future economy and succeed in it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Allow me to conclude this Malay section with a pantun: Sailing our boat on tranquil seas; Stopping awhile at Pulau Ubin; Knowledge acquired, talent grows with ease; Progressing together, a secure future is attained. : Mr Speaker, as I said at the outset, there is considerable common ground between the aspirations in this Motion and the direction already set out in the ESR.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The question is therefore not whether our economic model must evolve.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The question is how it evolves and which foundations of Singapore's economic success we must preserve even as we strengthen local enterprise, resilience and inclusion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One such foundation is our openness and connectivity to the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can build stronger Singapore companies, strengthen resilience and broaden participation in growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But these objectives should complement our global orientation, not substitute it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our task is to create convergence upwards, so that more Singaporean companies and workers benefit from the technology, capabilities, investment and opportunities flowing through our economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Because the choice is not between being global and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The ESR recognises that the global economy is changing in ways that are structural rather than cyclical.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My speech will focus on Thrusts 6 and 7 of the ESR.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While their broad aims are laudable, I hope to advance some different recommendations for consideration, in the shared hope and spirit of better preparing and protecting our Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I will frame my suggestions through three questions.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: What is the journey for Singaporean workers who find themselves displaced in the workforce or at risk of being made obsolete?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: What is the destination for those who undertake skills training or upgrading and how can we ensure that such retraining or upskilling results in a job on the other side?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The third question ties the previous two together.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: What is the proof that our continuing education system actually works?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: What is the journey like for Singaporeans who undertake reskilling or retraining opportunities?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, how can we make sure that these workers can and do benefit from these opportunities, and what can be done to make the journey easier for them?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My answer is two-fold: one, is to offer a robust safety net so that workers, especially those who are displaced, can pursue retraining and reskilling opportunities without anxiety or worry; two, is to unlock sources of funding for those who may wish to pursue deeper mid-career upskilling.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Upskilling and retraining sounds good in the abstract as a response to job displacement.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: But we have to remember that Singaporean workers are not video game characters, progressing through a skill tree to get an achievement unlocked.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: To workers made redundant or are on the verge of losing their jobs, upskilling and retraining may not sound like solutions in the immediate moment, but rather as another source of stress and uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Let us not understate the psychological distress and desperation that precarious employment can cause.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Other than anxiety and disappointment, workers can also feel shame and embarrassment, especially if they are breadwinners with children or elderly depending on them.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We must thus manage workforce transformations and transitions with sensitivity.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We need our Singaporean workers to feel secure and have confidence that they can and will overcome an employment disruption if and when they face one.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We need affected workers to be confident that they have the full backing of society and the Government as they endeavour to overcome this setback.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, I want to ask whether this alone is sufficient or even fair for the affected workers who have sometimes contributed years of service.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Crucially, employers are encouraged to abide by the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower and Responsible Retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As a result, retrenchment benefits remain at the discretion of the respective employers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Because every worker pays into it, every worker will be eligible to benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Workers will not have to go through an application process or face an agonising wait about the outcome or stress themselves out further about what they should do if their application was rejected.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Our proposal offers displaced workers the assurance, peace of mind and financial buffer to properly reskill and seek a better job fit since the worker would not need to jump at the first offer that comes along.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This will also reduce the prospect of underemployment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I want to reassure them that our redundancy insurance features the following "4Cs" to address this.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The 4Cs are coverage, conditionality, caps and cushion.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: First, coverage is restricted only to cases of involuntary redundancy, thus eliminating the concerns that workers may quit in order to collect benefits.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Second, conditionality payouts for the second and subsequent months will be made conditional on the individual's job searching and/or retraining efforts.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The payouts are modest and limited by a double-40 cap, that is, only 40% of the last drawn salary, which is also further subjected to a cap at 40% of median income.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These payouts are time limited and not meant to fully replace lost income.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Rather, it is intended to merely cushion the harsh impact of retrenchment and provide a semblance of security and assurance to the worker and his/her family and dependants in their immediate future.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Beyond the 4Cs, Mr Speaker, let me make a more fundamental point about the redundancy insurance scheme.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I am glad to see that the Prime Minister is here in the House, because he would perhaps best appreciate how our universal redundancy insurance scheme can reflect and foster a "we first" spirit by pooling our resources collectively and engaging in risk sharing.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It is a reminder that all of us Singaporeans are in this together and that we mutually help and support each other when things get difficult.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: What else can we do to better support workers who are retraining or upskilling?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: What I want to suggest here is especially pertinent for Singaporeans who have spent time in the workforce and may now want to upskill in a major and deeper way.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This could mean taking on a postgraduate degree.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In doing so, workers would then gain the qualifications and competencies needed to either value add to their current work or even to pivot to new industries.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, such deep upskilling is often more demanding, very time- and energy-intensive, and involves a longer-term commitment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I have two specific proposals in this regard.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: What I have in mind here is something like the MENDAKI study loans, which has a repayment arrangement that scales up over a period of time.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Finding the funding for postgraduate studies is often a challenge for many working professionals.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Yet, postgraduate degrees remain useful in improving employability.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For instance, employers sometimes reduce the years of working experience needed for applicants with a postgraduate degree.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I left the Public Service to pursue a postgraduate Juris Doctor (JD) programme at Singapore Management University to become a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The temporary transition back to being a full-time student was difficult, not least due to the loss of a stable income for the three years of the JD programme.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, securing an interest-free education loan from MENDAKI was helpful for me.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Also, while being a JD student, I was in a slightly better financial place as a result of holding a Master's in sociology, that enabled me to secure part-time employment teaching at Singapore Institute of Management, which helped me with my day-to-day expenses.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Today, retraining and upskilling is something unavoidable for the Singaporean worker.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, we in this House would do well to recognise that the process of retraining and especially deeper upskilling involves opportunity and real cost, some of which can and should be alleviated.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Training by itself is not an economic outcome.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Obtaining a certificate does not necessarily translate into a livelihood.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If retraining ends with the worker returning home to search job portals alone, then we have merely replaced one form of insecurity with another.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I am thus encouraged by the opportunity presented last month by the merger of SkillsFuture Singapore and Workforce Singapore into a single Statutory Board.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I believe that this is in line with the recommendation in Thrust 7 of the ESR.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As such, SWDA should avoid merely becoming a larger training administrator.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Instead, it should be connecting together employers, training providers and workers so that retraining culminates in a real opportunity for employment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Jobseekers will meet with the caseworker for a one-on-one guidance on the job search process.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: After a careful consideration of the jobseeker's circumstances, skills and experience as well as the expected vacancies in the job market, the caseworker can then either match the jobseekers to available jobs or else recommend retraining or upskilling courses that can prepare these jobseekers to transition into another role.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: To properly fulfil this bridging and matching function, SWDA will have to do two things in tandem: (a) tracking the macro developments in the job sector; and (b) ensuring that its programme offerings are fit for purpose.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The first task is for the SWDA to have a good understanding of the ever evolving needs and demands of the job market so that they can better match or train jobseekers for these jobs.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Here, SWDA can work with employers to understand which sectors are expanding, which firms are expected to have vacancies over the next six to 12 months and which industries face persistent worker shortages.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The second task requires the SWDA to build a culture of rigorous evaluation so that taxpayers' monies are funding courses and training programmes that actually provide good employment outcomes for workers or at the very least provide skills needed by the industry.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For example, in many industries, there are companies that compete commercially but require many of the same foundational competencies.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: SWDA can work with industry partners to build training programmes that focus on sector-wide skills during the first few months, followed by a shorter company-specific immersion.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: SWDA should also work with industry professionals to design training curricula for workers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It should regularly collect employers' requirements across each industry or perhaps even receive curricular proposals from these employers, as suggested before by two of my hon friends, Mr Gerald Giam and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Training providers should then demonstrate how their own programmes meet these industries' identified needs.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If this is not the case already, industry representatives should sit on these curricula's steering committees.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: SkillsFuture providers should also be governed by tougher quality assurance frameworks with frequent audits on providers and trainers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: There should also be industry input on the assessment standards for SkillsFuture courses.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Every SkillsFuture programme, from curriculum to assessment, should require sign off from three stakeholders: an employer or industry representative, the Government and the training provider.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This will demonstrate that they are solid training programmes that can prepare workers to enter new jobs or new industries.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I believe that a new SWDA can best serve our workforce by becoming the national convener for matching displaced workers, employers and training institutions into a single coherent system of retraining and rehiring.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: SWDA can then develop a niche in creating the career bridges which the ESR talks about in Thrust 6 – those structured pathways for at risk workers to gain employment in more resilient occupations.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: How can we be confident that our system of continuing education actually works?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Where is the evidence to tell us that our training programmes actually succeed?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I understand that SkillsFuture and continuing education more generally should not be narrowly evaluated in terms of employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: SkillsFuture also serves the purposes of enrichment and lifelong learning, which is why one of my hon colleagues shared with me even her 88-year-old mother receives SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If the Government is primarily relying on SkillsFuture as a platform to deliver workforce retraining and upskilling, then surely our evaluation of SkillsFuture and its offerings must reflect that priority.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The availability of such data will transform accountability throughout our training ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Providers will be forced to complete on outcomes rather than marketing and workers would make better informed decisions before going for training.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Government spending should then flow towards programmes that demonstrably succeed.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has built one of the world's most generous systems of continuing education.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Without a doubt, the Government has invested significantly in our people, But as always is the case with Government expenditure, where the money goes and how it is spent matters as much as how much is spent.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The recently released report of the Auditor-General raises questions about whether the money has been fruitfully used.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Auditor-General's Office (AGO) flagged some issues with the Career Conversion Programme and Mid-Career Pathways Programme.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While I understand that Workforce Singapore has addressed some of these findings, my concern is about the vulnerabilities in the system that can be exploited.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Government must remain vigilant in detecting any abuse of the system and plugging these gaps, so to ensure public monies can deliver genuine training of our workforce, because every dollar diverted and wasted is a dollar not spent to re-train or upskill a worker to stay employable.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And we must ensure that taxpayers' money that we spend to support reskilling and career conversion should produce genuine workforce outcomes and meaningfully help displaced workers rebuild their careers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: To recap the proposals in my speech: one, legislating mandatory retrenchment benefits; two, implementing universal redundancy insurance; three, introducing interest-free education loans and allowing CPF to be used for postgraduate studies; four, consolidating SWDA into a one-stop shop for employment and upskilling, with dedicated caseworkers; five, collaborating more closely with industry partners to finetune SkillsFuture offerings and curricula; and six, publishing more public outcome data by provider and course.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And to maximise our competitive advantage, we must enable Singaporeans to move confidently from one stage of their working lives to another.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Ideally, the worker should begin re-training or upskilling with a clear idea of the destination ahead, he or she should be able to see, right from the start, a credible career bridge, rather than resting on some vague hope that re-training will lead to some hazy notion of somewhere better.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: With that, I reiterate my support for the original Motion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: I would first like to declare my interest as a faculty member at an autonomous university.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It also calls for a more dynamic enterprise base, stronger support for career transitions and AI that augments workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The movers of the original Motion have described it as complementary to, but distinct from, the ESR.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And I agree with many of the aspirations in paragraph (a) of the Motion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Entrepreneurs should be able to experiment, businesses should have room to succeed and workers should thrive and innovation should flourish.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But agreement with those aspirations is not the same as support for the original framing of the Motion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: My concern is that the wording does not adequately address the trade-offs involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: I will begin with fairness, then turn to enterprise dynamism and the relationship between workers and innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: A more equal outcome is not always a fairer one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Equal pay for equal work may be fair, but we also give more help to households with greater needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It can also be fair to reward greater contribution or responsible risk-taking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The appropriate principle really depends on the issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: So, the question is not simply whether outcomes are equal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: This does not mean we should simply accept inequality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Large differences in income and wealth can generate wide social and economic costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: They can entrench advantage, weaken mobility and leave people with very different capacities to pursue opportunities or recover from setbacks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Where essential costs overwhelm lower-income households, greater support should be provided.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Where family resources determine access to education or career opportunities, the pathways available to those with fewer means should be widened.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: So, the response to the social and economic costs of inequality should be to target those specific costs, rather than assume that equality is always the appropriate remedy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: We should also not only look at the distribution of wealth, but also, at how that wealth is put to use.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: This points to a broader understanding of inclusion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: People should not only have access to opportunity at the outset; they should have the ability to change direction throughout their lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The ESR's proposal for proactive career bridges for workers in at-risk roles is an important step in that direction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And I would extend the same principle more broadly – across education and work, employment and entrepreneurship, and transitions between different careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Consider university students who discover during their first year that they have chosen the wrong course.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But the ability to correct an early mismatch can then depend on family means.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: This is not a case for unlimited switching or subsidy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It is about ensuring that an early mismatch does not become financially irreversible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It may also reduce the pressure on families to secure the "right" course at the first attempt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Our systems can sometimes behave like conveyor belts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: They work very efficiently when the destination is known, but they are a lot less forgiving when someone needs to change direction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: So, a more adaptable system should allow people to switch pathways without losing all the progress they have already made.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: That is how I would calibrate the Motion's reference to inclusion: not identical journeys or destinations, but real opportunities to change directions as people develop.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The ESR is right to emphasise enterprise renewal, including restructuring and exit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, enterprise dynamism must work for people too, not just for capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Experimentation involves uncertainty, so some ventures will pivot, others will end.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And when that happens, the learning should not be lost and the entrepreneur should not be permanently penalised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: A worker who leaves a job to pursue a venture should be able to return to employment, regardless of the venture's eventual outcome.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Employers should recognise the judgement and practical experience gained, rather than viewing that period as a blemish in that person's career.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, business success should not be defined only by scale or profitability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Its value lies not only in its commercial activity, but also in the skills and opportunities it helps create.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Bettr Group reminds us that enterprise dynamism should make room for a wider range of enterprises and forms of value.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: A healthy economy should allow experimentation and exit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It should also give enterprises that create wider societal value a fair opportunity to develop.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And so, my final point concerns the Motion's call for opportunities for workers to thrive and for ideas and innovation to flourish.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Both the proposed and amended Motions' use of the word "thrive" is one I support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It sets a higher aspiration than simply keeping people employed and it is worth striving for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Workers should be engaged in their work and able to build a good life through it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: As routine tasks become more automatable, workers will need to exercise more judgement and deal with problems that do not have formulaic answers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Workers must be willing to apply what they have learnt and take on new responsibilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Employers, in turn, can decide how technology changes work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: They can use it mainly to do the same work with fewer people, or they can use it to help the organisation grow and create more valuable roles for workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: This does not mean preserving every task or preventing disruption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It means that workers should take responsibility for adapting, while employers should use innovation not merely to reduce costs, but to grow the organisation and share the resulting benefits with those who produce them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It is with compressing distinct principles and trade-offs into a single proposition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But inequality should not become a lasting barrier to opportunity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Enterprise dynamism requires room for experimentation and exit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: I would have preferred a more nuanced and calibrated formulation, one that preserves its aspirations while making the trade-offs and responsibilities clearer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The full report of the ESR released on 24 June goes to the heart of what kind of economy and what kind of society we want to build for Singapore and for our workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is situated within a world increasingly shaped by AI, technological disruption, geopolitical fragmentation and intensifying economic competition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, the ESR speaks extensively about jobs and strengthening resilience, with section (b) of the report specifically devoted to it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My speech expands on this and will focus on worker resilience, the reality of how retrenchment hits our workers and how we can better support them, because a resilient economy cannot be built on the backs of insecure workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is why I believe the time has come for Singapore to legislate minimum retrenchment benefits, a subject I have pursued previously in this House, most recently in April this year, and separately, in the context of the ongoing review of the Employment Act.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In advocating for the legislation of retrenchment benefits, my speech will cover four broad sections: first, I will provide an overview of the retrenchment situation in Singapore; second, I will summarise the legal position on retrenchment benefits in Singapore. thirdly, I will explain why retrenchment benefits are important for workers; and fourthly, I will address the common reasons against the legislation of retrenchment benefits and how they should be reviewed in light of the ESR's broader recommendations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Last Friday, The Straits Times published an article titled "Singapore adds more jobs in Q2 even as retrenchments rose".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Over the last 12 months, Lazada, Gardenia, Shopee, Asia Pacific Breweries, Agoda, DHL and Yeo Hiap Seng are just some of the household names that have announced retrenchments, which made the headlines in Singapore, with some moving operations across the border to Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2024, the major technology companies in Singapore such as Meta, Tiktok, Dyson, Microsoft and Google collectively cut at least 9,000 jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This bodes well for a baseline legislated minimum retrenchment benefits starting point for all workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This data point provided by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM), however, does not specifically reveal how many workers receive the unionised norm of one month's salary for every year of service, although I understand this is not uncommon in many collective agreements.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is not a small number by any stretch.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Outside contract, retrenchment benefits remain largely governed by tripartite norms and employer practices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To receive retrenchment benefits, workers in Singapore are dependent on the goodwill of employers, the terms of their employment contracts, or the strength of their bargaining position after they have already lost their jobs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This legislative omission in our employment laws sits in stark contrast to the reality our workers face as set out by the ESR report: first, that Singaporeans should not assume that economic growth will automatically result in the same extent of job creation as before; and secondly, that despite Singapore's positive employment situation, worker anxiety has increased across a wide range of sectors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I now move on to the second section of my speech on the legal position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's courts and tribunals have reaffirmed a legal position that does not sit easily with workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In JIF v JIG, the Employment Claims Tribunal held that section 45 of the Employment Act does not create a statutory entitlement to retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The tribunal held that retrenchment benefits are payable only when they arise from a contract of employment, collective agreement, or some other legal basis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Tripartite guidelines do not create such a legal basis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, this position can be traced back to the Court of Appeals decision in Bethlehem Singapore Pte Ltd v Ler Hock Seng, which made it clear that section 45 does not compel employers to pay retrenchment benefits simply because an employee has completed a qualifying period of service.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The significance of the tribunal judgment in particular is magnified by its timing and it forces us to confront an important policy question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the very moment, the ESR is asking Singaporeans to prepare for an era of more frequent restructuring, more rapid technological disruption and greater economic uncertainty, the Courts have reminded us that workers facing retrenchment possess no general statutory entitlement to retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The question before Parliament is whether the law remains adequate for workers and the economy that the ESR hopes to evince.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my view, the law has fallen behind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: China legislates economic compensation for workers affected by redundancy and restructuring.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: South Korea imposes significant legal requirements before redundancies may be carried out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These countries differ enormously in their political systems, labour markets and stages of economic development.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet they have all reached a common conclusion: business flexibility for employers and worker protection are not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I now move on to my third section on why retrenchment benefits are crucial for our workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Retrenchment benefits matter because they support workers and their families precisely at the stage of life when financial obligations can often be at their greatest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They represent an important layer of support provided by employers, complementing taxpayer-funded assistance such as the Jobseeker Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the Singapore context, this additional financial relief is especially important, given how leveraged many households are.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Outside these age bands, when a worker in his 50s loses his or her job, the consequences extend far beyond immediate income loss.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Retrenchment is not merely a labour market issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For many, it is also a retirement adequacy issue, a housing issue, a family issue and a social stability issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As Singapore transits towards a high wage, high-cost economy, the effects of retrenchment will become even more severe, if workers are unable to secure employment at a comparable income level.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The mental health dimension of job loss and financial insecurity cannot be understated either.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Taxpayers are playing their part financing the Jobseeker Support Scheme, and the Government and Labour Movement are devoting significant resources towards retraining.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The fourth section of my speech will deal with the arguments against the legislation of retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Throughout Singapore's history, many worker protections were initially criticised as threats to business competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When Workfare was introduced, concerns were raised about costs, even as Workfare was taxpayer-funded.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When the progressive wage model was expanded, concerns were raised about costs, especially after Government wage support tapers off.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When platform workers were granted stronger protections, concerns were again raised about costs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, when the Government announced the review of the Employment Act last year, the Singapore National Employers' Federation cautioned that the review should not, and I quote, "inadvertently mandate progressive employment practices that may reduce flexibilities for employers and undermine business competitiveness".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet, advancing major pro-worker reforms are always important because economic growth alone is never enough.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, we regard things like Workfare as part of a mature and balanced economic system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Retrenchment benefits should be viewed in exactly the same way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Over the years, MOM has advanced several arguments against legislating retrenchment benefits for our workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the risks it has hitherto identified should be carefully examined and weighed afresh against the increasingly unpredictable economic landscape facing workers in the years ahead, as outlined by the ESR report.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first argument is that mandatory retrenchment benefits may make employers more hesitant to offer long-term or permanent employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet, the existence of mandatory retrenchment benefits in many economies, including advanced economies, has not eliminated permanent employment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is clear that such demands are influenced by a range of factors, including labour demand, skills and manpower shortages, productivity and broader labour market regulations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the Singapore context, a generally tight labour market could have the opposite effect with employers competing to hire the best with a permanent contract, an important lure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, the Government has argued that legislating a minimum retrenchment benefit may result in employers converging on that very minimum.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the facts do not fully support this concern.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are already collective agreements that prescribe retrenchment benefits and the vast majority of employers converge at those benchmarks anyway, with a very small number paying more than the one-month norm for each year of service.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is therefore not obvious that legislation would necessarily result in a different status quo with employers prevented from paying a higher amount should they deem it appropriate to do so.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This concern must be weighed against the reality that financial difficulty does not automatically extinguish obligations of distress firms, such as unpaid wages, CPF contributions, taxes, supplier debts or bank loans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Businesses do also account for employee leave encashment, gratuity obligations, contractual liabilities and debt repayments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Retrenchment benefits can be similarly treated as a foreseeable employment cost as they are today by progressive employers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, this argument assumes that retrenchments only occur when companies are losing money.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many retrenchments occur when profitable firms restructure, automate functions, consolidate operations, relocate activities or seek to improve profitability – as we have seen in Singapore over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In such circumstances, retrenchment is often a strategic business decision rather than a last resort.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, this helps explain why some unions have successfully negotiated for enhanced retrenchment benefits in the absence of statutory protection, precisely because not all firms retrench workers due to financial distress.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Like earlier efforts to strengthen worker protection, legislating retrenchment benefits will inevitably attract concerns from businesses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As I mentioned earlier, this can serve as the starting point for legislative retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would largely formalise an existing practice while ensuring that workers who fall through the gap that cannot be bridged by non-binding tripartite guidelines are protected.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Responsible employers would no longer be disadvantaged relative to those who provide the bare minimum or nothing at all.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The ability of smaller employers to pay retrenchment benefits often comes up as a concern against legislating retrenchment benefits completely.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The concerns of these small businesses are not irrelevant or unimportant.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A business with a revenue of half a million dollars is certainly a different enterprise compared to one that records $50 million in revenue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Various countries address this particular issue differently, even as they legislate for retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are not uncharted waters, and a perfect legislative retrenchment benefits regime does not need to be the enemy of a good regime that protects more workers than it does today in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The ESR calls on more international enterprises to set up regional headquarters Singapore and is fundamentally an economic plan for the future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It sees international trust in the Singapore brand as a strategic asset that Singapore rightly seeks to leverage in advancing its economic value proposition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet that trust hosts an important domestic dimension that builds that very Singapore brand.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I support the original Motion in the names of Members Kenneth Tiong and Jamus Lim, which calls for an inclusive and equal economy for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have been in session for close to five and a half hours, so I propose to take a break.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.00 pm until 4.20 pm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is, without doubt, critical for Singapore to sustain an inclusive and dynamic economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We are building on firm foundations and the ESR provides a robust blueprint to take our economy forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: That said, more ideas to spur inclusive economic growth should be welcome.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: There are many dimensions to this Motion and I will focus my remarks on our workforce and people as the key to an inclusive and dynamic economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, the main channel through which economic growth benefits Singaporeans is good jobs and incomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This remains the central socio-economic strategy, as affirmed in the recent debate in this House on an AI transition with no jobless growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: While we will have to consider new ways to strengthen social support and protection, and to step up redistribution for more equitable outcomes, we must continue to prioritise employment and good jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The first limb of today's Parliamentary Motion speaks of providing opportunities for workers to thrive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is worth reflecting on what this means.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: To me, it means that workers are not locked into pre-set pathways or dead-end jobs on their basis of the past educational qualifications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, they must have opportunities to continually grow and develop in their careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It also means that workers are not confined to tasks that are mundane or repetitive because all the interesting work has been taken over by AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, workers must have autonomy to express their talent and creativity, and to find meaning and self-actualisation in their work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore tops the world in test scores of 15-year-olds, but can we top the world in the skills and learning agility of 45-year-olds?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We should set our sights high, not just to have the world's best students, but also to have the world's most agile, adaptable and innovative workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We must reaffirm that people are our key competitive advantage, and not just technology or infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we often say that people are our only resource, hence, the sustained investment the Government has put into education and human capital development through the years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Today, it is not just about developing hard skills and competencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The human skills, or critical core skills, are coming to the fore, and the meta-skill of learning to learn is perhaps the most important of all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We need to emphasise learning agility and adaptability amid disruption, and dynamic innovation beyond static excellence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: AI and automation will analyse and execute, but it is human beings who set the agenda, prioritise tasks, frame the questions, weigh up the options that AI suggests, make decisions and ultimately, take responsibility for outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: All this requires judgement and creativity rooted in continual learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As individuals, we must get out of our comfort zones to seek new opportunities to learn and grow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We must also plan for our careers and invest in our career health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We should not limit ourselves to being just students, employees, freelancers or employers at any one time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone can be a worker-learner and a worker-entrepreneur.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: And because learning never stops, there should be no hard boundary between Pre-employment Training and Continuing Education and Training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: And everyone, regardless of occupation, needs to have the mindset and instincts of an entrepreneur to contribute and succeed in the future economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Second, let us focus on what organisations can do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: They must transform to activate the skills of the workforce and unleash the creativity of their people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, the gains from training and reskilling will not be fully realised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Learning must therefore be dovetailed with organisational strategy and not treated as a standalone activity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Enterprises must become learning enterprises, where learning is embedded in corporate DNA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is important that employers conduct regular structured career conversations with employees across all career stages and not just older workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Such conversations help individuals understand the strengths, aspirations and development opportunities, while enabling organisations to better develop and deploy talent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In a complex and uncertain environment, it is particularly important for workers to make sense of the evolving context and to be empowered to co-create solutions with opportunities to hone their instincts and build their confidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Workers' tacit knowledge is also valuable in human-centric work redesign, where involving workers in redesigning work can lead to greater ownership and better outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Third, a refreshed, integrated work and learning ecosystem is necessary to foster an agile, adaptable and innovative workforce, along with a labour market characterised by quality jobs, skills alignment and strong labour mobility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: There is generous support for training and reskilling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We have a common skills taxonomy and a Careers and Skills Passport that support skills certification, recognition and portability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: There is also a network of training providers whose quality standards are closely monitored.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Labour market intelligence is made available to individuals, firms and training providers via a suite of online tools and dashboards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: First, I think we need to accelerate efforts at making skills-first practices more prevalent and indeed, the default for firms and organisations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we need to develop robust skills credentialing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Today, there is a gap in the Careers and Skills Passport in that it primarily captures formal training and credentials, along with work experience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As workplace learning becomes an increasingly important part of lifelong learning, we need to be able to assess and recognise skills acquired on-the-job and demonstrable at the workplace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This is important, as a more complete skills passport would enable and encourage adoption of skills-first practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: IHLs, too, can support this by designing student testimonials to better reflect skills acquired through coursework, internships and co-curricular activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Third, there is a need to support enterprises in becoming learning organisations by providing practical tool kits and resources to strengthen organisational capabilities, while helping leaders, HR and organisational development professionals place learning at the heart of organisational strategy and unlock the potential of their workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, there is scope to further invest in personalised career guidance and job-matching capabilities, not just recommending jobs based on skills, but also on values, aspirations and personality fit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: A senior consultant psychiatrist recently told me that job fit is a major factor for human health and happiness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: He observed that different kinds of work may be better suited to different personability types.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Forcing a square peg into a round hole may lead to stress, burnout and poor mental health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Conversely, a good job fit is likely to result in personal fulfilment, more engaged and energised workers along with higher productivity and creativity on the job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: A more comprehensive and effective system of career coaching and guidance, not just for displaced workers but also for those in employment, can moreover support better career health and resilience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Fifth, we can strengthen support for micro entrepreneurship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Thanks to AI, individuals can now put their business ideas to the test with much lower barriers to market entry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Every chief HR officer I spoke with recently has shared that one of the central challenges facing their organisation is AI and its impact on work and their workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In this new reality of rapidly advancing AI, no organisation or government has all the answers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We need to experiment, test, iterate and scale up what works in AI-enabled learning, work redesign and employability across a range of sectors and organisation types.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We should bring to Singapore the world's leading experts – not just academic researchers but practice-oriented academics who can bridge the world of academia and industry with timely research that informs practice in a fast-changing landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Let us match our ambition for our workforce with sustained investment in expertise and capability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Our guiding star should be to give our people the best chance of succeeding and contributing in the AI age, which is critical to a dynamic and inclusive economy and fundamental to renewing our social compact.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This resulted in vast improvement of the quality of life for large swathes of our population.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For many, the promise of a better future for our next generation was a beacon of hope for which we worked towards.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, in recent years, it is not unheard of for our residents to ask: should economic growth be our ultimate endgame?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The latest ESR report provides us a valuable opportunity for reflection and to rethink what progress means to Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But at a time when retrenchments dominate newspaper headlines, anxious residents worry about unstable livelihoods and our little red dot feels ever-rising heat from climate change, it is timely for us to think how we can put economic growth in service of broader societal progress.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need a Singapore economy that provides breathing room for each and every one of our people to be the best version of ourselves.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A few years back, I spoke about Kate Raworth's concept of doughnut economics, which envisions an economy that places at its heart a collective well-being and equality to achieve a safe and just space for humanity whilst protecting our earth from further environmental destruction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our economic policies must embody an ethos of equity, and collective and planetary well-being while providing opportunities for all in our society to thrive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I will address three key areas today towards this goal: first, tackling our care system; second, providing the right ecosystem for creatives and entrepreneurs to thrive; and third, protecting our planet.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If our economy is to be rooted in equity and collective well-being, we must first look at who determines how our economic pie is sliced.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even as we recognise their insights, organisations representing migrant workers, women's rights and persons with disabilities should also have been more clearly represented.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our economic trajectory must be shaped by the people, with the people and for the people.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Diversity and perspective, representing the diverse stakeholders in our economy, must be used to identify potential blind spots and marginalised communities, and how these diverse communities live and experience our policies, economic and otherwise.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When we talk about economic contribution, our economic structure often focuses on the elite worlds of finance, tech and commerce.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, our economy is kept dynamic by a very diverse group of professionals whose contributions are invaluable for their collective economic success.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In particular, our care economy comprising both paid and unpaid labour in childcare, eldercare, healthcare and various social services.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A foundational building block for any economy, our care infrastructure is what leads to the broader growth, well-being and human development for current and future generations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Building our care infrastructure must be seen as a priority, not just an afterthought, a problem to fix due to demographic changes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many proposals were raised, such as job redesign, clarifying progression pathways, and strengthening skills development and certification.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: An example can be seen in action by the UK's latest attempt to reform social care, which is envisaged to be a long and costly process involving difficult decisions even as there is room for statements that carers need to be the best paid in society rather than the worst.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet even in Singapore, wage support is solely needed for our caregivers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These numbers are lower than the overall median gross monthly income from employment of $5,775.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even as we acknowledge that wage support is overdue, care workers must also be better acknowledged and supported for their invaluable contribution towards our society, regardless of their ability to weather AI-induced disruptions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Wages in the care economy must commensurate with the rising cost of living.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We also need to address the heavy emotional toll faced by care workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Another study conducted in the second half of 2024 in our National University Polyclinics also found that nearly 10% of participants stated that they intended to leave their current position in the next six months.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The authors of the study found this concerning, noting that the resignation rate of healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic was just 4%.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just as the Law Society recently started to review the prevailing work culture for lawyers, it is time for our regulatory bodies to work with industry and non-governmental organisations in care economy segments to officially track workplace well-being and examine prevailing workplace standards.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Support for local entrepreneurship in the care economy is also key.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The care economy is highly labour-intensive, and our general grant supporting capital needs in entrepreneurship and capability building needs closer scrutiny.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The efforts of our caregivers often come at a cost – sacrificing health, careers and leisure time to care for loved ones.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also why I have been calling since 2020 for official regular time-use studies for us to better understand our carers' needs and to measure the hidden economic and personal costs behind care.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Carers also need better support, which is why our Party's manifesto has called for, amongst others, compensation for family caregivers and the expansion of respite care.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore must bridge the gap of seeing care beyond being a cost.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must see caregiving as a growth segment that builds not just the economy of today, but the society of tomorrow.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our society of tomorrow must also support creatives and entrepreneurs who dare to dream and pursue their own passions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How do we ensure that our local entrepreneurs and dreamers can have their passion made possible in Singapore?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To create the conditions for entrepreneurship to grow, we must first, as a society, foster a culture of self-discovery and exploration from young.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Expanding entrepreneurship-related programmes in schools and encouraging critical thinking and empathy as prescribed in the ESR report only goes so far if our system does not reward risk-taking or having room to make mistakes and learn.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How do we explain the gap between the decades' long efforts to build an education system to be more holistic against the reality that these additional layers simply create new pathways for education arms races?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What do we need to do to address parents' or would-be parents' fears for the next generation in an age of million-dollar HDB resale prices, ever-soaring Certificate of Entitlement prices and the never-ending sense of scarcity?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While this is a whole other topic, it is relevant to our economic policies for the future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For today, I would like to instead focus on our creatives and entrepreneurs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They turn ideas into commercial and cultural value and inspire the wonder that a thriving society needs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet a career in the arts remains a difficult choice in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Regulatory hurdles have forced artists to alter or remove public artworks while beloved art spaces have shuttered under rising costs and redevelopment pressures.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They kill the very activity we say we want to nurture.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The one-off Culture Pass is only a first step.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What our creatives need is sustained support, dedicated work, display and commercial spaces to hone their craft and earn a decent living, backed by sensible commercial space regulations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These should sit alongside spaces for budding entrepreneurs, much like the creative and cultural parks we see in cities, such as Beijing and Taipei, proof that culture and commerce can thrive side by side.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, supporting the growth ambitions of our businesses, large and small.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
