text: Small home-based businesses can be a testbed for aspiring founders to launch businesses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But the next step is often daunting, with commercial overheads quickly becoming prohibitive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Can the Government, across agencies, provide more affordable short-term stalls and shop spaces across HDB, URA and JTC-managed properties for first-time entrepreneurs, taking inspiration from the now ubiquitous shared office facilities to offer smaller modular units with lower renovation and deposit requirements and allow tendency periods that are shorter or easier contractual conditions for potential exit?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Together with the Equity Market Development Programme, this can improve liquidity in our domestic equity market and attract more liquidity into these companies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such companies should also be explicitly tracked on the impact they have beyond returns, for example, their contribution to activity and employment in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is similar in spirit to Ireland's Strategic Investment Fund which has a double bottom-line mandate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To further encourage would-be entrepreneurs, we also need an ecosystem with structural measures to protect necessary risk-taking for success.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After I spoke in early May this year about supporting entrepreneurship amongst youths, including a call to adapt our current bankruptcy framework, a Straits Times' article on 26 May indicated that business failure is among the top reasons why individuals go into personal bankruptcy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, working out a bankruptcy is often difficult, with practical limits on day-to-day activities and no automatic discharge.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This can hold back those with bold ideas from taking the plunge.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Pro-data reforms have been found to be linked to better entrepreneurship and innovation outcomes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I will thus repeat our call to see if our bankruptcy regime can be reformed to encourage more would-be entrepreneurs to step up.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the relentless pursuit of economic growth on this planet has resulted in the over extraction of precious natural resources, damaged ecosystems and disruption to communities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thrust 8 of the ESR recommended that businesses prepare for a low-carbon and climate-resilient future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Noticeably, a heavy emphasis was placed on preparing businesses to shield themselves from the harmful effects of climate change, while not acknowledging that historically, it has been corporations and industrial development that have been the very reason we are now experiencing planetary distress.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need more attention and details on how our policies will make our enterprises and economies to be part of the solution to climate change, particularly in Thrust 2 of the ESR involves making Singapore a global leader for AI.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As I said during the debate on Singapore's use of AI, there's undoubtedly potential to harness the power of AI for greater economic and societal good.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, we, at the same time, hear about how low-wage workers, in developing nations are forced to view explicit content to train AI, as well as concerns about adverse effect on cognitive development and critical thinking.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More expressly, data centres driven by AI-induced demand, guzzle up large amounts of energy and water, increasing carbon emissions, driving up utility prices and disrupting the lives of nearby communities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This has caused disamenties for local communities, even prompting a group of Johor residents to protest against the construction of a nearby data centre.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving data centres further away also does not solve the problem.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: During my trip to Thailand in June, I noticed that while policy-makers were excited about investment and growth opportunities for AI in partnership with countries, like Singapore, there were also concerns about the environmental and sustainability impact of such investments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the planned resumption of data centre construction in Singapore requires the use of greener energy sources, how exactly are we balancing the needs for our precious land?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Does this result in land that could otherwise be maintained to be for nature and green spaces to be ultimately razed to meet industrial and housing requirements?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such green spaces are key to bolstering our heat resilience and are rapidly disappearing in the name of growth and economic survival.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Intensifying business and industrial operations ultimately affect our energy consumption.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The situation is worse for water, particularly with data centres being huge consumers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What are we doing to mitigate this impact?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even before we craft our policies to address the impact on the climate, we must first measure the environmental impact.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As I first mentioned during my Budget speech in 2022, a critical first step will be to track and monitor our policies, environmental outcomes via an environmental dashboard.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This could be aided by the recent introduction of the Singapore classification for environmental purposes, which is used to classify data relating to environmental activities and products.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We would do well to remember that Mother Earth is not humankind's personal automated teller machine (ATM).

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must ensure that our economic policies should not result in further destruction of our planet and a transparent accounting of its environmental outcomes would be a helpful tool keep us on our toes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Progress means that we, as a society, support balance and well-rounded lifestyles with strong safety nets for our people, recognise all who contribute meaningfully to society, provide opportunities for everyone to dream big and uphold our responsibility as stewards of Mother Earth.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The society of tomorrow that is built in Singapore must be one where all of us will thrive and enjoy the fruits of our effort together, and I believe that we can achieve that, and so much more for us and the generations that come.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The aspirations expressed in this Motion to support local businesses – help workers succeed, build a Singaporean footprint overseas and ensure shared prosperity – are aspirations that all of us in this Chamber can support.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Indeed, these have been central to the work of NTUC and the Labour Movement, our unions and our tripartite partners for many decades.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are also aligned with the spirit and direction of the ESR.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For many Singaporean workers and business owners, the future economy is already being felt in very real ways in uncertain demand, rising costs, sharper competition, new technologies and industries that are changing faster than ever before.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am now into my 25th year in NTUC, and currently serve as the Executive Secretary of the United Workers of Electronics and Electrical Industries (UWEEI).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Over the more than two decades, I have walked with workers through many storms, from Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS), to the Global Financial Crisis to the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Every transition was painful in its own way.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But the lesson was the same: workers must never be treated as collateral damage in economic change.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At every phase of Singapore's development, we needed clear national direction and most importantly, the assurance that those who work hard, adapt and contribute will not be left behind.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The ESR is our latest national roadmap to create a broader range of good jobs, stronger enterprises and growth that benefits Singaporeans fairly and tangibly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Today, I want to focus on three priorities, what I call the "3S" that are essential to build an economy that works for all.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First "S", safeguard the rules; second, share the gains; and third, strengthening our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Part (a) of the Motion speaks of an economy where "workers thrive".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They need fair rules, fair opportunity and fair protection.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: When the economy changes faster than workers can adapt, many feel that the odds are stacked against them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our duty is to level the playing field for them to compete fairly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It can raise productivity and create new possibilities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But if poorly managed, it can also widen insecurity, compress career pathways and place too much risk on workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Workers must not be asked to carry the burden of this transition alone.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: NTUC and the Labour Movement, including many of our union leaders and unions, we have been negotiating collective agreements, unionising companies to ensure that they are well protected in the event that there is a lay-off and retrenchment benefits can be paid out.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In fact, we have such strong existing mechanisms, such as conciliation and MOM, and even the Industrial Arbitration Court – very unique, creature of statute – which I appeared before on multiple occasions to support and obtain retrenchment benefit payouts for workers, including PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is in the common intent of everyone, I am sure, in this House, to ensure that affected workers are taken care of as every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These are things that we have been raising and I believe it is a journey, a journey which require all our tripartite partners to work closely together so that we achieve what we always say, a win-win-win outcome.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is always in the NTUC's and the Labour Movement's interest in our agenda to look after workers and their families, especially if they are affected by lay-offs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And there are a whole plethora of measures and support measures to help them land the next job, support them well in the company as well as on many occasions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I have done this, in fact, in the last couple of years in my capacity as Executive Secretary of the UWEEI, I have been very, very involved in the many lay-offs that you see in the manufacturing sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The key is, we will continue to lobby, advocate on behalf of our workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But more importantly, to work with our tripartite partners closely to ensure that we have the regime and the mechanism.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We are also observing that the tripartite partners are very open to see new ways and mechanisms to overcome this to ensure no worker is left behind in the event of a lay-off or retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: What is unique about the scheme is that, unlike in an unemployment insurance, where there are premiums to be paid by both employers and employees, this is a situation where Government picks up the tab and gives that needed support through and with active labour market policies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: That is something which will lessen the burden on workers having to fork out premiums.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Or even another new scheme to support PMEs now that we know they are equally vulnerable as rank-and-file workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Local PMEs, I must say are a definite group which I have constantly spoken up for in this House.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They form the broad middle of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are also those most exposed to technical or, should I say, technological disruption and yet, may not always enjoy sufficient representation and protection.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Over the years, NTUC has worked closely with our tripartite partners to build stronger institutional safeguards, for example the Complementarity Assessment Framework (COMPASS) framework for Employment Passes to the newly enacted Workplace Fairness Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am therefore heartened that the ESR recognises PMEs as a group deserving enhanced support and that it prioritises investment in AI technologies that augment rather than displace workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Initiated by NTUC, this Jobs Council brings together unions, employers and Government as a central node to coordinate existing and new programmes to help workers reskill, and to help businesses redesign jobs responsibly so that AI becomes a tool for uplift, not displacement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I think the difficulty of landing a new job is not a new discovery – I have raised this on numerous occasions – and we must pay particular attention to younger PMEs entering the workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They may be among the hardest-hit if AI compresses entry-level roles and creates a "broken rung" of sorts at the very start of their careers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And we unanimously agreed that if our young graduates cannot get that first meaningful foothold, their long-term progression may be affected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We cannot allow the first step of a career to become the weakest link in our labour market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is why I have lobbied also for, in this House, coaching, mentoring and expanding the SkillsFuture credits for use in the area of coaching and mentoring which has been supported, and really to have a stronger mechanism to help those transiting from school to work effectively, efficiently and seamlessly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Through the GRIT programme, NTUC works hand-in-hand with Government and employers in sectors such as financial services, information and communication technology, manufacturing to give young graduates structured, industry-relevant experience.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Beyond the traineeship period, NTUC and Workforce Singapore, through the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) and Careers Connect, help these young workers move into full-time roles and build confidence with AI tools so that they are not just job-ready for today, but career-ready for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And I have suggested for this scheme before in this House to be further expanded, to cover more areas, more sectors and maybe a review of whether it should be made permanent to really help new job entrants entering the job market which remains an issue and challenge.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Part (b) rightly highlights the importance of healthy domestic demand.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But for a small and open economy like Singapore, external demand is equally critical.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am glad that the ESR has identified a dynamic enterprise ecosystem for Singapore-based companies to succeed globally as a key thrust.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Domestic demand and external demand are not competing choices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The real test is whether that growth translates into better jobs, higher wages, stronger skills, and expanded opportunities for Singaporean workers and local businesses.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Global enterprises locate in Singapore not only for our domestic market, but to tap growth in Asia and beyond.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But if Singapore is to remain a trusted global node, our workers must also move up the value chain.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is where the NTUC Company Training Committees (CTCs), play a critical role.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: When companies modernise or adopt new technologies, our unions sit down with management to ensure workers are trained for higher-value roles and that productivity gains are reflected not only in company results, but also in workers' pay packets and career progression.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Through a CTC Grant project, a company introduced automation to its production process so it could take on more orders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is what real sharing of gains look like.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Not theoretical redistribution, but negotiated, sustainable outcomes where better productivity leads to better pay.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This works in tandem with the National Wages Council, a tripartite body which responds to the uneven and sometimes unpredictable outlook for different sectors and different companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The last "S" is strengthen our Singaporean core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As our economy globalises, we must ensure that Singaporeans are not bystanders to our own success.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need both global enterprises with substantial operations here, and dynamic local companies with the ambition to venture abroad.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But wherever Singaporean capital flows, Singaporean talent must flow too – to lead, not just to support.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Singaporeans must have a fair shot at leadership, regional exposure and global careers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Local SMEs cannot grow well and grow fast on the domestic market alone.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In high-tech manufacturing and commercial services, many local firms have scaled by first becoming trusted partners to global MNCs based in Singapore; then, using that credibility to venture into overseas markets, including high-tech and industrial parks in Southeast Asia, China, and India.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They build operational strength at home so that they can seize opportunities abroad.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Enterprise Development Grant supports SMEs in building core capabilities to compete internationally.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These schemes help our local enterprises take the first step ahead with greater confidence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But as Singaporean capital expands overseas, we must be intentional about building Singaporean corporate leaders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our workers and PMEs must not only support regionalisation from the back office.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is work that NTUC and our unions have carried out for decades, sometimes visibly, sometimes quietly, but always with one purpose – which is to safeguard the rights, wages, welfare and work prospects of our workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In fact, I want to use this opportunity to thank my fellow union leaders who stand in line, to lend a hand, to watch their backs, give a shoulder to cry on sometimes in events of ups and downs in the economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But make no mistake – tripartism is not easy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Balancing the needs of workers, businesses and the nation is not easy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But precisely because it is hard, it forces us to find practical solutions that endure.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The ESR gives Singapore a comprehensive roadmap to stay globally competitive.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our task is to make sure that this roadmap is also worker-centric, inclusive and fair.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: So, let us continue to strengthen this practical, tripartite partnership.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Let us Safeguard the rules, Share the Gains, and Strengthen our Singaporean Core anchored by strong and lasting tripartite relationships.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I support the amendments by hon Member Edward Chia to the Motion.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last July, the Prime Minister noted that the Association of Southeast Asian Nations' (ASEAN's) per capita GDP today is around $6,000.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And that if it reaches $10,000 or more, it is, in his words, a complete game changer.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A young region, a rising middle class on our doorstep.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The latest ESR report identifies Southeast Asia as an engine of growth.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Emerging Stronger Taskforce in 2021, under its Stronger Together pillar, had called for the deepening of partnerships, especially with Southeast Asia.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So did the Committee on the Future Economy in 2017, in the first of seven strategies.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Every major economic blueprint of the past decade has named the region as key to Singapore's future.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the question is not whether Southeast Asia matters.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have consensus that it does, but what have we actually done about it?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Motion believes that an economy of the future that works for all includes an economic engine driven by Singaporeans and Singaporean capital venturing abroad.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ESR is explicit about the latter and several Members of the House have echoed this.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The report asks that more of our own companies start, scale and succeed globally.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It seeks deeper trade and supply chain links across the region and it envisions a Singapore where capital is raised, structured, deployed and recycled across the region and the world.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Around each sits a familiar architecture of support, grants and market entry support for our companies, while our public institutions co-invest, de-risk and finance their expansion, which draws private Singaporean capital out alongside them.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The WP supports all of this, but capital does not manage itself in a market it does not know.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Someone has to be there to turn capital that has been deployed into capital that is productive.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The more successful we are at sending capital and our companies into the region, the more pressing the question that ESR does not answer: who are we sending with it?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two weekends ago, the Government unveiled the new SG Youth Plan.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A separate blueprint for young Singaporeans just a month after the ESR report, guided by the same conviction that our future lies in the region.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It picks up on this threat that the ESR left hanging.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If half of us are already willing to go, then what we should be looking at is whether the state invests in building us something worth going to and something worth coming back to.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And on this note, I want to highlight three gaps.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SG Youth Plan outlines a game plan focused on supply.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Every one of its regional commitments is about sending young Singaporeans out.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But what happens when we come home is the most decisive, because if we return to a job market and promotion board that treats six months in Jakarta as a detour rather than an asset, then only one obvious conclusion will be drawn – that such experiences are a penalty rather than a premium.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do enough employers in Singapore value and reward regional experience?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I cannot speak for all employers, I would like to share a perspective from our largest employer, the Government.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In April, I filed a Parliamentary Question asking where Government scholars have studied in the past decade.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also asked if there were minimum targets for scholars to study in non-English speaking countries and or regions.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not doubting the quality of an Oxford, Cambridge or an Ivy League education, but these numbers mean that when we select and invest in young Singaporeans who will return to serve in the Public Service, a small group of whom might even take public office in the future, 10 out of 20 of them stay home, while another nine go west.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Government is not prioritising and encouraging region readiness in the Public Service, how can we ask young Singaporeans to believe that there is market demand for this?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Exposure does not equal fluency or capability – 17,000 young Singaporeans spending some time in the region is not 17,000 region-ready Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SG Youth Plan included the story of an Institute of Technical Education student who came home after being sent to Hanoi.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: She was more confident and eager to explore opportunities beyond our shores.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Real region readiness is built over years, not weeks.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The language learnt, the workings of the market understood from the inside, the network that answers when you call.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Have we invested sufficiently in structures that will deepen this?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we are serious, is it not time to ask whether Thai and Vietnamese also belong on that list?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Language and cultural understanding are often the difference between a visitor and a partner.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third, and perhaps most important, gap is whether and how any of this will be measured.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because we have heard this aspiration before, especially in 2018 during our term as ASEAN Chair.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was appropriately a year of speeches about how the region was our future and how the Government will help Singaporeans seize it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In September 2018, in a written reply to a question on our progress in going regional, then Minister for Trade and Industry, Mr Chan Chun Sing, set out what we were doing for talent.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We had the Youth Talent Programme, which targeted sending 1,000 students each year for work opportunities in overseas markets.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We had a Professional Conversion Programme for Southeast Asia Ready Talent to reskill professionals for roles in the region.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also had an ASEAN Leadership Programme to help senior business leaders understand and grow into Southeast Asian markets.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It appears that the first two, in one form or another, are still with us.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Professional Conversion Programme was renamed and runs today as the Career Conversion Programme for Internationalisation Professionals.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But what is less clear is what outcomes they have achieved eight years on.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The 29,470 figure for the Global Ready Talent Programme includes both domestic and overseas placements.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is only starting this April that local internship support has been discontinued.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And of those who did, where did they go?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many of them went on to work in the region or in a region-facing role?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the Career Conversion Programme, how many professionals converted?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have been generous in announcing schemes to build region-ready Singaporeans but seemingly less willing to measure whether they worked.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some figures that I do have are from the ESR report.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, with the new SG Youth Plan aspiring to 17,000 regional immersion opportunities for young Singaporeans, I would like to ask what has changed this time, so that in 2030 we will be able to say whether it worked.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How will the Government track not just how many places were filled, but how many young people go on to work in region-facing roles or to build a career in the region?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because if not, we are simply announcing a larger number to not measure.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And as we chair ASEAN again in 2027, I hope we will not only articulate our ambition to plug into the region but actively track and report on our investments in resourcing this ambition.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The OMIP aims to give young Singaporeans real regional work experience, not just a taste of it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SG Youth Plan will expand the OMIP, not by scaling it so there are more places but by widening the eligibility by dropping the two-year rule so that younger professionals may qualify.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means more will be eligible without a commitment to send more people.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Widening the gate is not the same as sending more people through it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Eligibility without capacity is an invitation without a seat.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On behalf of fellow young Singaporeans, I have two asks: one, complement the eligibility widening by scaling the number of available places; and two, de-link it from employers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An employer-led scheme means a young Singaporean can only go if a company chooses to send them.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is dependent on the company having the HR capacity to manage an overseas posting.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rather than run a people scheme through companies, let us focus it on the people instead.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fund the OMIP directly as a fixed-term stint, at fair wages, open to all graduates from our tertiary institutions.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us select based on our graduates’ drive, curiosity and seriousness, rather than our companies’ ability to shoulder the administrative burden of overseas postings.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We would not be the first to do this.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: France's Voluntariat International en Enterprise (VIE), the International Corporate Volunteer Programme, proves that it is possible to do more and even shows us how.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The VIE places more than 11,500 young people abroad every year.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can directly search and apply for open positions that range from six to 24 months on the VIE platform.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When selected, these young people sign a contract with Business France, a state agency, instead of the host company.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Business France looks after payroll, health coverage and social protection.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The host company picks the candidate, supervises their work and pays the allowance to Business France.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The state sits in the middle and absorbs the friction that neither an individual nor a small company can carry alone.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the French government has the numbers to prove it because they measured it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More than seven in 10 come back fluent in the language where they were posted.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a scheme that produces more than inspiration.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And tellingly, Singapore is among its top 10 destinations.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are on the receiving end of another country’s talent pipeline but are struggling to build our own.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not saying that we copy the French VIE programme wholesale.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us fund the appetite that young Singaporeans have and measure outcomes rather than output.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And finally, we should go beyond the scheme and consider how we can tear down the wall that young Singaporeans find ourselves up against.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It correctly identifies the very things that weigh on a young person deciding whether to take an overseas work opportunity.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But these are not just facts to be explained.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are structures that will need to change for those who aspire to be regionally mobile.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A young Singaporean weighing three years in Bangkok or Ho Chi Minh is not only weighing salary against salary.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: She is weighing it against a BTO queue that rewards those who stay home; against CPF contributions a regional employer will not make; against the challenges of coming home to a housing and healthcare system she stepped out of.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have built a domestic architecture so finely tuned for staying home that leaving often means accepting penalties.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During his Institute of Policy Studies lectures last year, Mr Philip Yeo acknowledged this wall.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: His account of his EDB years was blunt – send officers out while they are young and single, because by their mid-30s with children and a mortgage, it becomes too hard.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, developing region-ready Singaporeans means we should also consider how we can better support those who choose to go out.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These cost only a fraction of the benefit they could bring and could go a long way to quell a family’s hesitation.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ESR speaks of creating good jobs and the SG Youth Plan echoes it with the moves to help young Singaporeans land them.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But for too long, we have pictured the good job as a high-value role inside an MNC that chose to base itself here, in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a good job that depends on someone else’s decision to come.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is another kind of good job; one we seize because a field is taking shape around us and Singapore is well placed to lead it – the growing social impact sector in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And here, I declare my interest as a professional in the social impact space.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the public and private sectors in the region turn towards impact to close gaps in issues ranging from health and education to financial inclusion and climate resilience, someone has to convene players, develop benchmarks and innovate for solutions.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are building blocks of a new pool of good jobs that a small country like Singapore can punch above our weight in.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it is also the kind of ambition that goes unrealised if we do not build a pipeline to seize it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For years, our answer to the regional talent gap has been to draw in the region’s brightest, educate them here and hope they stay.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That worked well when we were the obvious best choice.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But our region is catching up and this advantage shrinks each year as our neighbours close the gap.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As fellow Member, Mr Edward Chia, said earlier, we must attract the best from the world while developing the best in Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The talent we import appreciates for a while then goes home.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A region-ready Singaporean holds capability that is hers – portable, not contingent on a company’s decision to base itself in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have been slow to build the bridge that carries our people out and quicker to build a wall that keeps them home.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, next year, when we assume the Chairmanship of ASEAN, it will, once again and appropriately so, be a year of speeches about how the region is our future and how the Government will help Singaporeans seize it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that this time around, we will not only name the potential of the region as we did in 2018 but also help more Singaporeans seize it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I rise in support of the original Motion tabled by my colleagues, Mr Kenneth Tiong and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is whether it reaches the worker who needs it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is the work of NTUC and NTUC’s e2i, connecting workers to jobs: our youths who are taking their first step.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And those who start further back than most.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That has been my conviction since I first stepped into this House.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The ESR gives us a clear direction, and our task now is to turn that direction into something a worker can feel.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Together with fellow Member, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, we co-chair the Committee for Economic Resilience, or Jawatankuasa Daya Ekonomi, for the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And our job is to mobilise the community, so that these strategies become opportunities for our youths, businesses can scale further and higher wages for our workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And we should be honest about our size.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our domestic market is limited, and we have to tap demand in our region and beyond.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The global enterprises based here support a large number of local workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They have been a source of innovation, management practices and technology that helped our local businesses grow.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They have also spurred the development of startups and new local enterprises.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What I want from our global enterprises and our local enterprises is the same thing – stand by our workers; help those who are retrenched bounce back with dignity; and help the rest become AI-ready before the changes arise, rather than after.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, I will speak on three things: first, supporting our lower-wage and mature workers; second, on building career clarity and safeguarding mental well-being as AI transforms our workplaces; and third, strengthening pathways for our underserved communities and our youths.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, on supporting ourr lower-wage and mature workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When we talk about lifting the bottom, the conversation usually turns to where the floor should sit.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is a fair question, and I understand why it is being asked.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But a floor on its own only tells a worker where the first rung pays.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It does not tell him whether there is a second rung or who will help him reach it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is the thinking behind the Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It sets a wage and it attaches a ladder to it, with training and a higher wage at each step, differentiated by different sectors.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Cleaning, security, landscape, retail, food services, waste management, lift and escalator.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Each of those sectors took years of negotiation because wage floors do not rise on their own.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Alongside it, we have the Local Qualifying Salary that sets a floor for local workers in firms that hire foreign workers and Workfare tops up the income and CPF for our lower-wage Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, the question is – has it worked?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That gap is narrower in 2020, and narrower than it was in 2015.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To put it plainly, over the past decade, workers at the bottom of our ladder have been climbing faster than workers in the middle.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But I will not pretend that our work is over.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is progressive, it is sector by sector.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A segment of our lower-wage workers still sits outside these layers, many of them in platform and freelance work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Platform Workers Act now gives our delivery riders and private hire drivers CPF contributions, work injury compensation and formal representations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But as that segment continues to grow, I would ask the Government to study how our wage and protection floors can follow the worker rather than the job title.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is why the NTUC set up the Job Security Council in February 2020.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Retrenchments edged up in the first quarter of this year, though the incidence remains within the non-recessionary norms.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In an economy that keeps restructuring, some displacement will happen and we should be honest about that.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But the majority of these retrenchments came from businesses re-organising themselves and restructuring.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Firms are reshaping themselves and they will keep doing so.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, the test is not whether the retrenchments happen.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The test is what happens to the worker afterwards.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: On that test, unemployment has held steady even as retrenchments rose.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We also watch closely whether the help actually works.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Taskforce for Responsible Retrenchment and Employment Facilitation brings together MOM, NTUC, e2i, Enterprise Singapore and SWDA, and it has tracked our outcomes carefully.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Between 2022 and 2024, about seven in 10 retrenched workers who received career coaching from our agencies and e2i were placed within six months.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The median time to placement over that period was around three months.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Close to half of those placed came in at similar or higher wages than before.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And more recently, among workers who took up the Taskforce's help before their last day of employment, about two-thirds were back in work within six months, better than the median for retrenched residents.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is the case for reaching our workers earlier, and not later.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Mary Ho is a senior worker at Mandai Rainforest Resort.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Through an agreement between the resort, e2i and the Food, Drinks and Allied Workers' Union, she was offered a redesigned role suited to her needs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What stayed with me was what Mary said herself.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: She was struck by how we had been involved at every step, making sure she was placed in a role that suited her.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Someone walking beside a worker until they land a job.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That brings career, training and employment support closer to where our workers already live and work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my Budget speech this year, I shared the story of a mid-career worker who had completed several courses over three years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Effort with direction builds confidence and clearly, it gives a lot of clarity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And that is why I welcome the formation of the Tripartite Jobs Council.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It brings our partners together to help workers reskill and to help businesses redesign jobs responsibly as AI reshapes our workplaces.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For this Council to succeed, its work must reach workers where they already are.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That means the trusted touchpoints that I had mentioned earlier, on the ground, the very career centres and coaches that workers, like Mary, could turn to.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Through AI-Ready SG, we are already helping our workers and continue to do so, especially our PMEs, our youths, to gain practical confidence with AI, while supporting businesses to redesign jobs responsibly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our CTCs are where the real work happens.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And AI is now the centre of gravity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is what turning technology into practical help looks like.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Training that workers can use that same Monday morning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The fear of being too old to start again causes confusion.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That anxiety does not stay in the workplace.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It follows a person home and it wears on their health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I have long advocated in this House for a whole-of-society approach to mental well-being, including a Motion I had co-filed with fellow Members on this very subject.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the recent economic resilience dialogue with businesses and youths, may came forth and mentioned how important mental well-being is in a stage like this.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their ability to have support matters to them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And that is why the Committee for Economic Resilience will work very closely with community leaders and businesses to ensure that we give support for our community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we equip our workers for an AI-enabled economy, our support must address not just their skills but their peace of mind.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Only then can they face the future with confidence, with clarity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The ESR focuses on strengthening lifelong learning and on linking training more closely to employment outcomes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some workers start further back than others, whether because of their age, their background or simply because they lack the networks to open doors for them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Part of my role at e2i is to sharpen our focus on reaching these groups, our lower-wage and mature workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The aim is for our career services and programmes to be designed around their needs, like what we did with Mary, rather than around conveniences.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For our young people, clarity has to begin before they graduate, and we will come forward to them at an earlier stage than before, ensuring that they have the right clarity and a pathway to go into areas and sectors that have been assigned in the ESR.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A student who has stood inside a real workplace and who has a mentor she can call, makes a very different first decision from one who is guessing.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And that is why early career exposure and structured mentorship and internships matter so much, and we will have many of those in the pipeline.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For our young people, their first foray into the working world is often the most daunting.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, that a young person does not have to figure out their first steps alone.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This complements the work of the Tripartite Jobs Council that I mentioned earlier, as well as the Graduate Industry Traineeships programme, so that our young people are supported throughout their first transition.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is also why NTUC signed a memorandum of understanding with the MENDAKI Foundation this year.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It aims to strengthen the skills of Malay/Muslim workers, and to help more of them secure employment in growing sectors.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Within the Focus Area of M3+, NTUC, e2i, NTUC LearningHub, SWDA and the Lifelong Learning Institute have collaborated with MENDAKI.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Nearly 20% of them went on to receive more in-depth mentorship.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Now, as AI begins to transform the way we work, the same worry is felt in our homes too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: NTUC and e2i are ready to move forward together with our Malay/Muslim workers, especially our young people.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We will help them upskill, adapt, and access meaningful employment opportunities, whether in global companies or in local enterprises, where we want them to develop further. : Mr Speaker, before I entered this House, I spent nearly 25 years as an educator.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I learned that no one should be written off just because of a label that has been placed on them, not the academic stream that were put at them in schools and not the sector that they happen to work in.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And that belief still guides me in my work today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: At the heart of this Motion is an important aspiration: that Singapore remains an economy where our people have opportunities to succeed and our workers can look to the future with confidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: I believe every Member of this House shares this aspiration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: It has always been at the heart of our economic strategy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Our objective is not simply to grow the economy, but to improve the lives of all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We do this by creating better opportunities, better jobs and raising incomes, by ensuring that the benefits of growth are widely shared.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Our approach has delivered good outcomes for Singaporeans across the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Lower-income workers have seen faster income growth than the median worker.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Few advanced economies have been able to achieve all these outcomes at the same time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Some Members have contrasted Singapore with other industrialised economies, arguing that their greater reliance on local champions had produced better productivity models and better outcomes for their workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: But on comparable measures, Singapore's wage outcomes are higher than these economies, not only at the median but also at the lower levels of income.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: In recent years, real wage growth has also kept pace with and exceeded productivity growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: From 2021 to 2025, real value added per worker increased by about 0.7% a year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Over the same period, real median income of full-time employed residents rose by about 1.8% a year while real income at the 20th percentile grew much faster.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This did not happen by accident but through sound growth policies and strategies and tripartite efforts like the Progressive Wage Model, Workfare and the Local Qualifying Salary that have uplifted wages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: More recently, despite a challenging external environment, Singapore's labour market has remained resilient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: While retrenchments in some companies may have dominated the headlines, employment expanded for the 19th consecutive quarter in the first quarter of 2026.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Resident employment continued to grow, unemployment remained low and firms continued to hire.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: These outcomes are the result of deliberate policy choices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We have kept our economy competitive while ensuring that Singaporeans have access to opportunities, better jobs and clear pathways to progress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This has only been possible because Government, employers and unions have worked closely together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Thus, the evidence does not support the conclusion that Singapore's economic model is a failure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We are navigating a structural transition, however difficult and uneven, from a position of strength.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The system has served us well, but we must and will remain adaptable to the changing world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We know the pace of change has accelerated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Those who are displaced worry about how long they will take to find another job and whether the next job will be as good as the previous.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: As an open and small economy, Singapore's prosperity has always depended on our ability to compete successfully in global markets while ensuring that Singaporeans benefit from that success.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: I am glad that there is broad agreement in this House on this fundamental point.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The ESR provides an actionable blueprint to address the very challenges that our economy faces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: It was shaped by engagements with more than 7,700 stakeholders, including businesses, unions and workers, and grounded in Singapore's realities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The ESR also puts workers at the heart of its strategies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: First, it is to make it easier for Singaporeans to access career and skills support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: After more than a decade of SkillsFuture, we have built a stronger culture of lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We will now focus even more sharply on employment outcomes so that training leads to better jobs, better wages and better career progression.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi asked about the outcomes of our workforce programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Among jobseekers who received career-matching services in 2023, about six in 10 found employment within six months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Our Career Conversion Programmes show what we can achieve when we journey with our workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: These are not perfect outcomes and we must continue to improve them, but it made a real difference to those 62,000 jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: They show why we should strengthen the system, not dismiss it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi also called for more robust reviews of SkillsFuture training programmes and for funding to be channelled to industry relevant training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We have been strengthening quality assurance and sharpening our focus on courses that address identified skills gaps, improve employability and support workforce transformation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We are also looking at to strengthen signals of industry demand so that training remains relevant and delivers value.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: At the same time, we recognise that we can do more to tighten the nexus between training and jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This is why we merged SkillsFuture Singapore with Workforce Singapore into the new SWDA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: SWDA will enable us to align future skills more closely with future jobs, identify at-risk workers earlier and provide more seamless support from training to placement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This will help us close the gap between learning and earning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We will share more at the SkillsFuture Festival Launch event in September.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Second, a stronger first step into work, giving young Singaporeans a stronger start.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: In today's uncertain economic environment with AI reshaping entry level tasks, many fresh graduates and their parents are understandably anxious about entry into the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The WP argues that entry pathways for young people are broken.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: But the current picture is more resilient than suggested.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: I believe my learned colleague from the WP has also highlighted a similar point.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The system has served us well, but must continue to evolve with a new generation of workers and a changing work environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: As part of the ESR, we saw the need to bring learning and work closer together, including formally recognising on-the-job training as part of qualifications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We do this precisely because we want our young to have a good headstart in their jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: In this regard, we agree with Mr Andre Low on the value of expanding work-based pathways like apprenticeships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This is already a key direction of our efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The task now is to broaden and deepen these pathways to connect education, work experience, skills recognition and employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We share the aspiration of giving every young Singaporean a fair start.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Our goal is not just to help young Singaporeans get their first job, but to build strong career health from the start.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This means giving them more opportunities to learn through work, gain recognised skills and credentials, and access tools and support, including the Careers and Skills Passport, to better navigate their careers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We will continue to strengthen these pathways so that more young Singaporeans can build skills, gain experience and make a confident start in a changing economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Third, we are helping workers bounce back better.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We did this because we understand what a challenging operating environment we are in and we believe that Singaporeans who fall on hard times should receive support to enable them to return to work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: That is why we designed the Jobseeker Support Scheme to support re-employment, not unemployment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi suggested the introduction of an unemployment insurance scheme that is funded through premiums and conditional on job search and retraining, time limited and capped at a certain percentage of your last drawn pay.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: It is not clear how this differs from the Job Support Scheme, except that the Job Support Scheme places more emphasis on re-employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: But I suspect both schemes are similar to one another.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Instead of coming up with a new mechanism, the ESR has recommended that we strengthen schemes like the Jobseeker Support Scheme, especially for PMEs navigating more difficult career transitions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We are also studying how to do so, including whether the Jobseeker Support Scheme should be enhanced to cover more PMEs and give them greater confidence and assurance in their search for their next job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi and Mr Pritam Singh called for mandatory retrenchment benefits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: In fact, NTUC had long advocated that workers affected by retrenchments should be fairly compensated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: I believe Mr Patrick Tay had also mentioned this in his speech earlier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We will study this further under the Tripartite Workgroup on the Employment Act Review.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We have to get it right by creating job opportunities, helping Singaporean workers access them, and when they face the effects of economic disruption, ensuring that they will never have to navigate difficult and uncertain times alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Fourthly, we are putting in place strong ladders of mobility to ensure inclusive growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We have consistently put inclusive growth at the heart of our strategies to make sure that no worker is left behind.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: It is not about creating a fast lane for a few and a slow one for the rest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: It is about broadening our shared lanes to give every Singaporean the space to move forward and to get to their destination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Our efforts like the Progressive Wage Model and Workfare have been critical to this outcome.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Beyond uplifting the bottom, we are also building more pathways for good jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This includes jobs in domestic and essential services, where many workers are currently employed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: To this, let me briefly address Mr Gerald Giam's suggestion on uplifting the skills trades.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We share the aspiration for the skills trades to offer better wages, stronger professional standing and clearer career progression for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We expressed that aspiration in the Forward SG exercise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The ESR similarly recommended broadening the range of good jobs, including by uplifting skills trades and making work-based learning a more recognised route to mastery.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We are already working to realise this aspiration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This initiative seeks to address many of the issues that Mr Giam had raised.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: But more broadly, the sustainable route to better jobs is higher productivity, better job design, stronger certification, modern tools and processes, and employers who are willing to share productivity gains with their workers – all of which the Government will double down on to strengthen.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Enterprise transformation and workforce transformation must work together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We support enterprises because their success creates opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This is especially important for SMEs as they employ about two-thirds of our workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: When firms invest, innovate and raise productivity, they create better jobs, build deeper capabilities and sustain wage growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We also want Singaporeans to have different pathways to contribute and succeed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: For some, that will mean building a career in an established enterprise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: For others, it may mean starting a venture of their own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: With AI and new technologies lowering the cost of developing products, reaching customers and scaling across markets, entrepreneurship is an increasingly viable pathway.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: That is the nature of enterprise and risk-taking.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: But we are expanding support for promising startups to build, grow and reach global markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: And the ESR recommendations will strengthen access to growth capital, technology, networks and overseas markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Successful ventures do more than reward their founders; they create job opportunities for other Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Some Members may call for stronger Singaporean representation in our economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We too, want more of our local businesses to thrive, but the answer is to build them up, not to shut them out.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Founded by three NUS graduates, Carousell began with a simple idea – to make selling pre-owned items as easy as taking a photograph.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: What started as a mobile-first classifieds app, it has since grown into a leading online marketplace and omnichannel e-commerce business operating across Southeast Asia, Taiwan and Hong Kong, serving tens of millions of users across the region.
