speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This illustrates how Singapore firms grow as they access international markets, overseas customers, global technologies and world-class business networks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We will continue to support young Singaporeans to go abroad and gain exposure through programmes, like the NUS Overseas College and the Overseas Market Immersion programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Strong local enterprises and global companies are not mutually exclusive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Let us also not forget that MNCs support Singaporeans too, not just Singapore businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: My final point is on the importance of tripartism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: In many countries, economic debates have become increasingly confrontational and divisive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Singapore has avoided this outcome, but we should never take this for granted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: I have listened carefully to how this Motion frames its vision of our economic engine – entrepreneurs, households, businesses, workers, capital.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Two partners are notably missing from that list: employers and unions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: It is precisely the space in which wages are negotiated, jobs are redesigned and disputes are resolved without a single strike in decades.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Any vision for our economic future that is silent on how we will work with these partners is an incomplete one.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Our tripartite partnership brings Government, businesses and workers to work together to expand the economic pie and ensure that gains are fairly shared.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: That is what turns inclusive growth from an aspiration into practical outcomes – more investment, better jobs, rising wages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The Company Training Committees (CTCs) are one practical example of tripartism in action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Through the CTC Grant, companies and unions redesign jobs, build new capabilities and translate business transformation into better wages and career prospects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We will continue working with both NTUC and SNEF to build on this model, so that more enterprises and workers can benefit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We want an economy where Singaporeans can participate, contribute and succeed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: An economy where workers can build meaningful careers, enterprises can innovate and grow, and more Singaporeans can create opportunities not only for themselves, but for others as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This is precisely what the ESR seeks to achieve.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Not by choosing between growth and inclusion, local enterprises and global connections, or competitiveness and worker protection.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This is how we turn economic growth into broad-based progress – through better jobs, better wages and better pathways for advancement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: That is how we have and will continue to build an economy that works for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi, you have a clarification of which Member please?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: However, I would like to address the Minister of State's statements on the Jobseeker Support Scheme in comparison to the Redundancy Insurance Scheme.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: He suggests, if I caught his point correctly, that both schemes are broadly similar, but I just want to make the following point.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: Because the Redundancy Insurance is funded by joint contributions from employers and employees, the payouts are automatic and seamless.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: The Jobseeker Support Scheme, however, requires the retrenched worker to go through an application process and face the prospect of rejection.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: Hence, there are three questions, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Yes, Mr Fadli Fawzi if I could invite you to ask your clarifications promptly.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: One, would it not be better if retrenched workers did not have to go through this arduous application and waiting process which can be very stressful to such workers in that situation?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: Again, would a universal Redundancy Insurance Scheme not be better in providing 100% coverage to our retrenched workers?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister of State Dinesh Vasu Dash, would you like to reply to those three clarifications put to you?

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Maybe just to highlight that the positions are not really very far.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: So, I will probably frame it from that perspective and to add that friction in the process is not one that is intended to make it difficult for someone who is already going through difficult times but it is to make sure that they can bounce back, and bounce back stronger.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I have a clarification to seek from Minister of State Dinesh.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: My question is: the upgrading certification and tools only work if certified practitioners are not continuously undercut in the open market.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, how will this initiative address this structural problem of uncertified operators who drag down market rates for properly accredited local tradespersons?

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: I would just add that we are still studying that particular perspective.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: It is still being studied and perhaps we can have a fuller discussion when the scheme is a bit more ready to be discussed.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: There being no further clarifications, we will move on with the debate on the Motion and the amended Motion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: At the heart of this debate is a fundamental question: How do we ensure that Singapore enterprises can continue to thrive in a rapidly changing world?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The answer matters because our enterprises are central to Singapore's success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: SMEs create good jobs, strengthen our communities and bolster Singapore's economic competitiveness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: But all the Members who spoke before us also shared that the environment that the SMEs operate in is becoming more challenging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And global disruptions have become a recurring nature and feature in the global economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The recent Middle East crisis is the latest reminder of how quickly external events can affect our businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our response is not just to help the enterprises weather the new storm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It is to help our enterprises become stronger, more competitive and more resilient over the long term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our economic strategy has always been centred on improving the lives of Singaporeans, because strong local enterprises are indispensable to that goal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: That is why we will continue to stand alongside our businesses, help them build stronger capabilities, expand with confidence and innovate and grow beyond Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Businesses today compete not just on cost, many of the Members said that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They do not just compete on cost but on innovation, on quality, productivity as well as speed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Yesterday's strengths are no guarantee of tomorrow's success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Enterprises that continue to build new capabilities will be better placed to stay ahead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Those that do not do so risk falling behind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: During the ESR, we engaged widely with trade associations and chambers representing SMEs and various businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Most SMEs recognised that transformation is no longer optional.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The question is not whether to transform, but really how to do so in a practical, in an accessible as well as sustainable manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Every enterprise starts from a different position, serves different markets, customers and faces different opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: That is why we tailor our approach to support the company's needs, whether it is adopting AI, improving productivity, developing new products, services expanding into new markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Through Enterprise Singapore, businesses can access a wide range of Government support to build capabilities and transformation their operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, Sin Chwee Mini Mart started as a wet market seafood store by Mr Goh Thiam Chwee in Bukit Gombak in 1990.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Faced with changing consumer preferences, the second-generation owner Mr Jimmy Goh, his son, made the decision to reinvent the business.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: He launched Tankfully Fresh, transforming what had been a traditional wet market seafood stall into an omnichannel retailer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With Government support, the company accelerated its transformation by implementing an integrated inventory management system to support its growing omni-channel business.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: What used to be a wet market, small minimart, grew into new retail, B2B and online sales channels through contract manufacturing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: If anything, this example reminds us that every successful transformation begins with a decision by the business itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The aim of our efforts is to help enterprises build the capabilities that matter most to their business at that point in time, so that they can become more productive, more competitive and more resilient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Members over the last few hours have spoken about the challenges facing our F&B businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We Singaporeans, we love our food and we treasure our distinctive food culture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Operators face higher manpower, rental and operating costs, while consumer expectations continue to rise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Around the world, diners are demanding greater convenience, better value and more differentiated experiences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Digital platforms, food delivery and social media have transformed how customers discover and consume food.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: These trends present challenges, but also new opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In fact, many of our F&B businesses are responding with determination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They are redesigning their operations, they are embracing technology, they are centralising food preparation and adopting AI and digital solutions to improve productivity and to serve their customers better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our role is to support these transformation efforts with practical assistance that helps businesses become more productive, competitive and resilient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our objective is not simply to help F&B businesses cope with higher costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It is to help them operate differently and compete more effectively because that means improving productivity, redesigning their processes, embracing technology and finding new ways to deliver better value to their customers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: That is why Enterprise Singapore has put in place a range of initiatives to support the transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Smaller businesses can lower costs and achieve greater scale through FoodX, by sharing manufacturing and food preparation facilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We also offer help for businesses to adopt digital and AI solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Forty hours a day is almost equivalent to allowing them to avail four full-time staff to focus on greater value-add services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Another group of businesses close to our heart are the heartland enterprises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They help define the character of our neighbourhoods, bring communities together and contribute to our social fabric.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: But like all businesses, they must adapt to changing consumer preferences and new technologies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar will be glad to know that we have been the heartland enterprises through the years with many initiatives, such as the Heartland Enterprise Placemaking Grant and the Enhanced Visual Merchandising Programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, whether young or established, traditional or modern, every enterprise must continue building new capabilities to remain competitive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will continue to support our businesses in this journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And this journey includes going beyond Singapore to the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Because our domestic market is limited, enterprises must venture beyond our shores to grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our small economy also needs strong external demand in addition to healthy domestic demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To help enterprises go global, we have established support for enterprises across their different stages of internationalisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: From grants like the recently enhanced Market Readiness Assistance, which helps businesses springboard overseas, to programmes like the Scale-Up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Enterprise Singapore's Scale-Up programme helps high-potential Singapore companies build the capabilities they need to scale effectively and compete internationally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is a steel foundation solutions company specialising in waterfront and underground construction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It sharpened its market entry strategies through Scale-Up just about four years ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Since then, the company was able to, in the last four years, secure large-scale infrastructure projects in Southeast Asia markets and the Middle East and Africa.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As a result, Mlion saw a fourfold increase in their revenue in 2024.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Another example is Space Matrix, a workplace design and build firm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The company accelerated its international growth by sharpening its strategy and strengthening its supply chain and procurement capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Within two years, it has expanded into India, the Philippines and Dubai, and moved into the life sciences and data centre sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The company's revenue has grown more than 25%, and their profitability more than 200%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: While the decision to internationalise is one that the enterprises must make for themselves, our goal is to create the conditions and provide the support that will spur them to compete and to succeed on the global stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will continue to monitor the global economic landscape and refine our globalisation schemes and support for Singapore enterprises to become global champions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Every successful enterprise operates within a wider ecosystem of partners, networks and institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Over the years, the Government has invested in building a strong and vibrant enterprise ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our goal here is to create an environment in which enterprises can succeed, one that enables them to innovate, to build deeper capabilities, to gain access to talent, technology and market, and to be able to seize opportunities to enter new markets overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And Ms Mariam Jaafar shared very eloquently earlier, a key element of this vibrant enterprise ecosystem is that mutually beneficial, mutually re-enforcing partnerships between our SMEs and our larger companies, including MNCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As Mr Edward Chia and Ms Mariam Jaafar mentioned earlier, local and global enterprises in Singapore can work together to strengthen their capabilities, accelerate innovation and in doing so, create better jobs and opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Look around at the MNCs' C-suite executives over the years, the positions are also taken up by Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I recall, as an EDB officer some 26 years ago, I had worked on the Local Industry Upgrading Programme that matched the SMEs and the MNCs, company by company, sector by sector, matching them based on their workplan, their vision, their ambition and their values, but in a win-win partnership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And the programme allowed the MNCs to gain a strong base of suppliers, while allowing the SMEs to learn from the larger industry players and upgrade their capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Today, the programme has evolved to become what we call the Partnerships for Capability Transformation (PACT) programme, While LIUP focused primarily on strengthening supplier relationships between MNCs and SMEs, PACT brings the companies together to skill up, to innovate and in fact, to capture new opportunities together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: PACT has progressively expanded to support a broader range of partnerships.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Members will remember that last year, in this House, we announced expansion of the PACT programme to include internationalisation, corporate ventures and capability training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This has enabled SMEs to gain entry into regional as well as global value chains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In addition, SMEs get access to new customers and valuable chance to build stronger capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They also co-create solutions and grow with the larger partners in their overseas operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Take the partnership between ForeFront AM, which is a local additive manufacturing firm, and GlobalFoundries MNC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Due to their collaboration, Forefront AM was able to increase its capabilities in additive manufacturing to create critical, highly customised parts for GlobalFoundries' high-value semiconductor manufacturing tools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And on the part of GlobalFoundries, the company qualified nine local SMEs to produce more than 200 critical tool parts as a result of the two PACT programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We also partnered industry leaders to help companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Louis Chua called for greater support for AI adoption and acknowledged that the Enterprise Compute Initiative was announced last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is a scheme that where we work with leading cloud service providers like Google and Amazon as well as consultant partners to give enterprises access to cutting edge AI tools, cloud credits, training and certification.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The Enterprise Compute Initiative is meant to kickstart adoption and to build momentum.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, we will continue to monitor the take-up closely and refine the support where needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Partnerships like these have enabled our local enterprises to capture fresh opportunities, build stronger and deeper capabilities, and compete in higher-value segments of the economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As shared by Mr Saktiandi Supaat, attracting MNC investments and the support we provide to local enterprises are complementary strategies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: A robust economy needs the contributions of both the MNCs and SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: On that note, let me now turn to another important pillar in our vibrant enterprise ecosystem – our close partnership with trade associations and chambers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As Mr Mark Lee noted earlier, the trade associations and chambers play an important role as trusted intermediaries because the trade associations and chambers not only represent the enterprises and their respective sectors, they also help the businesses cope with shifts, like moving towards sustainability, digitalisation and workforce transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They are also instrumental in developing shared solutions as well as aggregating industry needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will continue to work closely with all our trade associations and chambers in Singapore as they lead initiatives that bring businesses together to address common challenges and to seize new opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And furthermore, the trade associations and chambers have contributed their insights and industry perspectives on the needs of their sectors as part of our ESR process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The ESR recommendations and the directions we are taking reflect our trade associations and chambers' input and feedback.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We value our close partnership and dialogue with our trade associations and chambers because we do not work in silos.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And as Mr Mark Lee pointed out, 24 of the 27 recommendations by the Alliance for Action on Business Competitiveness have been accepted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In fact, in April 2024, we sent up the Inter-Ministerial Committee for Pro-Enterprise Rules Review chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong as well as the various Ministers to oversee the agencies' efforts to improve regulatory efficiency and to reduce compliance burdens especially for SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And the Inter-Ministerial Committee has achieved progress in these few areas within two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Agencies have also reviewed their license validity period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In parallel, we also started the SME Pro-Enterprise Office last year to cut red tape and to help our businesses address regulatory challenges, especially where it involves multiple agencies or emerging nascent sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This approach keeps our enterprise ecosystem vibrant as Government and regulations stay responsive to the needs of our businesses and to the needs of our SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And recently, just three months ago, in May this year, JTC streamlined lease transfers for smaller industrial sites with remaining tenures, reducing the processing time from two months to one month, to help our businesses acquire space and respond more quickly to changing needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We recognise that many SMEs do not have dedicated teams for strategy, technology or business development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As mentioned by Mr Azhar Othman very passionately earlier, SME Centres help our SMEs identify opportunities, navigate available Government support and chart practical next steps for their growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: That is about 2,500 SMEs in a month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim earlier in his speech has called for simpler grant application processes and we have continuously been reviewing ways to improve.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This achievement is the result of the collective efforts of businesses, workers and the Government, that is, our tripartite partners.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Maintaining long-term, sustainable economic growth and ensuring that Singaporeans have good jobs and can live and work in peace and stability have always been our goal.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Strong local enterprises, especially SMEs, are crucial to achieving this goal.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They are a very important part of our overall economic ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: SMEs create many job opportunities for Singaporeans, strengthen community cohesion and enhance Singapore's economic competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Over the years, the Ministry of Trade and Industry, together with other Government agencies, has continued to roll out many measures and programmes to help local SMEs grow and thrive.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We have focused on three areas: (a) First, creating a pro-business environment and encouraging Singaporeans to start businesses; (b) Second, working closely with local TACs to strengthen the capabilities and resilience of each of the sectors; and (c) Third, encouraging and helping local SMEs venture into overseas markets.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In my English speech earlier, I also mentioned many successful examples of enterprises that have received practical assistance.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: When facing exceptional challenges such as the COVID-19 pandemic and the recent conflict in the Middle East, the Government will also adapt our measures based on the circumstances and introduce timely support measures to help enterprises tide over immediate difficulties.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: But Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we must remember that Singapore is a small country with no natural resources, a small market and an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In the last 61 years of our independence, although we have accumulated a certain level of economic strength, we cannot simply rest on our laurels and live off past successes.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Like businesses, the Government must also maintain an enterprising spirit, consistently upgrading, improving and adopting so as to secure a better future for our next generation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: These included local heritage businesses and representatives from heartland merchant associations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We listened to their concerns and gathered their views.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Every company is also at a different stage of development, with a different starting point, different customer segments and different challenges and opportunities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The key is whether the business owners, partners and employees have the will to find ways to ensure the business can sustain in the long term and achieve continued success.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We all know that yesterday's strengths do not guarantee tomorrow's success.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Businesses that continue to work hard to upgrade their capabilities will be able to go further.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We believe that as long as local enterprises commit themselves to upgrading their capability, seizing development opportunities at home and abroad and cooperating with one another, they will be able to sustain their operations and achieve sound growth.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Government will continue to create favourable conditions for businesses to flourish, and work hand in hand with businesses and Singaporeans to build a better tomorrow together. : Mr Deputy Speaker, we have debated this Motion and heard a range of views and suggestions.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We share the same vision – to see Singapore's economy succeed, businesses thrive and good jobs created for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Government continues to support and stand alongside our Singapore enterprises.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Our goal is not just to help businesses weather the new storm, but to help them grow, to help them improve their competitiveness and strengthen their resilience to scale and compete internationally.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We will continue to create the conditions of a vibrant and effervescent enterprise ecosystem to help them flourish and thrive.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: While we catalyse the ideal environment, it is the enterprises that continuously innovate, adapt and strengthen capabilities that will thrive and conquer new markets.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, do you have a clarification?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first concerns her point about internationalisation through Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: During her speech, she offered more than a few examples of local SMEs that have successfully internationalised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is without dispute something that both sides of the House can agree on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My second question has to do with the F&B sector, which Senior Minister of State Low also spoke about.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One notable difference between this sector and other SMEs is that the vast majority of our hawkers, coffee shop operators, restaurateurs deal with essentially a non-tradeable product.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is why suggestions that erase profits by scaling up often ring hollow to them, at least based on our conversations with them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I had suggested two channels in my speech on rental rate increase controls and different dependency ratio ceiling quotas, but if this is not something that the Government will entertain, I wonder what other suggestions, other than trying to scale up, which is something that these companies struggle with doing —

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, if I could invite you to promptly come to your second clarification?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Earlier on, when I talked about the range of support that we gave to SMEs, I had also taken a focus on F&B.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I talked about how we have within the last 12 months rolled out – and these programmes were not rolled out in isolation – for example, Enterprise Singapore rolled out what they called the F&B Process Optimisation Programme.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Allow me just one minute to explain what this is.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Like the Member mentioned, these are domestic companies, they cannot really go overseas unless through franchising.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They are very much looking at how they can overcome manpower constraints.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Based on our focus group discussion with them, we understand their pain points.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: That is why we came up the Process Optimisation Programme.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Kopi & Tarts example is a simple example, but it is quite powerful.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They serve really wonderful ayam merah – it is really good – and protein bowls.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They outsource the ingredient preparation for these two dishes.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This allows them to then redeploy their four full-time staff, who have to come in early into the kitchen and so on, into other positions.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The second one is FoodX that I talked about sharing of resources and so on.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to assure him that we are working with the trade associations, like what Mr Mark Lee has mentioned.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In this case, it was the RAS who addressed the issues and helped them to grow their top line and as well as bottom line.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: He asked about some of these big numbers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: If I could request for him to file a separate Parliamentary Question, we will surely look into it and come back to the Member.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: But suffice to say, within the enterprise ecosystem, it is not just Enterprise Singapore that account manages each of these companies.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I have talked about the 10 SME Centres.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And earlier on, some of the Members talked about GoBusiness.gov.sg.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Some of our business owners are very adept at that.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They are gleaning a lot of information from that as well.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We will continue, just like how earlier on I responded to the Productivity Solutions Grant processing time, we will continue to look at how we can use technology to ensure that we can serve our SMEs better.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On internationalisation, it is not just companies, like Space Matrix or the Mlion or the manufacturing company I talked about, ForeFront AM, let me cite an example called Hegen.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I have known Ms Yvon Bock for close to 10 years.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Ten years ago, Hegen was a startup, some Members are smiling because they probably used the company's products.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They took part in "double 11" back then.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: That was how we helped them to leapfrog to China, to various provinces.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Hegen has grown into a global consumer brand with a very significant international footprint.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I am using Hegen to say one thing.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I am using Hegen to say that, if we work together to ensure that in Singapore, we have a vibrant, effervescent enterprise ecosystem, our companies are not just selling products and services.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Our companies can also twin it with a Singapore brand, which stands for integrity, quality, reliability, which is what Ms Yvon Bock told me.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The first thing I did was set up a technical committee for space engineering, nuclear engineering and quantum engineering.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, we try to transform the Institution of Engineers Singapore from the built environment to the latest emerging technology cluster.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Last week, a famous Singaporean son, TikTok chief executive officer Chew Shou Zi, addressed the doctoral graduation ceremony at the Nanyang Technological University (NTU).

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: He noted that we are standing at a pivotal juncture, "Change is not just constant, but exponential and compounding." We all know that change is inevitable, but exponential and compounding are really another expression for disruptive and transformative.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, I sent him a message and said, "Can I quote you in my speech?" And he said, "Go ahead." That was on a Sunday evening, so I redrafted my speech.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, I will be quoting his various quotes, so I will not requote again.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: To thrive in this new landscape, I would like to propose "3Is": innovation, investment and internationalisation.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation – moving from a very fixed blueprint to embracing the messy unknown.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: As an engineer and educator, I have been championing the growth of our deep tech ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: However, true innovation requires cultural shift in how we manage risk.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: At NTU, Mr Chew challenged the doctoral students to take the superpower, which is their knowledge and research knowledge, and of course, it is not necessary that PhD students have the knowledge, everybody has the knowledge at their mastery.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: He said to take the superpower and apply it to the messy, ambiguous problems of the real world, adding that we must embrace uncertainty because that is where meaningful innovations happen.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Five years, six years ago, someone attended my class in NUS on technology entrepreneurship.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Blackstone deals with submersible robotics, things that swim in the water, which we cannot see.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And at that time, it is about just trying to do video analytics and – very much like student projects – we touch something so that it is accurate.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We tried to find some application for this.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And within five years, we looked at trials in Singapore, trials overseas.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, supported by Cap Vista; and Monk's Hill Ventures among the investors.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I am an angel investor, because when I see that they are really startup, I will put some money in for them, to help out.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, what we really need is much more aggressive regulatory-like sandboxes.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: It is not just domestic because in this kind of deep tech environment, domestic, sometimes, it is not applicable, so we should then look at sandboxes that are domestic, regional and even global.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot have sure bets, but we can actually give them opportunities to ride out that phase for the next generation of breakthrough technologies.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: In the first two years or first three years we were actually operating out of NUS labs.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, my suggestion is that we take a leave from the partnership between MOE and MCCY, where facilities that are unused – for example, badminton hall, football fields – if they are unused, then open it to the rest who can use it.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We can kick football on Sundays in certain school fields, right?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The same thing, whether it is universities, polytechnics or A*STAR, all these research labs, they have really expensive equipment and very sophisticated equipment that all these deep tech startups can use.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The question is how to manage it so.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: It is like facilities on a shared economy basis.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: If we believe in the Institution of Engineers Singapore, then maybe the institution can help you to manage it.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Coming to investment, the second "I", shifting capital to skill up revolutionary ideas.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chew Shou Zi noted that the massive shift in investments towards early-stage startups that emphasise the true impact lies in, "taking a single idea and giving it the scale to reach millions or billions," he said, "if you are lucky." The reality on the ground, for Singapore, is that it is really difficult to get Series A, and you have to prove profitability and the likes.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: That points us to a path for all these deep tech startups.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not depend too much on the venture capitals, maybe public money or public funding might be a better option or another option.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I convene a group of tech entrepreneurs, investors like Catalist sponsors, and investors, and we meet at the Singapore Exchange (SGX).

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: SGX is very supportive to give me the room.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I give you another case of space engineering.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I invited him to sit on my technical committee; I am going after all of these people.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And his business obviously is not really much in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, he would probably have one or two customers —

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I have given you 10 minutes of latitude.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I am beginning to ask whether you are going to draw any of your insights to the subject of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: And I turn you to Standing Order 50(1), and these are rules and Standing Orders that apply to all Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Could I invite you to draw a link from your observations, insights and experiences to the Motion or the amended Motion at hand?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng
text: And the system of innovation does not just have a couple of parties.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng
text: Competitors, especially MNCs, suppliers that are based here, are very important to help create this ecosystem to have a much more vibrant ecosystem, not just what you call – okay, I will stop at that.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng
text: I just want to declare one more interest.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng
text: I quote so much of Mr Chew Shou Zi and my mother maiden's name is Chew.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Dr Neo, you have got another few minutes.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Feel free to carry on if you can make your points relevant to the Motion.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng
text: Alright, so as far as the Motion is concerned, Mr Edward Chia took my technology entrepreneurship class in NUS also.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng
text: He understands that to build tech ecosystems, we really need a complete system and innovations, so I therefore support his amended Motion.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We carry on with the debate on the Motion and the amended Motion.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The next speaker is Mr Ng Shi Xuan.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I met companies involved in robotics, social enterprise and edutech, and that is just a very small subset of the thousands of entrepreneurs that the NUS Overseas Colleges have bred.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But every generation of startups and companies face challenges, and we are here to diagnose and address the gaps to help them succeed.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The aspirations expressed in this Motion are ones that Members on both sides of the House can support.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: An economy where Singaporeans can thrive, entrepreneurs can experiment, businesses can succeed, workers can progress and good ideas can flourish.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The more important question is how do we turn these aspirations into reality?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Businesses need skilled, confident and adaptable Singaporeans to grow.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Singaporeans in turn, need strong businesses that can create good jobs, invest in their capabilities and give them opportunities to lead.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: We should therefore avoid viewing workers and businesses as being on opposing sides.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: When businesses face genuine transformation pressures, our policies should help both companies and workers make the transition together.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: I have seen our enterprise landscapes from several perspectives, having worked in a successful startup, supporting Singapore companies in the Public Service and now running an SME.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: These experiences have convinced me that good ideas need "5Cs" to grow: customers, capital, connections, capabilities and confidence.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: I will trace the journey of a company through our enterprise ecosystem, from turning an idea into a viable product to winning its first customers, scaling through capital and global connections, and eventually reaching an exit that recycles capital, experience and confidence into the next generations of our enterprises.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Our enterprise policies should help promising companies to make each of these transitions.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: In the world of startups, it is no longer merely a contest of ideas.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: A good idea that nobody buys remains an idea.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: For Singapore startups, the domestic market is where they can prove themselves, but the region and the world are where they must scale.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: That requires more than grants, competitions and technical development.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: It requires someone willing to become the first serious customers.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Yet, every founder encounters the same dreaded question: "Who else has already used it?" This creates a familiar paradox.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: I recently met this company, Mottainai Food Tech, and "Mottainai" means "too good to waste" in Japanese.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: It is a local startup that turns food-manufacturing by-products, including soybean pulp, into nutritious food products.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Its technology supports food security and circularity, and it has developed a commercial product.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: But like many young companies, it still needs sizeable orders to prove that it can produce and deliver at scale.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: This challenge is not unique to food technology.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: This does not mean buying an inferior product, simply because it is local.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Nor should Government agencies become the permanent customers of every startup.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: It means giving credible companies a fair opportunity to test, demonstrate and improve their solutions.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: It means helping them to cross the difficult gap between having a technically viable product and building a commercially proven business.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: A reference customer in Singapore can provide more than just revenue.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: If a young company can show that its product meets the standards of an established corporation or Government agency, it becomes easier to approach customers abroad.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Our domestic market may be small, but Singapore's reputation for quality, standards and reliability is significant.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: I experienced the value of such an opportunity early in my career at Brandtology.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: It is a Singapore technology startup developing natural language processing and social media analytics before these capabilities became mainstream.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: A major Singapore Government contract gave the company both a credible reference customer and evidence that its team could deliver at scale.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Singapore's concentration of multinational and regional headquarters then amplified the value of that first reference customer.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Once we had demonstrated our capabilities here, many of their regional decision-makers were already based here and would ask us a very different question from before: "Do you want to follow us into our other markets?" A successful project in Singapore therefore became more than a domestic reference.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: If every major buyer insists on an extensive track record, new companies will never have the opportunity to build one.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Yet, buyers also have legitimate reasons to be cautious, especially when procuring critical or untested solutions.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: They must be confident that the technology is reliable and that the company can deliver.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: The challenge, therefore, is to manage these risks without allowing past track records to become the only measure of credibility.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: It is about ensuring that the bar measures what truly matters: whether the solution works, whether it meets the required standards and whether the company can deliver.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Leading global companies contribute more than investment and direct employment.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Their regional management, technical and procurement functions can connect local enterprises to sophisticated demand, new technologies, international standards and global supply chains.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Smaller companies may lack the information, networks or resources needed to identify suitable partners, understand overseas requirements or anticipate where an industry is heading.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: This is where industry associations and consortiums can play a much larger role.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: As the special advisor to Battery Consortium Singapore, I see how an effective industry platform can bring together startups, established local enterprises, MNCs and research institutions across the value chain.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: A startup may have a promising technology, but lack the production experience.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: An established enterprise may understand customers and operations, but need new technologies.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: An MNC may be looking for qualified partners that can meet its standards.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: A research institution may have valuable intellectual property that has yet to find a commercial application.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: The role of an industry platform is to then make these connections useful.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: It should identify actual market needs, bring suitable partners together and help promising solutions move from research and pilot projects to paying customers.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Foreign investment and local enterprise development are not competing strategies.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: The deeper question is not simply how many global companies we attract or how many local SMEs we support.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: It is whether they interact in ways that build lasting capabilities for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: The objective should not be to shelter our companies from competition.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: It is to ensure that they are sufficiently connected, informed and capable to compete.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Securing a major customer is an important breakthrough, but it often creates the next challenge: cashflow.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: A company may have to purchase materials, expand production, hire workers and provide bank guarantees before receiving payment.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: A healthy order book does not necessarily mean that there is enough working capital to fulfil those orders.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Penguin International's "Electric Dream" project illustrates how customers and capital must come together.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: The customer provided the demand and commercial validation, while suitable financing enabled the company to deliver an innovative project at scale.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: That successful delivery can, in turn, become a track record for winning future projects.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: And financing requirements change as a company grows.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Early funding may help develop and test a product.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Fulfilling the first major order may require working capital, while expanding production or entering overseas markets may require longer-term financing.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Deep-tech companies may need capital that is willing to wait several years before earning a return.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: We therefore need suitable financing at every stage, from developing a product and fulfilling the first major order to expanding overseas or preparing for acquisition or listing.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Different businesses will also require different forms of financing.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: These may include equity, venture debt, private credit and acquisition financing.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Not every promising company will fit the venture-capital model of rapid and exponential growth.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Some will grow more steadily while creating good jobs, accumulating valuable capabilities and becoming strong regional businesses.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Our financing landscape should have room for the whole range of companies.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Government intervention should not replace commercial discipline or protect unviable companies.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Our role is to address genuine financing gaps and crowd in suitable private capital.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: I also want to touch on a point on enterprise policy.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Singapore has built up a large and active startup community today.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Our next challenge is to help more promising companies survive, scale and expand overseas.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: This should also shape how we evaluate enterprise policies.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: These figures tell us whether support has been delivered, but not whether enterprises have progressed.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: We should also track how many companies move from pilot to first contract, from first contract to export and from export to scale.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: This does not mean that every company must follow the same path or grow at the same speed.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: It means each programme should be clear about the next commercial milestone it is intended to help companies reach.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Where companies repeatedly stall at the same stage, whether in securing their first major customer, obtaining working capital or finding overseas customers, that tells us where our support system must improve.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: In practice though, business progression ultimately depends on its people.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: While policies, financing and connections matter, businesses do not transform automatically.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: For an SME owner, AI, higher labour costs, overseas expansion and new regulations do not arrive as separate projects handled by different departments.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: The owner must manage cash flow, chase payments, retain workers, serve customers and resolve the day's operational problems, while still finding time to invest in technology and plan for the future.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: The owner must work in the business while also finding time to work on the business.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Enterprise transformation therefore cannot be reduced to giving a company a grant to purchase equipment or adopt a new system.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: This matters because entrepreneurship must remain a viable path for capable Singaporeans.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: We have strengthened protection, support and progression for workers, and rightly so.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: At the same time, we should recognise that business owners carry risks that are less visible and often less cushioned.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: We should not romanticise business ownership, because being your own boss also often means that every customer, creditor and employee becomes your boss.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Many will find a sustainable place in the SME landscape as employers and capability builders.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: But Singaporeans must continue to see starting and growing a business as a worthwhile path.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Entrepreneurs need confidence that a credible idea will receive a fair hearing, that financing will be available when real demand emerges and that one honest failure may not end their entrepreneurial journey.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: This returns me to the relationship between workers and businesses.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: It is tempting to view economic policy as a choice between supporting workers and supporting businesses.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: But businesses succeed through people and workers progress when their companies become more productive and competitive.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Every successful transformation therefore depends on whether employees understand it, contribute to it and share in its benefits.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: A grant may help a company purchase a new machine, but workers must learn to operate it.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: AI may improve productivity, but managers must redesign jobs and equip employees to use it effectively.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Internationalisation may open a new market, but Singaporeans must be prepared to lead teams, serve customers and operate across cultures.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Crucially, workers must share in these gains through better wages, stronger career progression and greater opportunities to take on skilled and leadership roles.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Workers also need confidence that the transformation will lead not simply to disruption but to better skills, wages and opportunities.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Workers and businesses are therefore not opposing interests.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Their success is interconnected and our economic policies must help them progress together.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: (In Mandarin):   As the sayings go, the lips and the teeth are interdependent.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Businesses and employees have to rely on each other.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Only when a business develops well can employees enjoy better salaries, and only when employees continue to improve can the business become more competitive.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Both must grow and benefit together. : In conclusion, there is considerable common ground between the aspirations of this Motion and ESR.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: First, help credible young companies secure their first major customers while maintaining rigorous standards and managing the buyers' risks.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Second, connect global companies, local enterprises and research institutions through industry platforms that are accountable for actual partnerships, projects and contracts.

speaker: [Mr Speaker in the Chair]
text: Third, ensure that companies can access suitable financing as they move from product development to order fulfilment, expansion and internationalisation.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Ng, you have about a minute left.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: Ultimately, an economy for the future must be built around its people.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Many have observed that our world has changed, constraints are tighter and our economic future could be more uncertain.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I am glad Members across the aisle recognise that Singapore must refresh our economic strategy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: And that is precisely why we started ESR a year ago.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The ESR was one of the most extensive reviews in recent years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: These included: business leaders of large and small enterprises; trade associations and chambers representing SMEs; unionists supporting and championing workers' interests; and experts with decades of experience, including academics, venture capitalists, senior civil servants and global CEOs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Many of these people are on the economic frontline, making decisions today that will shape the direction of our future economy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The ESR was a collective endeavour by all of these Singaporeans, and this is how we were able to produce a comprehensive economic blueprint grounded in experience and reality.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Today, we have heard several speeches from WP.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Sifting through the veritable grab bag of pet issues raised, nevertheless, I found agreement with quite a few of the WP's economic ideas.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: For instance, there were suggestions on how to better support our SMEs and startups and build a stronger base of local companies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: These goals are not in dispute and the ESR report sets out specific recommendations, whether on more broad-based support for overseas expansion or nurturing the next generation of Singapore global enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: While we can debate the details, it is clear that the suggestions from WP are not so much a different economic playbook but instead, very much in line with the direction of the ESR.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We do want an economy with dynamic local enterprises and good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: There are some differences over the means of achieving these goals, but there is no need to overstate these differences.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: However, there is one significant difference we need to address, and this is in how we understand Singapore's economic model.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: From the speeches I have heard, WP appears to believe that Singapore's economic model is imbalanced and needs to be fundamentally re-oriented.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: They have portrayed Singapore as a place where MNCs create wealth and there is some Faustian bargain where SMEs are held down, and Singaporeans receive the benefits through redistribution.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: And this is not an academic disagreement but one that is crucial to the policies that we will pursue.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: If the original diagnosis or assumption is wrong, the proposed remedy will send us in the wrong direction.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The wrong medication may cause us even more harm than good.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: One example, Mr Kenneth Tiong referred to the Government as having a universal land pricing model.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Land is priced differently at fair market value based on its intended use, which could be residential, commercial, industrial, community, educational or religious.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We can debate whether there is sufficient flexibility in the current framework and whether there could be or should be further differentiation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But that is quite different from suggesting that the current framework is fundamentally flawed.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: On the contrary, our clear and transparent framework ensures responsible stewardship of our limited land resources.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I want to emphasise that the People's Action Party Government's economic strategy has always been built around Singaporeans, whether as workers, professionals, investors, entrepreneurs or business owners.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Our people, not companies, are at the centre of everything we do.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Economic growth has never been an end in itself.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: It is a means to an end to create better jobs, higher incomes and better lives for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: And by that measure, Singapore's economic model has delivered for generation after generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The WP's view appears to be that MNCs and local firms are competing for a fixed pie.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But as my colleague, Mr Edward Chia, has already pointed out, this is a false choice.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: In a more difficult global environment, we have to compete harder for foreign investments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We must also work harder to support our local companies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: In fact, the growth of our local companies and our MNCs mutually reinforce each other.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Many enterprising Singaporeans start their own businesses to forge their own paths and strive for their hopes and dreams.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Senior Minister of State Low Yen Ling, has spoken in detail about the robust support ecosystem for SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: And the Minister of State Dinesh Vasu Dash, shared how we have built up our startup ecosystem over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I will not repeat what they have already covered.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But very few countries support local companies like we do here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Not all of these schemes are fully utilised today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Of course, if this was just about spending more money, we would already have many more world-class companies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But many of us understand that building a company is very hard.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Mr Mark Lee and Mr Azhar Othman have spoken passionately about their experience as business leaders themselves and also in their roles now supporting SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I had the privilege to serve as the first Managing Director of Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: My colleagues and I were deeply motivated by our mission.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We made it a point to use Singapore-made products in the office – locally made coffee and tea; chairs and cushions; even the snacks in our vending machines – as a small reminder every day that our mission was to support and champion our local enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Every success by a Singapore company – a new product, a new market, a new investment – was a success that we celebrated together.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Our companies know that we walked this journey with them side by side.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Because when Singapore enterprises thrive, they create more jobs and opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We all have a stake in their success.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: In a more fragmented global economy, it has indeed become more difficult for SMEs to venture overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The path from local company to global enterprise seems much steeper than before.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But that does not mean that we should turn inward.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The WP asserts that if external markets become more uncertain, we should retreat and rely more on domestic demand.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Mr Mark Lee, who leads the SBF, pointed out that domestic demand cannot be our primary engine for growth, and I cannot agree more.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: In fact, Castlery has pivoted so well that it has recently opened up its first brick and mortar store in New York City, which I hope to visit soon.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
