text: Even as we redouble our efforts to support our local companies, we must not forget that MNCs remain important to our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: MNCs are attracted to Singapore not just because of the incentives we give, but because of our entire ecosystem – our capabilities, our workers, our SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat spoke in detail about how, in turn, MNCs generate positive spillovers for the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: When global companies set up deep capability here – a research centre, a regional headquarters, an advanced manufacturing line – they do not simply occupy space that local companies might otherwise have filled.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But they bring in resources, capabilities and technology we do not yet have, and this includes AI capabilities which would take us years to develop on our own.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Many of our local companies grow and succeed because of their relationships with MNCs, not in spite of them.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: For example, Sunningdale Tech is a Singapore precision engineering company which started off as a small-scale manufacturer of plastic products, and it has grown to be a large company, alongside its blue-chip clients like HP, Illumina and Dyson.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: When I attended a major industrial trade fair last year, I was proud to see many more local manufacturers, smaller than Sunningdale, but ready to grow, showcasing their innovations and products to a global audience.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Just as importantly, global companies create good jobs – high-skilled, high-paying jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: These often have regional or even global responsibilities, which means Singapore can have a greater influence in economic decisions beyond our small size and population.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Many jobs are generated for young Singaporeans too.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Applied is an American company producing high-end equipment for semiconductor manufacturers, such as TSMC, Samsung and Micron.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: At Upper Changi, I met Ms Chua Khai Shuen.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Khai Shuen had interned at Applied while studying mechanical engineering at the NUS.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: She was very happy to be hired upon her graduation, so she could continue with the projects that she started.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Her biggest achievement, so far, unfortunately, is that she can put on her PPE faster than her colleagues.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I tried competing with her and I naturally lost out.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But Khai Shuen's story, as a young graduate, is not unique.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: There are many like her, building their budding careers in global companies based in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: During our house visits, I am sure many of us would have met parents who proudly tell us their sons and daughters are working in Google or Microsoft, BlackRock or JP Morgan, Micron or GlobalFoundries, Boeing or Rolls Royce.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: It would be much harder for a Singaporean to work in any of these companies, if the companies were not based here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The support we provide to attract foreign investment and the support we provide to local enterprises are complementary and mutually reinforcing.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: So, at a time when countries are spending more than ever to attract and reshore strategic investments, our response surely cannot be to do less.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Giving up these investments would mean fewer higher quality jobs and fewer opportunities for Singaporeans – and this cannot be our approach.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The ESR began with a simple but urgent premise.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The world is changing and Singapore must reinvent ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But as we do so, we should be clear about what needs to change and what should stay the same.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Our task is not to discard what has made Singapore successful, but to renew and strengthen our formula for a changed world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We are not choosing between SMEs and MNCs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Our job is to help our companies realise their ambitions and not hold them back.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We have stayed open, we have continued to build our capabilities, and we have always invested in our people.

speaker: The Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This is how we have earned our place in the world and this is how we will continue creating opportunities for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Mark Lee, do you have a clarification to ask of the Member?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: While we discuss the mandatory retrenchment benefits for workers, has MOM also examined the potential impact on employers, specifically whether mandatory retrenchment benefits could create unintended cost or behavioural changes in hiring, particularly for SMEs and firms?

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: This is something that we are looking at.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, do you have a clarification to make?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I think when I and my colleagues called for a rebalance, we were neither suggesting that SMEs and MNCs are competing for the same pie.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Nor are we suggesting that greater support for local SMEs must somehow either come at the expense of existing MNCs or punish these golden geese.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Indeed, I believe I was very careful to emphasise in the closing of my speech that we must not sideline our MNCs and GLCs, nor should we shut off foreign capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What Mr Siow attributes to the WP, I am afraid is a false dichotomy that we did not draw.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is a convenient strawman argument, perhaps to win – had we actually made it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Similarly, we are not blind to how domestic demand alone is insufficient to drive our economic engine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But saying that we want healthy domestic demand is not equivalent to saying that we do not need foreign ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Rather, what we want to urge is the growth of consumer demand that historically has been weaker here than in other advanced economies of our level of development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, my question then to the Minister is whether he believes that the state of our SME ecosystem is currently sufficiently strong to compete in regional economies as they internationalise and if he thinks that our current domestic demand is sufficiently healthy, that there is no need to push this up as we try to restructure and reform our global economy for the 21st century?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We had this impression, I had this impression largely because of the language that is used in the Motion, where there was no mention of global enterprises and the global economy.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And Mr Edward Chia had to specifically amend the Motion.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's speech, he specifically said that we should pivot towards SMEs.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, when we say pivot, I am assuming there is an impression of a zero-sum arrangement that he had in mind.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But if I was mistaken, I am very happy that he has clarified that the WP is certainly aligned with our economic strategy, that he sees that both MNCs and SMEs are important, and that we should strive to strengthen our strategies on both sides.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Specifically, to his question on whether the state of our SME ecosystem is sufficiently strong, or whether local demand is sufficient, I do not think there will be a threshold where we say today, we are ready and okay.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The colleagues at Enterprise Singapore and MTI are working very hard, continually strengthening our SMEs, continually making them globally competitive, continually creating opportunities and supporting them to grow.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And that is the spirit in which we see this, and we will continue to do this and endeavour to help our SMEs to succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With that point that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim raised earlier on to Minister Jeffrey Siow, perhaps, the Member would consider supporting and voting for the amended Motion.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have all heard different views, diagnoses and prescriptions, but also substantial common ground.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We want good outcomes for our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We all want entrepreneurs who are confident and willing to try, to innovate and to grow.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We all want more Singapore enterprises that are globally successful.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And we want Singaporeans to be able to face the future with confidence, even as technology and global competition reshape our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Kenneth Tiong said that, if he could sum up this Motion in one question, it would be: "How does an ordinary Singaporean get a lasting share of our country’s success?" It is a fair and it is an important question.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some Singaporeans will be able to do much more, such as by starting or growing a successful business; by turning an idea into a product or service; or by leading a regional or global team from Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But they are, in turn, shaped by the economy itself.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Singaporeans are not mere passive beneficiaries of economic growth.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We would never have gotten here if our people had been inert digits.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our people have always been active participants, contributors, builders and owners of this island-nation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And this has always been at the heart of Singapore's economic strategy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The ultimate purpose of our economic strategy has never been growth for growth's sake.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is about whether that growth pervades and percolates through the broader economy, that it improves people's lives through good jobs, rising incomes, social mobility and the resilience to withstand setbacks.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: By these measures, the Singapore model has delivered over successive generations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our responsibility now is to ensure that it continues to deliver in a very different, changed world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They are about widening practical pathways to success.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Can someone with an idea – whether a research breakthrough, a new service, an F&B concept or even a franchise opportunity – find the mentorship, the first customer and the capital to build a viable enterprise?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Can a professional gain the international exposure needed to lead a global business?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Can a worker acquire relevant skills before being displaced or find a credible path back into meaningful work after losing a job?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I began my own entrepreneurial journey when I was around 27.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Together with a few partners, I started Healthway Medical Group with one clinic in Yishun.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I have to declare I do not have any shares in Healthway, so I am not making a pitch.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We had zero experience in starting a business.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Nor did we have the wide range of support schemes which startups today can draw on.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There was no certainty that our venture would succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We were doctors, and I can tell you our medical training did not include courses on how to build a business organisation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We had to learn on the go – operations, finance, people management and quality control.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In time we also had to learn how to build an institution that could endure beyond ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some of the earliest companies that gave us a chance were MNCs like Sony, Aiwa, Shimano, Asahi TV Glass, Hewlett-Packard and Procter & Gamble.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In fact, a few of them no longer exist in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They were large at that time; they were established global companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We were a young Singapore startup enterprise who found a relatively white space in the HDB and industrial estates, when the concept of a corporate group practice providing healthcare in those areas was still nascent.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The trust of these MNCs gave us that foothold and enabled us to build a track record.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In my own experience, established global companies helped a homegrown Singapore enterprise to start, establish credibility and grow.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They gave us an opportunity to grow and to compete.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And I know this is the experience of many other SMEs in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We had to improve our service, we had to look after our people, we had to manage our costs, we had to earn our customers' trust again and again.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It transformed, it diversified, it achieved sustainable scale and all of us successfully divested.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Later, I built, I transformed and I scaled organisations at a much larger and more international level.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Starting a clinic did not equip me automatically to manage a network, let alone lead a healthcare group of tertiary hospitals with global operations, with more than 55,000 staff operating across Europe and Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I had to keep learning, moving beyond medicine into management, finance, technology and organisational leadership, and working with people and most importantly, mentors who knew far more than what I knew in so many areas outside my own training.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I graduated from business school only after turning 40, and hence, I am a believer in lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even now, I am still learning from all of you here.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Healthway was built with a few founders who shared that same vision – perhaps foolishly, they listened to me, they took risks alongside, with me – and staff who committed themselves to the organisation, customers who trusted us and partners who helped us develop.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That experience also taught me what the Government can and what the Government cannot do.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Mark Lee put it so aptly: the Government must build the runway, but entrepreneurs and workers must still run on it and take off.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government should maintain sound institutions, open markets and clear rules.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It must and should always reduce avoidable friction, reduce volatilities in policies, connect businesses to knowledge and markets, and share selected risks where there is wider economic benefit.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And I was taught by a very famous accountant during that period.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In Singapore, we have knowledge, but know-how, better.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But when you go overseas, know-who is the best.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, the Government cannot find the customers for us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It cannot build the business team, it cannot make commercial decisions or persevere on the entrepreneur's behalf.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Government support should be a springboard for enterprise.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But that does not mean leaving entrepreneurs and SMEs to fend for themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Senior Minister of State Low Yen Ling has set out comprehensively how we help enterprises manage immediate pressures, adopt technology, strengthen operations and venture overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These schemes are aimed at helping viable firms become more productive, more competitive and more resilient.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To be clear, not every idea or startup will bear fruit.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, this does not mean that these assistance schemes are futile or that the entrepreneur has failed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Every closure can instead mean avoiding years of opportunity costs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The efforts, capital and time saved can then be re-channelled to other more promising ideas or opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If you talk to enough successful entrepreneurs, where they eventually arrive – the destination, the final destination – often differs from where they intended to go at the start.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But that is the resilience, the tenacity and the perseverance of an entrepreneur.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some of you are old enough, alongside with me, to remember the series "Rocky".

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I presume he would have known who Rocky, the character is about. "Rocky" is like an entrepreneur.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: An entrepreneur, the exhortation is that, he is not someone who can throw the punches, but it is the person who can take the punches, get back up and keep moving forward.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our ambition cannot be measured only by how many companies are formed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It has to be measured by how many good ideas become viable businesses, how many viable businesses can scale, and how many anchor capabilities, intellectual property and good jobs in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I want to say that this is not exhaustive, but generally, the entire journey involves five difficult crossings: from aspiration to the first venture; from an idea or research breakthrough to innovation and enterprise; from a product or service to a first customer; from early traction to sustained scale; and from a strong base in Singapore to markets around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Government policy can undoubtedly help at each stage, but what it cannot do is make the journey risk-free.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The first gap is between aspiration and the first venture.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Dedicated spaces such as LaunchPad@one-north give founders a place to collaborate, learn from one another, meet investors, develop the know-who, the networks – and develop their ideas.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The aim is not to make everyone an entrepreneur.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is to give serious ideas a fair chance to be tested.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The second gap is between research and something that creates value in the market.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Many of tomorrow's founders may not begin in a clinic, in a shop or office, but in a laboratory.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Their initial asset may be a scientific discovery, a medical device, a new material, software or intellectual property developed through years of research.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As a medical doctor, I know that a good scientific result is not yet a treatment.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A promising prototype is not yet a product.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And a good product is not yet a sustainable company.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Scale allows it to create wider economic and social impact.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our long-term investments in the research, innovation and enterprise, RIE space are producing results.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Government spending has catalysed greater private sector R&D.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But creating knowledge is only part of the journey.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The harder task is how do we translate research into products, into businesses and economic value.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are strengthening this translation in several ways.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have also established translational platforms that bridge research and commercialisation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Through platforms such as MedTech Catapult and our semiconductor innovation facilities, companies can prototype, they can test, they can commercialise new technologies without bearing the full cost themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Translation also takes place when our public researchers work with leading global companies and local suppliers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Smart Manufacturing Joint Lab, which is established by Rolls-Royce, Singapore Aero Engine Services (SAESL) and A*STAR, is one example.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The collaboration has developed new technologies that improve fan blade manufacturing and aircraft engine maintenance, repair and overhaul.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It has also enabled local SMEs to qualify as suppliers to global aerospace companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is how we anchor investments deeply in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We connect global companies with our researchers and our local suppliers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is how knowledge is translated into industrial capability and local companies gain pathways into global supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our objective is to ensure that more research becomes useful technology; more useful technology becomes commercial capability; and more capability becomes enterprises, jobs and value anchored in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Earlier on, Dr Neo Kok Beng and Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh both argued that innovation and entrepreneurship require room for risk-taking and responsible failure.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am a custodian; we are all custodians of our Budgets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am not sure whether I can go to that extent of his support in terms of risk-taking and failure.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we will work within a responsible means of making sure that successes can be sustained.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, we will fund only ideas whose outcomes are already more certain.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we also cannot afford to only fund those outcomes that are already certain – because if we just do that alone, we will miss many of the breakthroughs that could define the future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This risk-taking, therefore, must be and will be matched by discipline.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government must invest in areas where Singapore can build meaningful advantages.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And entrepreneurs must solve problems that customers are willing to pay for because even the best technology cannot be scaled unless someone is prepared to use it and pay for it.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This brings me to the third gap – how do we bring the product to the first customer.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Ng Shi Xuan highlighted why a first customer matters.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It allows a company to test and demonstrate its solution, build a track record and show that it can meet demanding standards, making it easier to win the next customer or investor.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That was true when I started at Healthway.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is why EDB and Enterprise Singapore work to connect MNCs with local startups and SMEs through PACT.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will not go through that because Senior Minister of State Low Yen Ling already expounded on it earlier on.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our public sector can also be an early customer.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Under the Innovative Procurement Partnership, startups can participate in tenders and propose innovative solutions for pilot testing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If a trial is successful, agencies have the option to continue working with the same firm to scale and deploy the solution.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is the wider ecosystem we are trying to build: established companies, startups, research institutions and the public sector all coming and working together; and firms gaining the chance to prove themselves; and good solutions moving more quickly from pilot to scale.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The fourth gap is from early traction to sustained scale.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Different stages require different forms of capital: modest funding for a first venture; patient equity for deep-tech development; venture debt or private credit for growth; and then, public markets and credible exits for mature companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The ESR also recommends developing venture debt and private credit alongside venture capital.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: All these successful exits, they recycle capital, expertise and confidence, and trust, and reputation into new ventures.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But let us not just focus on finance alone.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Because finance alone does not build great companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Public capital should crowd in commercial capital and expertise, not replace them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The risk must still be properly understood and borne.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Governments cannot and do not create champions just by simply writing larger cheques.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is the journey we must strengthen: from the courage to start, to the capability to innovate; from a first customer, to the financing and leadership needed to scale; and eventually to markets much, much larger than our own.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Healthy domestic demand matters because it reflects confidence, it supports domestic-facing businesses and it gives firms a first market to test products and build brands.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: My second foray after divesting Healthway was joining and building the hospital business under Parkway.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Parkway Holdings itself began in Singapore as a Singapore company.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It owned, at that time, the three hospitals named Gleneagles, Mount Elizabeth Hospital and East Shore Hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But Singapore’s domestic market alone cannot provide the scale required for ambitious firms or advanced industries.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is a good platform to build your credibility, to build trust, to build your reputation, to establish a viable proof of concept, build that trusted brand and operating model; then, leveraging it as a platform, a springboard to expand into the region and eventually, globally.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And I believe it is getting even harder.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A company entering another market must understand different customers, regulations, cultures and partners.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A more fragmented world that we live in today makes diversification and good in-market support even more important.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Mr Azhar Othman said, Singapore must remain a bridge of trade and not become a barrier to it.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The answer is not to withdraw into our domestic market.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is to do more to help Singapore firms enter more markets, find credible partners and compete more effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Not every Singapore business can or must become global.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A neighbourhood service provider or heritage restaurant that serves the local community plays an equally important role in our society.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They directly meet the needs of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But for companies that aspire to become regional or global champions, they cannot be confined by the size of our home market.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we want the headquarters, the strategic decisions, the R&D, the brains of the company, the intellectual property, the finance, the product management, the regional leadership, the good jobs anchored here.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And that has always been what we worked towards.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, to put simply, we help firms go abroad to grow.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But as they grow, the stronger capabilities and opportunities will continue to be anchored firmly in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That does not make their stake in Singapore's success any less direct or lasting.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But it should also enable a person to build skills, experience and confidence over time.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I have considered this consistently as a doctor, entrepreneur, employer and when I was Manpower Minister, and of course, today, I consider it even more.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As an employer, I learnt that an organisation can grow sustainably only if its people can grow alongside with it.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A company that introduces technology without redesigning work and without developing its people will create anxiety and limit ultimately its own capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I have come to realise very early on that at the end of the day, we are all in the business of developing, growing and maximising our human capital.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Manpower Minister, I met workers for whom disruption was not abstract.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A job loss raises fears about income; whether years of experience still count; whether one is too old to begin again; and whether the next job will use one’s experience and abilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We should not answer them merely by pointing to aggregate statistics or the number of courses available.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A course completed is not yet a successful transition.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Dr Wan Rizal put it well: effort without direction creates frustration; effort with direction builds confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And Assoc Prof Terence Ho added that the gains from training and reskilling will not be fully realised until workers have opportunities to apply what they have learnt at work.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, support will therefore have to begin earlier and connect to real opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employers must treat workforce transformation – redesigning jobs, training workers and translating productivity gains – into better work and progression.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Workers, on the other hand, must take ownership too.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government can make training accessible, employers can create opportunities and unions, the Labour Movement's brothers and sister, can support workers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But no institution can learn on a person’s behalf.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I had to keep learning as the organisations I led became more and more complex.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Singaporeans will increasingly have to do the same – deepening expertise, moving into hybrid roles that combine AI with sector knowledge, making mid-career transitions or becoming entrepreneurs later in life.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Morris Chang founded TSMC, one of the world's most successful semiconductor companies, at age 55, after 25 years at Texas Instruments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This shows how accumulated knowledge and judgement can underpin reinvention later in life.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Financial support during unemployment or retraining gives individuals and families breathing space.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But it must be connected to a pathway forward.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is how a worker obtains a lasting share of economic success.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Not only through compensation after disruption, but through the enduring ability to contribute, earn, adapt and progress.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When a young Singaporean turns a scientific idea into a company.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When a local firm wins its first major customer and enters a global value chain.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When a technician progresses into a higher-skilled role.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When a displaced PMET can build on years of experience rather than start from zero.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When a Singapore enterprise grows abroad while strengthening its R&D and leadership functions here.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When a Singaporean in a global company develops the capabilities and networks to lead across the region – or even later starts a venture of his or her own.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And when someone who suffers a business or career setback can recover, learn, try and succeed again.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is not only a transfer received after value has been created.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is the opportunity to take part in crafting, in creating, in shaping and sustaining that value.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: All of these are mutually reinforcing parts of one united economic strategy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There is a famous Chinese saying that says: "tian shi di li ren he" (天时地利人和) – right timing and opportunity, right place, right people.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These are the elements often cited as requirements for success.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They must invest in people; workers must keep learning; investors take informed risks; and entrepreneurs build, compete, persevere and accept the responsibility.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We cannot guarantee that every venture will succeed, every job will remain the same or every transition will be painless.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That in itself is "tian shi" (天时) (In English): Right timing and opportunity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our beloved Singapore's success has never been guaranteed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Every generation had to build it by staying open, learning faster, taking calculated risks and pulling together when circumstances become difficult.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The next chapter will demand that same spirit.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The economy of the future will not be powered by one type of company, one source of demand or one Government programme.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will be powered by all fellow Singaporeans who can build, lead, own, innovate, adapt and grow.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is how we secure the best future for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And that is how we will ensure that Singapore's future economy truly works for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With that Mr Speaker, I support the amendments and the Motion as amended.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Dr Tan, you took a road less travelled and you have certainly come a long way.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: On a lighter note, we both come from the same era and, like you, I, too, enjoyed watching Sylvester Stallone and must admit I watched the movie Rocky quite a few times.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I would now like to call on Mr Tiong — Oh, sorry, there is a clarification?

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: In the context of just sharing mine as well in doing business, we know it is very difficult, but the reward is very sweet.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: My point of clarification is this: we compete in a global scale now.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: What we compete before, purely on company to company; and now we compete against China, against US, against everybody.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: And my point is that in the context of Singapore's unique strategy, the competition can be made easier with the help of what our company has grown.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: We have the support of Enterprise Singapore, SBF, we have the support of MTI and so forth.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: And I just want to clarify that I hope this support continues and hope this support strengthens even further because this is the unique story of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: How our company grows, not through the competition of what others sees from their government as a restriction, but we see our Government as a conduit to help fellow entrepreneurs, fellow companies to grow globally, irrespective of any country that we are going to go to.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, I thank every Member who spoke on both sides of this House.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We filed this Motion to provide answers to the economic worries top-of-mind for every Singaporean: whether there is a job and whether it lasts; whether the young person who has done everything asked of them can find work that goes somewhere; whether a flat is within reach; whether a small shop can survive its rent; whether the course a worker is sent on leads to a job; whether the growth we announced is felt in a wage; whether a Singaporean who wants to build something can afford to do it in spite of the high cost structure here.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is our structured view across the factors of production, land, labour, capital, productivity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In this Motion, we have addressed nine of those questions and answered them systematically.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Take a different tack from the lack of flexibility, once shown to NUS and the One-North area.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A zone authority that is able to make fast decisions on visas, space and procurement within weeks, with its own investment body to provide growth capital and take equity stakes in emerging enterprises.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is an investment in our young and Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: While we agree with his call for high-failure, high-impact state funding, we believe such public R&D spending must be paired with sovereign return mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And I thank Mr Ng Shi Xuan for his relaying of the "5Cs" approach to the startup lifecycle.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Fair market value is already a function of the interest granted and not a number attached to a plot.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, our state land and our rental policies should exercise maximum flexibility for our young and our young companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Wherever land is priced, market scarcity value remains the default benchmark.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We propose one zone where the benchmark is developmental cost and not scarcity and welcome what we perceive to be the Minister's posture of being more flexible.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How can we create a business climate where dynamic local firms can emerge as drivers of innovation and become future cornerstones of the economy?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, proposed turning the machinery from push to pull.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He proposed widening qualifying research spending and seconding experts into SMEs, because domestic enterprises carry one dollar in five of this economy's business research spending, and that gap does not close by a company deciding to try harder.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And he proposed tying Catalist listing to state co-investment because the capital that is missing is pre-initial public offering.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We appreciate his support for our core aspirations of a more inclusive economy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We agree at least on the vital goal of building a vibrant local ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We share his concern for the ground pressures facing micro businesses, particularly rising rents and labour costs that mid-career workers face today.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We gently note that we have already laid out these specific choices, including our positions on labour, rent and structural support throughout our speeches on this debate.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked whether our transmission mechanisms are strong enough to reach smaller firms and did not really answer his own question.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, if I may just ask him, what policy choices of transmission mechanisms to create upward convergence of smaller firms should we make?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How do we shed our rentier mindset by assuring that attractive affordable housing is available for every Singaporean household?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Mr Louis Chua proposed that land revenue maximisation stops being the primary aim of land policy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How do we ensure our tertiary students and young workers find meaningful opportunities and good jobs in a challenging economy?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He proposed to make entry-level hiring genuinely skills-based using verified skills evidence and practical assessments to match capable beginners to existing labour market demand.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He also advocated expanding the supply of properly paid apprenticeships, creating a national market, coordinating employers and shared training capacity, especially for SMEs with paid employment, CPF, structured learning and portable competence.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He proposed creating genuinely net new job opportunities via the use of targeted temporary risk-sharing arrangements and giving appropriate credit in suitable Government tenders for additional employee jobs and apprenticeships.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Minister of State Dinesh broadly agreed with Mr Andre Low's proposals and acknowledged that he shared our aspiration of giving every young Singaporean a fair start.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In particular, he agreed on the importance of expanding and strengthening work-based pathways, including apprenticeships.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh suggested a one-time course correction allowance, so, a first-year university course transfer does not depend on family means.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He suggested one or two subsidised semesters could be disregarded.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How can we create accessible pathways for tradespersons to earn a decent middle-class livelihood?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Mr Gerald Giam proposed a practitioner-led guild, with chambers grown out of the trade societies we already have, because an employer federation cannot impartially certify a worker's competence against his own members' interest in keeping him.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He proposed task-specific endorsements on a digital skills ledger, verified by practical assessment and he proposed licensing built into ITE curricula with an independent panel, an apprentice can appeal to.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We thank Assoc Prof Terence Ho for his valuable insights on the Career and Skills Passport and the importance of valuing workplace learning, acknowledging the gaps requiring enhancement to truly promote skills-first hiring as my colleague Mr Andre Low pointed out.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Does our system of continuing education actually work?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We thank Minister of State Dinesh for mentioning that our positions are not very far.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We hope this means that we will soon have universal redundancy support for all workers rather than just the Jobseeker Support Scheme for the 60%.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Mr Fadli also proposed mandatory retrenchment benefits because they are discretionary today and can lawfully be zero and a worker who has given years of service should not depend on goodwill.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He proposed interest free postgraduate loans, CPF for Master's programmes and outcomes published by course and by provider because deep reskilling is where the money runs out and we need to know which courses work.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Mr Azhar Othman asked for stronger monthly income support during retraining.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We also could not agree more with Dr Wan Rizal when he says that effort without direction builds frustration.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We need to give more direction to our people.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What does the Singaporean worker actually receive when the retrenchment comes?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our Party Leader Mr Pritam Singh asked what a retrenched worker in Singapore is entitled to and answered it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Every developed economy around us – China, South Korea, Taiwan, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines – legislates for this, but we do not.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We thank Mr Patrick Tay for his valuable contribution to the debate.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We find shared ground in our conviction that workers must never be treated as collateral damage during economic transitions and that we must proactively protect our PMEs from the displacement risk of AI.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: However, we respectfully frame our Motion as providing some of the legal force for the very protections NTUC has long lobbied for.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, we invite the Labour Movement to support legislative mandates for retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What parts of our economy do our national statistics fail to capture.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Ms He Ting Ru proposed a formalised wage ladder for care work, because a registered nurse, a social worker and a preschool teacher all earn below the national median in the very sectors that the ESR calls resilient.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We have not measured what it costs to the people who provide it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: She proposed an environmental dashboard tracking the environmental outcomes of our policies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How do we empower Singaporeans to seize the opportunities in the region and abroad?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Ms Eileen Chong proposed funding the OMIP to the person rather than through the employer on the French model, where a state agency holds the contract, because tying a placement to a sponsoring employer's growth plan caps it at that employer's ambition.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: She proposed scaling the places rather than only widening the gate, because the SG Youth Plan drops the two-year eligibility rule without committing to send anyone more.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And she proposed publishing outcomes at two years and at five because the 2018 scheme came with targets and no published outcome, and we still do not know whether going out pays you when you come home.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: She proposed tearing down the walls on coming home, around BTO queues, CPF and schooling re-entry for children.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We thank Mr Azhar Othman, who made policy suggestions for warehousing abroad, deal-making officers and tax incentives for reinvesting overseas profits back into R&D and capacity building.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar said, create before you capture.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The sentiment is real but the diagnosis is wrong.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Capability is what makes ownership possible, rather than the other way around.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we make rebalancing the organising principle of our strategy, we may not end up with more of these companies, we may end up with fewer.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Target ownership without capability and competitiveness and we do not own more of the pie, we own more of a smaller one.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But let us use the PSA example from her speech.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: PSA did not acquire terminals because it had a data advantage.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It got the data advantage because it owned the terminals.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Ownership came first and capability compounded from it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Ownership without capability is a dead end, but capability without ownership does not build resilience in a fracturing world.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: While we agree on the goal of building globally competitive Singaporean companies, we see ownership not as a premature target, but an essential next chapter.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: After 60 years of successfully creating values through MNCs, our Motion seeks to ensure that Singaporeans move through value creation to capturing and owning more of that value today.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I believe Minister of State Dinesh was making some suggestions that some people were saying that Singapore's economic model is failing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Minister Jeffrey Siow, I believe, mischaracterised our policies as saying we want to rely on the domestic market as a primary source.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is of course a non-starter to anyone who spends more than two seconds thinking about it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What we are saying is that domestic demand is necessary.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We are not saying that domestic demand is sufficient.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The hon Member Edward Chia moved four amendments.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This amendment does not simply remove a word.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our Motion says this House believes in these things.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The amendment says these things will follow from adopting the review.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Ours commits the House to ends, but this amendment commits it to a document.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A standard that is stated separately can test any plan, the Government and ours.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Many of the diagnoses we shared are set against the risks that one Government document comes to be treated as the whole of the House's thinking on the economy. "Notwithstanding" says only that our commitments are neither exhausted by that document nor derived from it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is how the word "notwithstanding" is used in our Constitution.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Article 148A of the Constitution allows the President to assent to a Supply Bill, notwithstanding his opinion that it is likely to draw on past reserves.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If he does, that opinion must be stated in writing to the Speaker and published in the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, the word "notwithstanding" does not overrule the President, it does not say his opinion is wrong, it just requires that the opinion be genuinely held, that it stands on the record and it does not settle the outcome.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The reason is because it is not a matter of simply including "global enterprises" into the text of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Had the amendment been "an economy powered by dynamic local enterprises supported by global enterprises", we would have less of an issue with the change.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We are not choosing between being global and local.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The WP believes categorically in an open economy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: As my hon friend Jamus Lim has said, we are "not calling for a wholesale overhaul of our GLC-heavy, MNC-led and foreign capital-reliant model." We must acknowledge the long history of how our domestic firms have not felt sufficiently supported by the state in their effort to grow their companies and compete in their home economy and beyond.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The proof of the pudding is in the eating.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If this model has succeeded historically in delivering for so many domestic firms, then why and wherefore the history of these concerns?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I ask all Members and especially Members opposite to honestly reflect upon these questions.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At this point, it is worth underscoring, as my hon friend Assoc Prof Jamus Lim pointed out at the end of his speech, that we are not seeking to undermine the contribution of MNCs to our economy, nor to stem access to foreign capital.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Rather, we are calling for an evolution of how dominant MNCs and GLCs have been in our economy and to re-orient it towards the younger local companies and SMEs as they are more inherently rooted and can be a source of disruptive innovation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To be clear, we are not pitting foreign versus local.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Can the ESR carry the standing that is placed on it?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There is much to like about the ESR.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is diligently put together, has consulted widely and it outlines real challenges.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But it is incremental and it sits within a tradition of reports that say the same thing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This is not about the ESR in itself, this is about the whole continuity of reports since 2010.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The ESR is the fourth national economic blueprint since 2010.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What is new in this report is AI.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But that is a new exogenous factor that all countries must react to.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Adding new chapters and footnotes to an existing playbook does not make a new playbook.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Have we arrived at those past reports' medium- to long-term targets or not?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is hard to tell with the decreasing level of tracking with each report.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, we do not know whether it was met.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The 2017 Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) set two targets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: One on growth – 2% to 3% per year – which was met.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Again, a topline figure, necessary but insufficient by itself as a goal.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: One on manufacturing – "The CFE recommends building a globally competitive manufacturing sector at about 20% of GDP over the medium term".

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In 2010, the target was 1,000 local companies by 2020.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In 2026, it is a recommendation that a target be set, and the companies counted have shifted from local to Singapore headquartered.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This strikes me as a government that maybe has become a little bit averse to being measured.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In May 2017, MTI wrote that every Industry Transformation Map has "tangible indicators and targets to measure the effectiveness of its strategies".

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In July 2024, its own retrospective told readers that sector outcomes should not be compared against these initial projections.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Targets are watered down to projections, goals into aspirations.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We are getting a bit familiar with this.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The food policy "30 by 30" was dropped last November for narrower targets, five years later.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: An unambiguous goal became a bit more of a challenging aspiration.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I have not understood from this Government what is the next level of economic target detailed beyond topline growth targets, such as the type of growth or its distribution that it will hold itself to.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Government wants us to know it will react swiftly once the monitoring alarms are triggered.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Review says so itself: on AI and workers, it recommends monitoring the impact closely and adjusting policies when needed.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What matters far more is which structural and falsifiable targets it will set itself between now and 2030.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: After all, what is the vision and what would tell us whether we had reached it?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Here is what we would hold ourselves accountable to beyond top-line growth: the indigenous share of national income rising, real wages in line with productivity growth and a widening range of what an ordinary wage can afford.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I have read the Review and in my view, it is short of report cards and targets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Nor has a consolidated report card for any of the four blueprints been published.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our Party Leader, Mr Pritam Singh, asked for one in February.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Separate the rhetoric about promises kept, from measurable outcomes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Surely, in spite of the uncertainties, there are macroeconomic targets beyond top-line growth that we can commit to.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A Member who supports the Review because he wants a more equal and inclusive economy and an engine driven by dynamic local companies already believes (a) and (b).

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: These are the ends the Review is meant to serve.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Voting for the Motion says that and nothing more.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It does not criticise the Review and binds no one to our proposals.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our Motion asks this House to commit to principles, the amendments ask it to commit to one set of operational plans.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like to ask Members of the House, especially Members opposite, to let the word stand and accept the Motion as originally worded.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans deserve a country that is prepared to try what is necessary to give them that strongest shot of success.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our Motion is thus written: opportunities for entrepreneurs to experiment because the ground and the capital to try are priced for incumbents; households and businesses to succeed because high land prices working their way through the economy make it structurally challenging; workers to thrive because the ladder above the wage floor must work; and for the wider swath of society, workers need room to experiment, pathways to succeed and a financial cushion to recover or pivot if retrenched; ideas and innovation to flourish because we need our R&D spending to lead to meaningful commercial outcomes; and an economic engine driven by dynamic local companies, healthy domestic demand and Singaporeans and Singaporean capital venturing abroad because Singaporeans need to understand that there is a system that encourages their economic flourishing and their dreams of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans do not lack drive, ambition or imagination.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What we need is to be further empowered and supported to achieve our next successes in a different global context.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We will leave no stone unturned in trying to better secure Singaporeans in uncertain times.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I am very grateful that he has clarified that he and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim support the idea that we are not in a zero-sum situation, that we are not arguing for a zero-sum pivot; both SMEs and global companies are important, and that a comprehensive economic strategy must have both.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The ESR, relative to what the WP has proposed, I see a lot of commonality, although Mr Tiong has characterised it as incremental.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Actually, in today's speeches, I have also not heard a "great big idea" that would replace the ESR.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In fact, I see very much as the WP building on what the ESR has recommended.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In fact, I think that Mr Tiong himself, I think during a press briefing, said that they were filling the gaps of what the ESR has set out.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, without a replacement or a big idea for us to be able to put side by side, I venture to say that a lot of what we discussed today are towards the same goals, moving towards the same objectives, perhaps differences in the details, differences in some of the parameters – but we are all trying to achieve the same thing.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Most importantly, we are in a very difficult world, a world where external competition has become stiffer.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think it is better for us to see if we can look for areas of commonality, areas where we are aligned, areas where this House can present a common front to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Better for us to be able to push together, rather than look for differences that perhaps do not exist and find a wedge to drive into gaps where we do not see.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, on this note, I would really lament that it is not possible for us to achieve common ground today.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I hope the WP, at a future situation, can reconsider whether or not to try to come together and support what I think is a comprehensive, complete and forward-looking economic strategy that will serve Singapore and Singaporeans well into the future.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: What I said was that our outcomes might be the same and that workers should be protected, supported, especially when they go through an exercise of retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: But I did not say about the fact that the insurance is the only way forward.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: It is really about the design, the funding approach, which may not be the same.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: What I also said was that our approach was always to support re-employment and not only unemployment.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: So, I just wanted to state that clarification on that over-simplification of what I have highlighted.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It built world-class port operating capabilities and then, it used that capability to go out and acquire other ports.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It did not set out a target from the beginning, to say "I want to own for ports in 45 countries".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It built the capability first and then, it went out.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The data advantage does not just come from ownership.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The data advantage comes from the capability in digital technology, AI and automation, without which, you do not have competitive advantage.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: So, I stand by my statement that in this case, capability came and ownership followed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But actually I do not want to belabour the sequence, as much as was in my speech.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But if I had to choose any day, what is going to make a company globally successful, it is capability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: And because this is an important issue, when we talk about retrenchment benefits and making it mandatory, the views of businesses should be taken into consideration.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: And I believe that some clarifications are needed to some of the points and proposals that has been put forth by the WP.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Second, would higher retrenchment cost make employers more cautious about hiring permanent staff?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Could companies rely more on short-term contracts or outsourcing, or in the worst case, hire fewer people, particularly inexperienced workers and career switchers who require longer training runway?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Third, if we legislate a minimum, what assurance is there that outcomes could improve?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: So, for the above clarifications mentioned, is legislation necessarily the best solution?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: And I hope that the WP would hear from businesses on the ground.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I believe the comments by hon Member Mr Mark Lee were directed at my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The three issues that he highlighted, in terms of what difficulties businesses could have, I think I was conciliatory enough in my speech to say that businesses will have their challenges, I accept that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not think it is a question of not taking them into account.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The issue here is the workers and the scenario painted by the ESR of the world they are coming into, of the Singapore they are coming into.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We will have our different points of view.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The three questions, the three particular points he raised were the same points that I believe then-Senior Minister of State Mr Koh Poh Koon raised when we had an exchange at this table.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I responded to all three of them in my speech, so I would invite the hon Member to consider how I responded, vis-à-vis those three points that both he and the then-Senior Minister of State Koh had raised earlier.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think the Ayes have it, the Ayes have it.

speaker: Mr Speaker

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The question is, "That this House, in line with the suggestions in the Economic Strategy Review on the future Singapore economy, believes: (a) in a more equal and inclusive economy, with opportunities for entrepreneurs to experiment, households and businesses to succeed, workers to thrive, and ideas and innovation to flourish; and (b) in an economy powered by dynamic local companies, global enterprises, healthy domestic and external demand, and Singaporeans and Singaporean capital venturing abroad." Those who agree say "Aye".
